Sir Billy Boston - 'the world-class athlete, whose story deserved to be told'
- Published
When Sir Billy Boston was knighted in 2025, it was a unique moment for rugby league.
For the first time, this rebel sport from the north of England had been recognised in such a manner; one of its heroes had been acknowledged for their contribution to history through the game.
Sir Billy was a fitting recipient of the honour and a world class athlete, whose story deserved to be told.
You can tell the importance of someone by how many statutes have been erected in tribute, and Sir Billy Boston wasn't lacking.
His name was chosen as one of just five to grace Wembley's monument to rugby league's Challenge Cup, while years after his departure north, his home city of Cardiff also ensured his legacy remained cast-iron strong as he formed part of a three-man tribute along with Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman.
Unsurprisingly, Boston is also captured in bronze in his adopted home of Wigan; the place where his legend really came to life.
Born and brought up in Cardiff's ethnically-eclectic Tiger Bay district, he learned his rugby skills on the streets and with the talent factory-esque Cardiff International Athletic Club.
Like all Welsh lads he harboured dreams of playing for his local club Cardiff RFC and hopefully the national team.
Like others before and after for a time, Boston found those routes blocked, having to travel to Neath and Pontypridd to trial before his military service took him north.
It was here where the league scouts came calling, and Wigan persuaded Boston to turn professional in 1953, forever ending his union dreams in the time of 'sine die' penalties for liaising with league personnel.
The money was life changing.
£3,000 could easily buy a house at that stage, while it proved money well spent as he took to the new code like a duck to water, scoring with his first touch in a Wigan A team game.
This prime specimen of Welsh breezeblock had everything; he was quick, he could step and as former player and BBC commentator Ray French put it - his fend was like "being hit in the face with shovel".
The sepia footage and slow shutter speeds of the cameras that captured his magic during his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance.
Whether it was bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston was a blur of speed, footwork and power.
Having swiftly progressed to the first team at Central Park, he would go on to score 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, and tales of his feats would be passed down through generations. There are very few down at the Brick Community Stadium these days who don't know of Sir Billy, young or old, his name carried a cache right until his last.
Great Britain gave him the international recognition denied to him by Wales, and he rewarded the selectors by racking up the tries, particularly against the Australians who would bear the brunt of his scoring ability.
He scored 36 tries alone on his maiden Great Britain tour, dazzling both Australia and New Zealand in 1954 under captain and fellow Welshman Dickie Williams.
Boston was a phenomenal rugby league player, but there is also a powerful message in how in post-war Britain a black athlete could become a hugely popular figure by communities adjusting to a new, more diverse world.
Others like Roy Francis beforehand, Johnny Freeman, and Colin Dixon, also became established names, but never quite sprinkled the same stardust as Sir Billy.
It paved the way for players such as Ellery Hanley and Martin Offiah to charm the public with their talents, while modern day talent such as Junior Nsemba and Kai Pearce-Paul continues to stand out in a sport which has broken down barriers for years.
Sir Billy had a unique unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community.
He was revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.
Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his passing, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.
There was a photo of him and his wife Lady Joan, who had died just a few weeks previously, on her seat with flowers at Wigan's game with Wakefield last week. There is a poignancy that Sir Billy departed soon after her.
His seat will always be reserved at Wigan, and he will be dearly missed but certainly not forgotten.

India’s pet care ecosystem is undergoing a structural shift. What was once a fragmented market dominated by neighbourhood pet stores, a limited number of veterinary clinics, and imported pet-food brands is steadily becoming a broader consumer category. Today’s pet parents aren’t shying away from spending on much more than just food. Because of this shift in behaviour, the pet care ecosystem now spans nutrition, medicines, veterinary care, grooming, accessories, diagnostics, insurance, boarding, at-home care, and even quick commerce. The shift gathered pace after the pandemic. Lockdowns pushed more people towards pet companionship, while rising disposable incomes, delayed marriages and smaller families created a growing pool of urban consumers willing to spend more on their pets. Now, as pets increasingly become part of the family, spending on them is moving from a discretionary expense to a recurring household priority. This has given a much-needed boost to India's pet care market that is expected to reach $7 Bn-$8 Bn by 2030, with pet healthcare and services growing faster than the traditional pet-food category. The opportunity has attracted startups across the value chain. Drools, Heads Up For Tails, Vetic, PetKonnect and JustDogs have built businesses around different parts of the ecosystem. At the same time, ecommerce platforms such as Amazon and Flipkart have expanded their pet offerings, while offline veterinary chains have increased their footprint. Supertails, however, is betting that the bigger opportunity lies in connecting these fragmented pieces. Founded in 2021 by Varun Sadana, Aman Tekriwal and Vineet Khanna, the company started as an online pet-food platform. It has since expanded into accessories, pharmacy, teleconsultations, private-label pet food, veterinary clinics and quick commerce. The expansion has translated into rapid top-line growth. Supertails' operating revenue rose from ₹109 Cr in FY25 to more than ₹200 Cr in FY26, while losses remained broadly unchanged despite investments in clinics, dark stores and healthcare infrastructure. The startup expects revenue of ₹350 Cr-₹400 Cr this financial year and now serves nearly one million pet parents. But the next phase is likely to be more difficult than the first. Supertails has spent five years building the infrastructure around pet parenting. Now, it has to prove that these different pieces can work together well enough to create a durable and financially sustainable business. "We've entered a phase where this is no longer just about growth. It's about building a business where the unit economics and profitability make complete sense," said Vineet Khanna, cofounder of Supertails. Supertails Factsheet Supertails’ Sustainability Push For years, the playbook for the startup was straightforward: acquire customers, expand the assortment, enter new cities and chase topline growth. Supertails is now at the point where simply adding another vertical or opening another location will not be enough. The startup increasingly has to make the existing ecosystem work harder. The company believes the path to sustainable growth lies in increasing the value of each customer while making its existing infrastructure more productive. Three pillars underpin that approach: Vertical Expansion: From Pet Food To The Entire Pet-Care Basket When Supertails started in 2021, ecommerce was the obvious entry point. The founders had identified a fragmented market where consumers bought food from one platform, medicines from another, consulted veterinarians separately and relied on neighbourhood stores for other needs. Rather than compete for a share of one category, Supertails decided to build across the pet-care value chain. But the startup did not attempt to capture everything at once. Pet food came first, helping the brand establish a recurring purchase relationship. Accessories was the next category. The startup then added pharmacy and teleconsultations before moving into physical veterinary care and, more recently, quick commerce. Each layer expanded the startup’s addressable customer relationship. The most important shift came with healthcare. Around 18 months ago, Supertails began opening veterinary clinics after finding that teleconsultations alone could not address every healthcare need. It now operates 12 clinics in Bengaluru and employs more than 110 veterinarians. The same logic extends to quick commerce. With pet parents increasingly accustomed to receiving products within minutes, Supertails has added a network of 45 partner-operated dark stores across three cities. Rather than building and owning the entire infrastructure, the startup manages inventory, technology and customer experience while relying on third-party operators. For Supertails, the objective is not simply to add revenue streams. It is to increase the number of occasions on which a pet parent interacts with the platform. “Supertails has already invested in clinics, healthcare infrastructure, inventory and delivery infrastructure. The next phase therefore cannot simply be about adding more categories. It has to be about improving utilisation of what the startup has already built,” Khanna said. That is why Supertails is currently resisting aggressive expansion into new cities, even as categories such as insurance, boarding and at-home care remain on its longer-term roadmap. Doctor Consultations: Turning Healthcare Into The Engagement Engine The second pillar is healthcare. For Supertails, veterinary care is not simply another revenue vertical. It creates a different relationship with the customer. Supertails assigns new customers a 'Super Companion', a pet relationship manager who interacts with pet parents. Purchase history, veterinary records and consultations are then combined to build a more detailed profile of the pet. This changes how the startup thinks about customer acquisition and recommendations. An eight-month-old cat has very different needs from a 12-year-old dog. A dog with allergies requires different products from an otherwise healthy pet. A puppy entering its vaccination cycle creates different purchase opportunities from an ageing pet requiring medicines and specialised food. Supertails' proposition is that repeated interactions across commerce and healthcare allow it to understand the pet rather than simply the customer. This data is also used to improve recommendations and support veterinarians. With AI now becoming mainstream, Supertails is building a recommendation engine for better understanding of a pet, more relevant purchases and potentially higher customer retention. Private Label: Bringing Margin Into The Ecosystem The third pillar is private labels. The decision emerged directly from Supertails' healthcare interactions. Veterinarians were prescribing specialised diets and recommending products that were either expensive because they were imported or difficult to source in India. The founders saw an opportunity between premium imported food and lower-priced domestic products. The result was Henlo, Supertails' premium pet-food brand positioned around products made for the Indian market. Private label gives Supertails something its marketplace business does not: greater control over product economics. That makes it strategically important as the startup moves from growth towards sustainability. The marketplace can increase selection and transaction frequency, healthcare can deepen engagement, and private labels can potentially improve monetisation and margins on that existing customer base. The combination is more important than any one vertical individually. A customer may enter through pet food, interact with a veterinarian, receive a recommendation for a specialised diet, purchase that product through Supertails and subsequently return for medicines or another consultation. That is the ecosystem flywheel Supertails is trying to create. Supertails Supertails Now Has To Make The Numbers Work Supertails more than doubled its revenue to over ₹200 Cr in FY26 while keeping losses broadly unchanged. While this suggests the startup has been able to grow without a proportional deterioration in its cost base, it also means the next stage cannot be built purely on topline expansion. The startup has already made substantial investments in three areas it considers foundational: delivery infrastructure, healthcare infrastructure and data infrastructure. The question is no longer whether Supertails can add another vertical. It is whether the existing customer base can generate enough frequency across food, pharmacy, healthcare and other categories to make the infrastructure increasingly productive. Quick commerce provides a useful example. Supertails says its quick commerce business is growing at double-digit month-on-month rates, with retention and repeat purchases improving as customers use the platform for medicines, food, toys and accessories. The startup also argues that the economics improve as demand scales because shorter delivery distances, negligible returns and higher infrastructure utilisation can make the model cheaper than conventional ecommerce. But the more important test is whether this increased convenience creates incremental frequency rather than simply shifting existing orders from standard ecommerce to a faster channel. The same question applies to clinics and private labels. More clinics can increase healthcare revenue, but they also add fixed costs. Private labels can improve margins, but only if Supertails can generate sufficient volume and customer adoption. Recommendations can improve conversion, but only if the underlying customer data translates into higher retention and purchase frequency. Supertails’ Next Act Supertails' first five years were largely about building. It built an ecommerce business, expanded into healthcare, launched its own brand, opened clinics and created a faster delivery network. The next five years will require a different kind of execution. The startup wants to become the largest specialised pet-care platform in India and expects to reach that milestone in the coming quarters. But market leadership alone will not pave the way for attractive economics. Therefore, three sets of metrics will become increasingly important. First, customer retention and purchase frequency. If pet parents use Supertails across food, medicines, healthcare and other categories, the startup can potentially increase customer lifetime value without having to reacquire the same customers repeatedly. Second, utilisation and economics of healthcare and delivery infrastructure. Clinics and dark stores only become assets rather than cost centres when enough demand flows through them. Third, the margin contribution of private labels and other owned products. These businesses could help SuperTails capture more value from transactions that it already generates. The startup is also targeting financial sustainability over the next 24-36 months, with a longer-term ambition of becoming public. Its IPO ambition put another layer of pressure on the business. Public markets tend to reward growth, but they also demand visibility into margins, cash flows and the path to profitability. For now, Supertails has become successful in building a large pet-care platform. The next part is making every cog in the wheel work together.

I first sensed a disturbance in the force in the early days of the first Trump administration. It wasn’t the president’s antics that got my Spidey senses tingling. Rather, it was a gnawing recognition of a fundamental shift in the way the world worked. Over time, the contents and contours of this new mindset became clear – to me, at least – and I called it “the new national security economy.”
While that administration’s declaration that strategic competition was the defining feature of the geopolitical moment made sense, it wasn’t clear how that concept would be applied. Unlike the Cold War, when the primary battleground was military, the U.S. and the West generally were squaring off against a real economic adversary, one that is deeply embedded in its supply chains and integral to its economic success.
The economic dimension transformed strategic – I use that word in its most elemental sense – calculations, particularly since this shifted attention to an arena, technology, where Western leadership has been taken for granted. Historically, discussions of technology in the strategic sphere zeroed in on its impact on military capabilities. Today, the civilian uses of that technology matter most. That is why David Lee and I titled our new book, which comes out today, “Tech-Gemony”: It explains how and why the future will be written by the companies and countries that lead in this field.

Trump envoy calls for Sudan-wide arms embargo as drone attacks escalate
- Published
US President Donald Trump's senior Africa envoy has asked the UN to extend its arms embargo from Darfur to all of Sudan, warning the war could spread across the wider region.
The UN Security Council "must act to stop external financial and military support to the parties, such as drones and related technologies, from entering Sudan," Massad Boulos said.
Drone attacks are escalating with both the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) accused of using them. Now in its fourth year, the conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and forced 14 million more to flee their homes.
But a wider arms embargo would require a Security Council vote, with Russia and China opposing the move.
They said it would affect Sudan's army's effectiveness. Sudan's UN envoy agreed, adding it would weaken protection for civilians.
The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.
As the UN Security Council heard appeals about the arms embargo, the army was reported to have carried out drone strikes on RSF positions in Nyala in Darfur.
Nyala airport has become one of the paramilitary group's chief logistics hubs - and the attack came hours after a large cargo flight landed in the city.
An arms embargo covering the Darfur region has been in place for more than two decades - and will expire next month if not amended or renewed.
Observers say it seems to have done little to stop the flow of weapons into Darfur, which has witnessed some of the worst fighting since the conflict erupted in April 2023.
Ethnic violence witnessed 20 years ago has reignited in Darfur, with UN experts saying atrocities allegedly committed by RSF fighters as they took over the city of el-Fasher last October showed the "hallmarks" of genocide.
At the council meeting, UN's humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, warned that fighting had in recent weeks been "characterised by the heavy use of drones".
Rosemary DiCarlo, the UN's under secretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs, told the council that civilians were facing "the unrelenting consequences of one of the worst humanitarian crises of our time".
"Drones launched by both sides have repeatedly struck markets, schools, fuel stations and water infrastructure," she said, adding that the UN had documented that 1,100 civilians had died in drone strikes between January and June this year.
DiCarlo noted that the true death toll since the war began was uncertain but was "likely to be in the hundreds of thousands".
The continued use of "sophisticated weaponry" pointed to ongoing external support to both sides, she added.
Boulos said the US plan included a proposal to increase the number of experts monitoring the embargo.
He asked the council to take steps to curtail "external actors" fuelling the conflict, adding that this "risks drawing more regional actors and neighbours deeper into Sudan's conflict".
Sudan's military chief seemed unfazed by the proposals under discussion by the UN.
"The continuing talk about the possibility of imposing sanctions on the country will neither affect us nor weaken our resolve," Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan told a police graduation event in the capital, Khartoum, on Monday.
The flow of weapons into Sudan has been analysed by various experts.
Amnesty International has in the past said it found evidence of weapons manufactured in Serbia, Russia, China, Turkey, Yemen and United Arab Emirates (UAE) being used in Sudan.
The UAE in particular is accused of being the main provider of arms and support to the RSF, who in turn is accused of using the UAE as a marketplace for illicit gold sales. Both parties have repeatedly denied these allegations.
Sudan's military has used Turkish and Iranian drones, and it receives political and other backing from Egypt, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.
The two warring rivals had been allies - coming to power together in a coup in 2021 - but fell out over an internationally backed plan to move towards civilian rule.

Is Mercedes' 2026 dominance over? F1 Q&A
- Published
Lando Norris beat championship leader Kimi Antonelli to claim his second win in a row with victoy at the Dutch Grand Prix.
Reigning world champion Norris moved up to fourth in the drivers' standings, 83 points adrift of Mercedes' Antonelli.
Four-time world champion Max Verstappen suffered heartbreak at his final home race when he crashed out heavily in the opening stages.
F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your questions after round 12 of the campaign in Zandvoort.
Is it fair to say the dominance of Mercedes is over? They haven't won a race since Spa-Francorchamps, and even then that victory wasn't consecutive. Are they focusing more now on scoring points than they are winning races?
There has been a very obvious shift in competitiveness at the front as the Formula 1 season has progressed.
Mercedes won the first six races of the season, but have won only two of the subsequent six.
Mercedes took 10 consecutive poles in the first 10 races, but have been beaten by McLaren's Lando Norris at the past two grands prix. And the fastest Mercedes was lower than second for the first time in Hungary, where Red Bull's Max Verstappen also lined up ahead of Kimi Antonelli.
Over the season as a whole so far, the Mercedes is the fastest car in qualifying by an average of 0.316 seconds over Ferrari, with McLaren a further 0.041secs adrift.
But what happens when you split that into the first six races and the next six?
Until the Canadian Grand Prix in late May, Mercedes were 0.453secs a lap faster than the next fastest team, which was McLaren at the time, and 0.489secs quicker than Ferrari.
Since Monaco, that gap has come down to 0.163secs over Ferrari and 0.270secs over McLaren. Red Bull's gap over the past six races is 0.353secs, whereas it was 0.813secs up to Canada.
There is a very obvious reason for this - Mercedes have upgraded their car less than their rivals. To a quite stark degree.
Each race, governing body the FIA issues a sheet showing the declared upgrades each team has brought to that race.
It's not a definitive list - teams don't have to put all the changes on that sheet, only the ones that are visible. But it gives an idea.
Since the start of the season, Mercedes have fitted a total of 24 new parts to their cars, compared with 37 for Red Bull, 38 for McLaren and 40 by Ferrari.
This is not a direct representation of relative spend, as some parts are more expensive than others.
But it's striking, for example, that Mercedes have also deployed fewer upgrades than Aston Martin, Alpine, Racing Bulls, Audi and Cadillac.
Even Haas, the team with the smallest budget on the grid, have had more upgrades than Mercedes, who have the equal lowest number with Williams.
This is all in the context of the budget cap, which is set at $215m (£170m) for all teams.
The question, obviously, is what is going on here?
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff says: "We haven't got the money to put developments on the car.
"We are trying to evenly split that through the season, based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimising the championship points. But we just can do what we can do."
Asked why McLaren and Ferrari appeared to have the money and Mercedes did not, Wolff said: "Well, you will see how towards the end of the season (whether) they are going to be able to deploy as much stuff on to the car as they do now.
"Someone might have a different strategy in spending more at the beginning and in the middle of the year than towards the end."
The obvious conclusion is that Mercedes either spent more money in the design and build process of this year's car than their rivals - which would make sense, given how competitive it was at the start of the season - or they have saved money to spend on their next upgrade, and/or next year's car.
That is due at the so-called Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the start of October, when there are either eight or nine grands prix remaining, depending on the situation in the Middle East.
On top of that, Antonelli will take a grid penalty at the next race in Italy for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts, and George Russell will also have one at a subsequent race, most likely Azerbaijan.

How did the alleged improvements go on the Aston Martin? Is there any sign of improved performance? - Chris
Honda gave a debut to its long-awaited 'spec two' engine at the Dutch Grand Prix, while Aston Martin added a new front wing and diffuser to the pretty much all-new car that was introduced at the previous race in Hungary.
Within the team, they were hoping that the Honda engine would reduce lap times by somewhere in the region of 0.3-0.5secs.
The weekend painted a confusing picture.
On the one hand, Fernando Alonso looked more competitive than ever before at various points.
But he qualified further away from pole in both positional and percentage terms than he had in Hungary.
There were, however, extenuating circumstances, in that he was 12th fastest before failing to improve on a messy final lap hindered by a sub-optimal 'prep' lap which left his tyres out of the 'window'. Without that, he probably would have progressed beyond the first session.
Nevertheless, that suggests the new Honda was little better than the old one. On the other hand, the new engine's drivability was definitely worse, which may have skewed the picture.
But then Alonso drove an outstanding race on a one-stop strategy to take ninth place, looking after tyres and measuring his pace with all the expertise and skill he has shown throughout his career to hold off two faster cars in Pierre Gasly's Alpine and Yuki Tsunoda's Racing Bull in the final stint.
Those are the first points Aston Martin have scored on merit all season.
As Alonso put it: "We scored one point in Monaco with nine DNFs (retirements). Today we scored two points with Max (Verstappen) DNF. It was well deserved."
Alonso said after the race that the team were planning a two-stop but changed during the race because they were stuck behind other cars.
"We are in traffic," he said. "We cannot use our potential. We are faster in the corners than the people in front of us and we are slower on the straights. We're stuck behind.
"So as soon as we have free track in front of us, we try to use it. Even if it's not the optimal performance and the optimal strategy, and it's what we did today."
On the car and engine upgrades, Alonso said: "Another step forward, especially on the chassis side.
"We brought four or five components here. Also the Budapest package was understood in the (summer) break. With all the data available after the race, we fine-tuned a little bit the set-up around that new spec. Plus the new parts. I think now we are optimising the chassis side and we are able to extract the maximum.
"The engine is more difficult. I don't think we can be black and white if we have more power or not.
"On the driver side of things, you change circuits one month after the other race. The drivability has been a difficult weekend. We struggled with the downshift again. We struggled with the engine braking corner to corner. It was a challenging weekend in that regard."
These engines are highly complex and it takes time for teams to dial into them so they are working at their optimum. So it may be a few more races before the new Honda can be judged fairly.
Did Charles Leclerc cost Ferrari and Lewis Hamilton a podium position by holding Hamilton up when he refused to pit when instructed to, and what will Ferrari do to ensure he follows team orders in the future? - Mike
Mid-race in Zandvoort, Lewis Hamilton came up behind Charles Leclerc on fresher tyres, their strategies offset, and asked to be let by to optimise his race.
The way the television broadcast was played out, it sounded as if Ferrari decided to pit Leclerc for fresh tyres to get him out of the way. He initially resisted that and did not come in, but then came in at the next call.
Team boss Frederic Vasseur addressed this after the race, in comments that were a little unclear.
First, he said, at that point, Ferrari were thinking of running Hamilton to the end, so they did not want him to push hard - but had not told him that was the case, because they wanted to keep the plan secret from their rivals.
As for Leclerc, Vasseur said they were "expecting him to pit" but then realised he was in danger of coming out in traffic.
Vasseur said: "Charles was supposed to pit, we extended one lap, and it was a kind of confusion, but I'm not worried about this. Everybody will be back in the briefing, they will have a clear picture about the race."
Some will inevitably say this was another example of Ferrari messing up their strategy, an accusation that is levelled at them quite often.
Vasseur said: "It's not so easy, but, if I look at the race now, my issue is that we didn't tell Lewis that we were expecting him to go to the end, and it was not a matter of (him) pushing (at that point)."
Did the delay cost Hamilton third? Hamilton thought so, but it's impossible to know whether he would have passed George Russell if he had had a lap or two more to try.
With Isack Hadjar hurting his wrist during the summer break, do teams not ask drivers to stay away from high impact or dangerous sports and activity during their time off to keep them ready for their return? - Dave
F1 drivers' contracts usually have clauses in them forbidding them from doing 'dangerous sports', such as skiing or scuba diving, although not every driver's contract is the same.
In Hadjar's case, the Frenchman suffered what Red Bull describe as a "minor fracture" while doing a boxing exercise which is part of his normal gym routine.
There is no suggestion of him doing anything that could have been outside the terms of his contract.
Red Bull are targeting for him to return for the next race, the Italian Grand Prix, but it remains to be seen whether that will be possible.

Where Do America’s Colleges Go From Here?
The Trump administration has a new series of questions for colleges about affordability, curriculum, and “national service”—how will they respond? And: W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington in a dubious battle over education, from the Atlantic archives.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts
On August 3, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to states and higher-education leaders with instructions to, as McMahon put it, “describe to the American public your commitments to rigorous teaching, pathbreaking research, and national service—commitments that make our universities a bedrock institution of the American republic.”
A request like that would be simple enough if not for the history between the Trump administration and higher education—a relationship that can fairly be described as antagonistic. Case in point: last year’s “Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education,” which critics from across the political spectrum argued effectively asked colleges to compromise academic freedom in exchange for privileged, if vague, access to federal funds. There’s also the suite of federal investigations targeting diversity programs on college campuses.
Questioning colleges is normal. There are outstanding concerns about the experience, the education, and the enterprise of higher education: How much does it cost, and is that more than families can pay? Who gets in, and why? Are faculty members treated with dignity? What is college even for? So, although college leaders argue that a few of the concerns voiced in the document are legitimate, they also see within it the bane of Ilium.
Read: A deal that would end universities’ independence
On this week’s Radio Atlantic, I’m joined by Jack Stripling, the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education, to consider higher education in the Trump era, and the purpose of college itself.
I also go back into the Atlantic archives to look at a debate between W. E. B. Du Bois and Booker T. Washington over their theories of advancement for Black people, and how it should inform our thinking about colleges today.
The following is a transcript of the episode:
Jack Stripling: We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.
Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Adam Harris, and around the country millions of students are getting ready to head back to school, if they’re not already in class. So today, we need to think about education in uncertain times.
Now, I was always a big fan of the first day of school. In grade school, I’d pick out my clothes the night before, have them sitting and ready next to my bed. My bag was packed with everything I could possibly need, and some things I definitely didn’t. In college, every new year meant new books, new ideas, and new challenges.
But over the last several years, there has been a battle raging for the soul of higher education in America that’s divorced from those idyllic memories—a battle that has many asking what college is supposed to be and whom it is supposed to serve. Earlier this month, Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent a letter to colleges asking them to respond to a series of questions. Questions about their institutions, their programs, and how they contribute to the American project. The letter gives college leaders one more thing to consider in an era marked by funding woes, by fears of enrollment stagnation and decline, technological advancements, and political pressures.
How will it all play out? And what will school leaders be thinking about throughout the next year?
Jack Stripling is the host of the College Matters podcast at The Chronicle of Higher Education and my former colleague. And he joins me now to discuss.
 
 Let’s get to questions.
Jack, welcome to the show.
Stripling: Adam Harris, so good to catch up with you.
Harris: Absolutely, man. I want to start with this letter that went out to college leaders recently from Education Secretary Linda McMahon that was effectively the administration’s call to action, right? To prod colleges to address what they see as a sort of outstanding concerns—affordability, viewpoint, diversity, right? That is to say, more acceptable, or more acceptance of conservative views on campus, job preparation, among other things. And it’s sort of been billed as a Compact 2.0, sort of building on the Compact for Academic Excellence in Higher Education that was criticized in 2025.
In The Chronicle, you all referred to it as either an olive branch or a gloved fist.
So, like, which one is it? How are college presidents viewing this?
Stripling: Well, I think that the backstory is important here, Adam, which you know, which is that this is an administration that has essentially been at loggerheads with higher education since day one. The Trump presidency has largely defined its domestic agenda around attacking higher education for its perceived “wokeness.”
So this was no surprise that they were going to head in this direction to some extent. They have used, as you know, different types of leverage against all sorts of universities: withholding money, threatening all sorts of things. But the one thing they did do last fall was to release this compact for higher education, which was to say Sign on to these federal priorities and we will, in exchange, give you favorable treatment for federal funding. And this was a total flop. No one really signed on to this thing. There were lots of objections to it. And I think where it really hurt this administration was college presidents saying, This isn’t even merit-based, and you’re supposed to be the merit people. You’re now saying you’re going to give favoritism to people who agree with you politically.
So there was a disconnect between two value systems of the Trump administration. So they end up going back to the drawing board and, as you say, this August 3 letter comes from Secretary Linda McMahon that’s called “a national call to action.”
It’s a little softer. It’s more coalition-y, to make a phrase here. It’s based on feedback from influential higher-ed leaders, although some of them seem to be distancing themselves from their role in this.
Harris: Wait, how so?
Stripling: Well, so, one case in point being the Association of American Universities. So this is the group of high-powered research institutions in this country. It’s an invite-only group; it’s very elite to be a part of it. And they have apparently been working behind the scenes in conversations with the Education Department and with the White House about what they would or wouldn’t want to see in such a letter, but they’ve distanced themselves in saying, Hey, we actually didn’t get to take home drafts. We only had these conversations in person, and some of what we said showed up in there, some of it didn’t.
Other people, like the president of Wash U, Andrew Martin, who I think is considered somebody who’s kind of in the “Trump has a point” camp, has said, Hey, I didn’t I didn’t draft this thing, but it does look like some of the things I said are resonating with the Trump administration and ended up in there. But that tells you something about how prickly this is, Adam.
So people want to look like they’re playing ball with the Trump administration, but then they have to answer to other constituencies who are deeply skeptical of the motives behind this quote, unquote “agreement” or “value exercise.”
Harris: One of the things I noticed as you mentioned is that you had not only liberal groups, academics who might skew a little bit more to the left criticizing this original compact, but you also had conservative think tanks who would say things like At least the previous attempts to change higher education had some sort of legal backing, some sort of legal argument. It was a Title VI, it was a Title IX, it was a Title IV. Is this compact different than things that we had seen in previous administrations?
Stripling: Well, I probably should have said more about what was in it, Adam, right? So some of these things are sort of the greatest hits of the Trump administration. They want institutions to answer questions about, like, how are you gonna ensure merit-based admissions? Well, this is a very conservative-coded phrase, right? Because the suspicion is that they’re giving advantages to minority applicants, etc., even though the Supreme Court has said they can’t. So what are you doing on that front? What are you doing to ensure intellectual diversity in your departments? This is another conservative bailiwick, that certain soft sciences and other disciplines are now dominated by left-wing radicals who are here to indoctrinate your children. So they want you to speak to that.
These have flavors of things that came in the old compact. I think the distinction here, though, is that they are saying rather than Sign on to all of this, it’s phrased more in questions. Put something in a public statement that says what you’re doing on this front.
I talked to one former college president recently who said Is the Trump administration going to consider it a win if a bunch of us change our websites? And I think that remains to be seen. Would a symbolic victory of that kind be enough for the Trump administration?
Harris: And is there a concern that if they do put something on the website, the administration might try to poke holes in it?
Stripling: Absolutely, yes.
There are several people that I’ve talked to in recent days who talk about this as a Trojan horse. Because you can’t divorce this from history, Adam.
So I had one former president—I’m not going to name names here—but from a high-profile institution tell me, Well, Jack, you know, what if this came from Obama or Biden? Would people be freaking out about this? And then said, Now set aside all of the things that the Trump administration has done that appear to be or probably are patently unconstitutional and illegal. Set aside the fact that they had their fangs out for higher education from day one.
Well, you really can’t, right? You can’t set that aside. There’s history here, and so there’s a complete lack of trust. And the idea that we’re gonna put a public statement on our website saying we ostensibly sign on to a lot of the things you like—there’s great suspicion about how that information might be used against the institutions at some later date.
Harris: But we’ve seen some institutions comply, right, and already respond to the administration. So who has been responding and what are they saying in their responses to the call to action?
Stripling: The early responses are coming from pretty expected quarters. So Florida’s universities and state colleges, as well as the University of North Carolina system. These are both university systems that have a lot of political and ideological alignment with the Trump administration. They’re governed by boards that are led by Republicans or people with deep ties to the party. So it’s not really surprising to see them come out. They both praise the secretary’s questions. You know, we were waiting to be asked. Thank you so much. And they said We’re already doing a lot of the work that the Trump administration cares about.
So things like cracking down on disruptive protesters or banning DEI-related measures or emphasizing civics education. This is all pretty standard policy, particularly in red states now at public universities, so that’s not a big surprise. They were also asked about things that I think are arguably pretty nonpartisan, like dealing with grade inflation, maintaining academic rigor in the AI age. These are things that universities across the country, regardless of politics, I think, are concerned about and thinking about, so they weighed in on that.
I think what’s distinct in the responses to this letter from these two states, at least, though, is the highly nationalistic tone. They’re being pressed to talk about how they will serve American interest. And these states are very comfortable with that type of conversation, perhaps in a way that left-leaning faculty, frankly, might not be. Florida’s saying, Hey, we’re capping undergrads from foreign countries. That’s one of the things we’re doing. UNC says We emphasize research related to national defense. It’s probably a bit rah-rah for some in the faculty set. It reminds me a little bit of post-9/11 America, what we saw in higher education after that. But I think to sort of sum it up, Florida and North Carolina are saying You’re preaching to the choir here. In fact, you’re preaching to the choir directors. We were already on this. And so it’s not surprising to hear this from them.
Harris: But it’s almost like serving up a little bit of red meat with a little bit of substance.
Stripling: I think so, I think so. This has been compared to what people do in an accreditation process, for example. We know the rules; this is how we’re obeying them. And it’s, you know, it’s sort of a statement of alignment as much as anything.
Harris: Yeah. And so for these states, which are functionally sort of aligned ideologically, they’re saying that they are already concerned about these things. They’re already working on these things. And you mentioned that other institutions are concerned about these things. Are they also working on those things? Like, how much of this is the rest of higher education already doing?
Stripling: Well, I think that we’re having a national conversation around things like the SAT, for example. Some colleges went test optional, or even test blind. And even, you know, the liberal state of California is starting to grapple with this question. Did doing away with the SAT mean that we got students here who weren’t prepared for the level of work they were going to get at a University of California campus? So that conversation is happening in states red and blue, and it’s something the Trump administration emphasizes and cares deeply about.
It’s part of this larger merit conversation.
Harris: And of the things that are in the actual call to action, how much of it are colleges already doing? I thought that was a really interesting critique, was that these questions are things that we’ve already outlined; they’re things we’re already trying to address. So how much of it are the colleges actually already doing?
Stripling: Well, your mileage may vary on whether they’re doing enough to control cost, whether they’re doing enough to address ideological capture within their own departments.
Cost you can’t argue with; we now have from the highly selective institutions that are charging over $100,000 to other privates that are much lower but still very much out of reach for most American families. Very hard to argue with that.
Then you have recent reports from Yale and one commissioned by the chancellors at Vanderbilt and Wash U that have both said there’s some credence to this idea that politicization has become a problem in our academic departments. So those voices are coming from within. Clearly there has been some recognition within higher education that some of these critiques have some merit.
Harris: To that point though, one of the administration’s plans, goals, is to address the high cost of going to college. But how much control do institutions actually have over the cost of education?
Jack Stripling: Well, Adam, you’ll know from our days working together at The Chronicle, which were the best of my life, I should say—2017 was a great year for me.
Harris: Incredible. I enjoyed it so much.
Stripling: But in any case, you’ll remember it was the same story that we were hearing then, which was that a lot of the drivers of cost have to do with personnel; they have to do with structural issues within higher education; they have to do with students wanting more amenities—that was kind of an old sall. And I think you’re hearing a lot of the same things, but the fact is they can’t get away from the reality that people are losing confidence in higher education as an institution.
If you look at the latest polling on this, I think it’s, like, four in 10 Americans that say they have high confidence or a lot of confidence in higher education now. And even Democrats who have historically supported higher education more than Republicans are starting to lose their affection for the institution.
So I think there’s a recognition that it’s a real problem, and I really do think that the money is the big factor. We keep talking about the politics, but when people are saying I don’t know if college is worth it, they’re usually saying I don’t know if it’s worth the money, not I don’t know if it’s worth risking meeting a liberal person.
Harris: I do want to talk more about the purpose of higher education, but I wanted to ask first about the pressures for ideological change from the administration and state lawmakers. You’re in Florida, and that’s a good example of the changes in terms of curriculum, institutional culture. So are you noticing any effects?
Stripling: I think it kind of remains to be seen, Adam. I still—and again, this is really more gut than data—but I still do think cost is the major thing families are worried about.
I will say that, to your point, I do live in Florida and, you know, this is famously the place where woke goes to die, as Ron DeSantis said. And a lot of action has been taken on the ideological front that is also connected to this question of What is college for?
So if you think about the core curriculum, the courses that colleges are saying everybody should take, there’s usually some menu of sorts. A lot of institutions over time—there’s been a lot of bloat there. There’s been a lot of things that we might not consider essential that have come into the core curriculum. So some of these ostensibly sort of ideological attacks resonate to some degree with faculty who say, Actually we have gotten a little out of control in what’s in this core.
But what you’re pointing to, Adam, is the key distinction, which is, is higher education about vocation or does it have some sort of more aspirational mission? And this is an old problem. Are you there to learn about how to prepare for your first job, or is it about preparing you for a life of greater intellectual enrichment? And I think that that’s at the heart of a lot of the conversations we’re having, even if they are politically coded. What is college for? continues to be something that, you know, sort of divides people.
What’s interesting is that parents and even students will tell you, I really want to go to college and be able to get a good job. And I want to be able to leave here with a credential that matters and that is seen as authentic, even though I use ChatGPT for half my classes.
But students also say they want more. If you look at the studies around mental health that places like the Harvard Grad School of Education have done, they are desperate for something real. And so when they come to an institution that seems like it’s all about pleasing the next corporate overlord, they chafe. That’s why they’re booing at commencement ceremonies when people praise AI, right? So students actually do want something more than something to punch up their résumé.
Harris: So, Jack, we’re in August, whole school year ahead of us. What will you be keeping your eye on the most as this year develops?
Stripling: I go back to what I said before, which is this collective sense of Is the Trump administration done with us?
I think that that is something that I’m starting to hear people in higher education ask. Like, Was this Act 1, or is this letter in and of itself a form of surrender, a sort of concession? They’re looking for a symbolic win. Using the DOJ and these other arms of the government to try to exact concessions or revenge is very expensive. It’s very time consuming, and they’ve lost in court in some big ways. Now these cases are still unfolding, but that’s the reality.
What I will be paying attention to is this question of purpose, though. And I know this is going to sound weird, Adam, but have you read Stoner?
Harris: Yes, I have.
Stripling: Okay. So for folks who don’t know, this is a 1965 novel by John Williams. We just talked about it on my podcast, College Matters. We had sort of a reading club.
And it’s the story about this professor at Mizzou, who’s this farm boy who goes to the University of Missouri thinking that he’s going to major in some kind of agricultural sciences. He’s going to come back and work on the family farm, and life’s gonna be happy for him and his parents. What ends up happening instead is that he goes into this class and he’s exposed to his first Shakespearean sonnet, and it immediately changes his world. He can’t explain why, but the way he sees people, the way he sees worlds, the way he interacts with the universe changes in some profound way. And the frustration of the novel is that he can’t really explain it to anyone. It’s just something he feels.
And that’s the problem with this product that we call “higher education.” When it works as it should, it’s transformational. It changes you in profound ways. But it’s nearly impossible to explain how.
And that makes it really hard to charge $100,000 for. And so what higher education is going to have to do this year, like it has every other previous year I’ve been covering it, is explain that transformational experience in a way that resonates with every constituency, whether it’s the Trump administration, the student who doesn’t have enough money to go to college, the parents who are skeptical about the the job return, the people who care about AI and how that’s changing credentials. Somehow they’re going to have to make that case, and maybe reading Stoner is a good start. But that’s what I’m always thinking about.
Harris: Well, Jack, as always, it is fantastic to see you, to talk to you, and you’ve given us a lot to think about as we head into this new school year. It’s great to have you on.
Stripling: Thank you, Adam. Let’s do it again. I really appreciate it.
Harris: We’re back in the archives this week with a look at a question that has troubled some of the greatest minds throughout history. It’s a question that Booker T. Washington and W. E. B. Du Bois tried to answer in The Atlantic between 1896 and 1903: Are colleges designed only to train people to work for their own improvement, or are they designed to train people to create a better society?
Booker T. Washington was the most powerful Black man of the late 19th and early 20th century in America. He was born on a tobacco plantation in 1856, and he was emancipated from slavery at the end of the Civil War. He was 9 years old then. Education changed his life.
Writing about his upbringing in the September 1896 issue of The Atlantic, Washington said: “After the close of the war, while working in the coal-mines of West Virginia for the support of my mother, I heard in some accidental way of the Hampton Institute.”
Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute, near the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, had opened its doors in 1868. It had a simple mission: “to train selected Negro youth who should go out and teach and lead their people first by example.” The students from Hampton were expected to get land and homes, to work for their money with knowledge of why they were doing the work—or, as the institution’s founder put it, “to replace stupid drudgery with skilled hands.”
Washington would later write in the pages of The Atlantic in 1896 the education he received at Hampton changed him, it “caused me for the first time to realize what it meant to be a man instead of a piece of property.”
He was ready to proselytize, to spread the word on this industrial, practical education that wasn’t just a mirror of what was popular. It wasn’t just teaching French for the sake of saying that it did or the piano while expecting nothing but a future of poverty in return for its graduates. It was a functional education, which would help Black people less than a generation removed from slavery learn the skills they needed to advance.
In 1881, Washington went to the Deep South, to the Black Belt in Alabama, to establish a school in Tuskegee. The school opened with one teacher, 30 students, and not a lick of property to speak of save a shanty and a church. But Washington was a savvy dealer; he coaxed donations from wealthy people in both the North and the South by preaching a philosophy of self-reliance. The students worked to build buildings on campus while they received an industrial education. And by the time he was writing in The Atlantic in 1896, that little college in Tuskegee had grown to 800 students, taught by 79 faculty members, spread across 1,400 acres of land which housed 30 buildings.
Washington’s reputation grew alongside the institution, not least because of what he was willing to set aside to achieve his goal.
His philosophy would have allowed—at least in the short term—the continuation of Black Americans’ second-class citizenship.
Black people, Washington argued in his Atlantic essay, were to find their dignity through their industrial labors and the financial gains it brought them. He wrote that “it is through the dairy farm, the truck garden, the trades, and commercial life, largely, that the negro is to find his way to the enjoyment of all his rights.”
Now, despite the critique that Washington’s school only taught Black people to do the same jobs that they did during slavery, even his critics were forced to admire his brilliance and thrift and ability to make a tangible difference in the lives of Black people in the Black Belt.
Perhaps most prominent among those critics was W. E. B. Du Bois, who argued that the training students received at Tuskegee was necessary but insufficient on its own. Sure, it might lead to the economic advancement for some of its students; it might make them self-sufficient, able to eat and clothe themselves. But Du Bois argued that there was more to life than food and clothing.
Du Bois thought a true college education—a liberal education of the kind taught at Fisk, Atlanta University, Wilberforce, Howard, and Lincoln, among others—was the foundation of advancement. In the September 1902 issue of The Atlantic, Du Bois argued that there needed to be teachers for would-be students. Those colleges like Fisk that were training Black people to go back and teach their kin were of the highest importance. Du Bois wrote: “In a single generation they put thirty thousand black teachers in the South; they wiped out the illiteracy of the majority of the black people of the land, and they made Tuskegee possible.”
The schools Du Bois praised developed not only workers but full men. They produced people capable of critical thought. The Bible says that man shall not live by bread alone; Du Bois had his own version. “We shall hardly induce black men to believe that if their bellies be full it matters little about their brains.”
The reality that both men acknowledged is that both forms of teaching—the one that begins with the theoretical and the other with the practical—are necessary to improve the situation for Black people in America, to unwind the damage done by generations of laws which banned Black education.
Washington thought enough of his critics to respond, which he did in the October 1903 issue of The Atlantic, where he wrote: “I cannot understand how any reasonable person can object to such education for a large part of a people who are in the poverty-stricken condition that is true of a large element of my race, especially when such hand training is combined, as it should be, with the best education of the head and heart.”
But the issue was that Washington’s idea of a practical education which would disregard social equality was weaponized: It was treated as the only way rather than a way.
As Du Bois noted in his 1902 essay, “I sit with Shakespeare and he winces not. Across the color line I move arm in arm with Balzac and Dumas, where smiling men and welcoming women glide in gilded halls.” Reading the classics gave him a sense of the ties that bind humanity; they welcomed him to the great brotherhood of mankind.
The question animating the debate between Washington and Du Bois is as relevant as ever: Is college meant to train people for the workforce of today or to produce graduates capable of building a better tomorrow? It’s a question that we should all be considering.
That’s all for today’s show.

Former Union Minister for Finance and Home Affairs, P. Chidambaram, on Wednesday said there had been “no corruption or virtually nill corruption” at offices of the Registration department and the State power utility after the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) took over the reins of the State.
Citing public feedback as the source of his information, Mr. Chidambaram, in an interview with The Hindu 360, the Tamil YouTube channel of The Hindu, at his residence here, said that during his interactions with people at his home district Sivaganga, he heard that there was “no corruption” at the time of registration of documents or in teachers’ transfers. “Corruption has almost been eliminated at the offices of the Electricity Board . I also understand that sanctions for the appointment of teachers in [government-aided] schools and colleges have been sent by post,” he observed.
He was replying to a question regarding his assessment about the functioning of the State government. “Only 105 days have passed,” Mr Chidambaram remarked, “it is a short period.”
To another question about the 2026 Assembly election result, the former Union Minister, said political parties, the media and commentators had failed to read the political scenario and had been under the impression that the two Dravidian parties, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), were occupying 80% of the space. “What they held was 80% of the legislature space in view of the two parties sharing between themselves nearly 200 Assembly seats all these years, but not 80% of the political space,” he explained. Referring to the role of the Gen Z, he added: “This time, they all exercised their franchise.” In his constituency, for instance, by 11 am on the polling day, Gen Z had finished casting their votes.
On the need for continuing with subsidies in Tamil Nadu, Mr. Chidambaran said the question was whether there were externalities associated with any subsidy scheme. “If externalities are there, we can welcome the scheme. In the absence of externalities, the scheme can be rejected,” he observed. For instance, with the free bus travel for women scheme, he pointed out that in Karaikudi , where a women’s law college had come up, people from villages within a radius of 20 km to 25 km were saying that but for the bus service, they would not have sent their girl children to the college. “So, the scheme has got externalities,” he explained.

The Velotric Discover M e-bike we reviewed earlier this year had a feature I found somewhat annoying: It would sporadically block much of the display with an alert telling me I should be in a different gear. While the implementation bugged me, the concept made a certain degree of sense; most e-bikes now know your cadence, how much torque you’re generating, and how that power is being translated into speed. That’s everything you need to know to determine an optimal gear.
Somewhere in the back of my mind, I thought, “If you’re so smart, why don’t you just shift for me?”
I was completely unaware that Shimano had already developed a system that did exactly that. And for the past few weeks, I’ve been using it on a $4,500 cargo bike from Xtracycle called the Swoop ASM that let me see what it’s like to hand control of my gears to an electronic brain.
The short answer is that the electronics on the Swoop really are smart enough to figure out when it should be shifting. But the system is less adept at the actual shifting process, making for rides that are less smooth than they could be when it’s active. But you can shut that feature off, and the Swoop will shine as a fantastic cargo bike.
Swooping in
Xtracycle got its start providing cargo trailers for mountain bikes and then branched into dedicated cargo bikes. The Swoop ASM is a long-tail cargo bike with what’s called a mullet setup: a larger tire up front and a smaller one in back. The small wheel is designed to help keep the weight held by the large rear rack a bit closer to the road. It also has a front suspension to help cushion the ride.
Notably, the bike is built with steel tubes. Most manufacturers’ lineups use a mix of either carbon fiber and aluminum because those two materials can be made into the exact same shape, simplifying manufacturing. But other materials still have their fans, as they can offer distinct combinations of weight, stiffness, and vibration dissipation.

I haven’t owned a steel tube bike since the 1990s, but the Swoop was a good reminder of why it still has its fans. It’s relatively lightweight (just under 70 lbs/31 kg) for its size, its ride is very comfortable, and it was surprisingly responsive when I stood in the pedals to accelerate away from stops. Despite its highly specialized geometry, the Swoop felt like a fundamentally good bicycle.
There are limits to how well a single frame size can adapt to different body sizes, but Xtracycle does its best to widen the comfort window. It includes a double-telescoping seat post to maximize the seat-pedal distance flexibility. There’s also a quick release on the front handlebar clamp, making it easy to tweak the angle where the grips meet your hands. I found settings that were relatively comfortable but still a bit short of ideal for my 6-plus-foot (188 cm) frame—even with the seat post at its recommended maximum, I could touch the toes of both of my feet down while seated.
Beyond that, plenty of nice touches make this a solid cargo bike. These include protective covers for the rear wheel and chain to keep clothing and limbs from accidentally getting entangled. A robust U-shaped kickstand keeps the bike stable even if you park it when fully loaded, and there’s a front cargo rack that can hold some baggage.
The rear rack can be outfitted with a large range of accessories; mine came with the default setup meant for carrying passengers. This means footrests extending out at the level of the rear hub and two handgrip bars running parallel to the bench seating. But remove a soft cover, and the metal beneath reveals a series of slots that allow a wide variety of attachments to be fitted into place.
You can also use one of Xtracycle’s bag attachments in this setup; I was provided one that ran the full length of the rear attachment and held a fair amount of cargo. Adding a second would have handled all of my typical shopping needs. (While having only one bag might seem awkward, the bike performed very well with everything I was carrying loaded on one side.)
The only problem is that this hardware makes the rear wheel extremely difficult to reach. I struggled to lock the back tire to anything, and I considered myself fortunate to not have to figure out how to deal with a flat.
Smooth assistance
All those basics make the Swoop a solid entry into the cargo bike market. What sets it apart is its use of a Shimano Cues Di2, one of the component maker’s low-end electronic shifting systems. Its mere existence surprised me, since I thought Shimano was reserving electronic shifting for higher-end component lines. But the company not only took it lower in the range; it added a couple of surprise features to its electronic shifting.
First, the basics: the drivetrain uses a single chainring on the cranks and a 10-speed rear cassette. The rear derailleur requires only a power source and control signals—no cable required. Once properly aligned with the cassette gears, it executes a perfect shift every time it’s told to. This shift includes a brief period when the derailleur over-travels to ensure the chain engages the next ring along, then drops back into the optimal location for continued cycling.

Everything in the system—the derailleur, the controllers, and the motor—takes power from a single removable battery. If the battery’s charge is good, you’re set to ride.
The mid-motor offers three levels of assist, adjusted through a controller on the left side that also includes the power button and a simple display. Shifting is controlled by the one on the right, which lacks a display. Separating the two allows each to be fairly minimalist, making it easy to find the control you need by feel.
On its own, the system worked beautifully. Shifting was fuss-free, and each change was blissfully silent. The assist worked well, and its three levels seemed to cover any needs short of going up steep hills with lots of cargo. This is not a bike that lets you skimp on pedaling in hot conditions; there’s no throttle, and even the highest setting of assist still requires you to exert some force on the pedals. But the motor definitely cuts down on the effort you have to make.
The battery, while looking fairly compact, easily handled dozens of miles without needing a recharge, which means several days of typical errands. While the battery lacks a carrying handle, it’s easy to take it out to charge it, as it pivots sideways out of the frame. When in place, it acts as a protector that keeps anything on the left side of the bike from sliding through the frame and getting tangled in the chain.
This is the first Shimano e-bike system I’ve tested, and it was just as good as you’d expect from a company that has come to dominate cycling drivetrains. Shimano Cues may be its lower-end system, but there’s no apparent skimping on the quality. And that’s before the bonus surprises Shimano has included.
The fun stuff
Somewhere in one of the controllers, Shimano’s software gathers all the relevant information about your ride: how fast you’re going, how much force your feet are exerting on the cranks, what gear you’re in, and how fast your legs are churning (and possibly more?). And it uses that data to do a couple of interesting things.
One is what it calls Free Shift. Normally, a bike can’t shift to a different gear unless you’re turning the pedals to move the chain, which can potentially create problems. For example, you could move the derailleur down a gear but not complete the shift before stopping, meaning that the shift would be made when you start pedaling again, and the chain is under a lot of tension as you crank away from a full stop. Or you could move the derailleur several gears over without the chain following.
But the whole point of having a motor is to move the chain. So if you shift without pedaling and the bike isn’t stationary, the Cues system will use the motor to move the chain just enough to complete the shift. It does so without speeding up the bike at all.
Getting at the rear wheel may require removing the mesh panel that keeps passengers’ limbs and clothing from hitting the spokes.
Credit:
JOHN TIMMER
Getting at the rear wheel may require removing the mesh panel that keeps passengers’ limbs and clothing from hitting the spokes.
Credit:
JOHN TIMMER
Practically, this means that as you coast to a stop, you can simply hit the downshift button a few times, and the system will go into a low gear to make it easy to start up again without requiring you to turn the cranks. It’s … weird. Decades of cycling experience have programmed me to instinctually move my legs when I shift. Those instincts are suddenly superfluous.
It gets even weirder if you enable the automatic transmission. Shimano has included two settings, one for general riding and one for hauling cargo or passengers. When the system recognizes that you can get more out of your pedaling in a different gear, it will simply move you into that gear. That includes doing all the downshifting as you’re coasting to a stop and rolling back up through the gears again as you accelerate away from it.
Let me make that clear: You can coast to a stop without turning the cranks or touching the shifter, and you’ll still be in a different gear when you start up again.
The system is remarkably good at matching when I feel a shift is needed—Shimano’s programmers have done a fine job. Because of that, it’s pretty easy to induce a shift by altering your pedaling, as well. You can tell when it’s close, and just a bit more force will cause the system to send you up a gear. It’s kind of pointless to do so, since the buttons that shift up and down still work when it’s in auto mode, but I found myself doing it regardless.
The downside is that these shifts are not situations where instinctual actions are superfluous. To execute a smooth shift, you have to ease tension off the drivetrain by pedaling with less force, allowing the chain to slide over onto a neighboring gear with a bit less stress. Failing to do so can make for a clunky, inefficient shift and wear down components over time.
A nice touch: a quick release on the stem lets you adjust their angle to match your height.
Credit:
John Timmer
A nice touch: a quick release on the stem lets you adjust their angle to match your height.
Credit:
John Timmer
My problem with the automatic transmission mode was that I could tell when a shift was likely to come, but I couldn’t predict its precise moment. So it typically came while I was pedaling away happily, with full tension on the chain, making for a loud and awkward shift. This was especially unpleasant when accelerating away from a stop, when the bike would make three or four clunky shifts in rapid succession, each emitting a noise that told me I’d just done something I’d spent years learning to avoid. Living in a neighborhood with lots of four-way stops meant I sometimes experienced that every single block.
Shimano is not stupid, and these systems use parts that are specifically hardened to handle the added strain and wear. But it still felt bad every time I heard and felt that clunk.
A solid contender
The Swoop is not an inexpensive bike; at $4,500, it sits somewhere between the Trek Fetch+ 2 and the Urban Arrow Family I’ve reviewed previously. While it lacks the latter’s capacious cargo tub, the longtail form factor provides a much more bicycle-like riding experience. I’d rate its ride as superior to the Trek because of its frame and front suspension made for a more pleasant ride.
I also prefer Shimano’s drive system to the Bosch used by the other two bikes. It just felt better integrated with my pedaling, plus a bit quieter and less intrusive. The electronic shifting is a bonus—it’s not needed, but it definitely makes for a nice experience, and one where Shimano’s integration means you don’t have to worry about the status of the two additional batteries needed by many electronic systems. I don’t think I’d use the automatic shifting, but I could see where a less experienced cyclist might feel they benefit from it.
So while it’s on the pricier side, the cost seems to be in line with the features it offers. If those features are important to you, the Swoop is definitely worth consideration.
In the end, though, I’m not a huge fan of electronic shifting. I hate worrying about battery levels just to ride my bike, and I like the feel of a well-aligned mechanical shifter clicking into place. But even I have to admit that Shimano’s software does a fantastic job of shifting at the right times, and I think the system could really work well for anybody who hasn’t learned to associate a clunky-sounding shift with bad things.
The good
Steel-framed long-tail provides a good ride experience for a cargo hauler
Electronic shifting comes to budget components
One battery powers it all
Solid array of options for hauling cargo and/or kids
The bad
Supposedly rated for riders taller than me, but I found it a bit small
