The Nishad community finds itself at the centre of the fish row in Ayodhya ahead of 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly polls.
At a time when many Hindu devotees traditionally give up non-vegetarian food during 'Sawan', fish has acquired an unlikely political importance in Uttar Pradesh.The row began earlier this month with Uttar Pradesh minister and Nishad Party chief Sanjay Nishad's remark that fish cooked without garlic and onion could be considered vegetarian. It escalated on August 23, when a video purportedly showing fish being prepared at a Nishad community event in Ayodhya, attended by UP Congress president Ajay Rai, surfaced on social media.But behind the sparring over what was - or was not - on Rai's plate lies a larger electoral calculation. The Nishad vote has shifted political loyalties before, and with the BJP seeking to retain its non-Yadav OBC coalition and the opposition trying to prise open that support, the community could once again become an important factor in the 2027 contest.
The 'fish on your plate' row
The controversy began earlier this month when Sanjay Nishad said at a programme: "Bina lahsun-pyaz ki bani machhli shakahari hai."The remark came during Sawan, a month when many Hindu devotees observe dietary restrictions, and quickly attracted attention because of the community he represents. Nishads have historically depended on rivers and water bodies for fishing, fish-rearing, boating and related livelihoods, making food and fishing practices part of a broader social and economic identity.
Then came Ayodhya.On August 23, UP Congress president Ajay Rai travelled to Tarun, around 30 km from Ayodhya, after visiting Hanumangarhi, reciting the Hanuman Chalisa and offering prayers at the Ram temple. He attended a programme organised by members of the Nishad community. A video showing fish being prepared at the venue subsequently surfaced.
Sanjay Nishad said fish preparation mattered.
The timing and location gave the BJP an opening.BJP state president Pankaj Chaudhary described the alleged fish feast as "highly condemnable and unforgivable", while Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath accused Rai of "duplicity" for visiting a temple and then attending a fish feast during Sawan."You saw the conduct of the Congress state president yesterday. He goes to Hanumangarhi for darshan and, after coming out, enjoys a fish feast and then shouts 'Ram-Ram'," Adityanath said.Rai denied eating fish and challenged the CM to produce evidence. "If he can produce any pictures, I will be ready to resign immediately," he said.Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera defended the hosts, saying they belonged to the Nishad community and had their own traditions of eating and drinking.Later, cabinet minister Om Prakash Rajbhar entered the controversy, backing Nishad's earlier claim and asking Congress to clarify whether the fish allegedly served at the event had been cooked with garlic and onion."Sanjay Nishad machhli ke mahir hain, unhe zyada jaankari hai, hum thode kam hain," Rajbhar said.The political argument, however, goes well beyond the menu at one event. The larger story is the political importance of the community that hosted it.
Ajay Rai dared CM Yogi Adityanath to provide evidence.
Nishads — the 'jal kisans'
The Nishads are a cluster of riverine communities whose traditional livelihoods have been closely tied to rivers, ponds and other water bodies. Community organisations have increasingly used the term 'jal kisan', or water farmers, to describe this relationship.Fishing, fish-rearing, boating and the sale of fish have historically been central to these communities' economic lives. Questions over access to water bodies, fishing rights, sand mining and regulation of traditional occupations therefore have a direct political resonance.The term Nishad is also used as an umbrella for several communities and sub-castes, including Mallah, Kewat, Bind, Kashyap, Dhimar, Batham, Kahar, Manjhi and Turaha. Not all of these communities necessarily identify themselves as Nishad in the same way.
Organiser of the event defended the decision to keep fish in the menu.
In Uttar Pradesh, Nishads are classified among the Other Backward Classes (OBCs).Political estimates put the core Nishad population at around 4.5-5 per cent of the state's electorate. Estimates that include a wider set of related riverine communities put their combined share considerably higher.There is no recent official caste census providing a definitive figure, but the community's electoral importance comes less from its statewide percentage than from its concentration.Nishad voters have a significant presence across the Ganga-Yamuna belt and eastern Uttar Pradesh, including Gorakhpur, Varanasi, Azamgarh, Ballia, Mau, Ghazipur, Mirzapur, Bhadohi, Jaunpur and Prayagraj, besides parts of Sultanpur and Fatehpur.The community is considered electorally influential in more than 160 Assembly constituencies, with around 80 seats often identified as having a particularly substantial Nishad presence.That geographical concentration explains why a community accounting for a relatively small share of the state's electorate can command such political attention.
Estimated data based on reports.
Nishadraj and Ekalavya: The epic roots of identity
The Nishad political identity is also deeply connected to stories from the Hindu epics.In the Ramayana, Nishadraj Guha, the boatman-king, is described as an ally of Ram during his exile. Guha receives Ram, Sita and Lakshman and helps them cross the Ganga.
The 51-foot-high statue of Lord Ram and Nishadraj at Shringverpur Dham, 40 km from Prayagraj.
For the Nishad community, the story has long been invoked as a marker of their place within the Ram narrative — not as an identity created by contemporary politics, but as an older cultural association that acquired renewed political meaning during the Ram Janmabhoomi movement.The community also invokes Ekalavya from the Mahabharata, who is traditionally identified as belonging to the Nishad community. His story - of a skilled archer seeking to learn from Dronacharya and ultimately giving his thumb as guru dakshina - has come to represent a different strand of Nishad memory: talent, exclusion and the struggle for recognition.The two figures capture contrasting elements of the community's epic imagination: Nishadraj represents proximity to and loyalty towards Ram, while Ekalavya represents ability denied recognition.These narratives have subsequently been woven into the community's assertion of a distinct historical and social identity.
The Ram Janmabhoomi movement
Sections of the community found their cultural resonance in the Ram Janmabhoomi movement.As the campaign for a Ram temple in Ayodhya gathered momentum in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Nishad organisations and leaders participated in the wider mobilisation. The story of Nishadraj Guha gave the movement an immediate cultural connection for sections of the community, while the broader call for 'Ram Rajya' resonated with those who saw the temple campaign as a civilisational and cultural cause.The political landscape changed sharply after BJP leader LK Advani's Ram Rath Yatra in 1990, which transformed the temple issue into a mass political movement. The demolition of the Babri Masjid on December 6, 1992, further entrenched Ayodhya as a defining issue in BJP politics.
Source: Centre for Study of Developing Societies Lokniti.
As the BJP expanded its support among non-Yadav OBC communities, sections of the Nishad community also moved towards the party.But that support did not become a permanent political contract.
From support to sense of being left behind
Among sections of Nishad political opinion, a recurring grievance emerged: the community had supported the Ram movement but did not receive a commensurate political return.The complaint has, at various points, extended to BJP leaders associated with the Ram movement, including Advani and former UP CM Kalyan Singh, with Nishad voices arguing that their support for the Ram cause did not translate into adequate representation or resolution of longstanding demands regarding representation and farming on the riverside.In the coming years, the same community that participated in the Ram movement subsequently moved towards the Samajwadi Party, created its own political organisation and entered into an alliance with the BJP.That fluidity became particularly visible in the 1990s.
Phoolan Devi and politics of representation
Before the emergence of the Nishad Party, the strongest political association for sections of the community came through the social-justice politics of the Samajwadi Party.Phoolan Devi became the most recognisable symbol of that phase.A Mallah woman from Uttar Pradesh, Phoolan Devi contested the Mirzapur Lok Sabha seat on an SP ticket in 1996 and won. She retained the seat in 1999.
SP has given key post to Phoolan Devi's sister ahead of 2027 polls.
Her rise gave the community an unusually prominent political figure and turned caste identity into a language of representation.Her political legacy continues to be invoked in Uttar Pradesh.
Nishad Party enters equation
The next major shift came in 2016, when Sanjay Nishad founded the Nirbal Indian Shoshit Hamara Aam Dal, popularly known as the Nishad Party.The party sought to consolidate riverine communities and give political expression to demands involving reservation, representation, fishing rights and livelihoods.Its first major electoral breakthrough came in an unlikely place.In the March 2018 Gorakhpur Lok Sabha bypoll, Praveen Nishad, Sanjay Nishad's son, contested as an SP-backed candidate and defeated the BJP.The result was politically significant because Gorakhpur had been Yogi Adityanath's parliamentary stronghold for five consecutive terms.The defeat demonstrated that the BJP's support among non-Yadav OBC communities could be disrupted when Nishad mobilisation combined with the SP's wider social coalition.But the equation soon changed again.Before the 2019 Lok Sabha election, the Nishad Party moved into the BJP-led NDA. Praveen Nishad joined the BJP and contested the Sant Kabir Nagar Lok Sabha seat on a BJP ticket, winning the election.The BJP-Nishad Party alliance became an important part of the BJP's strategy to consolidate non-Yadav OBC support in eastern Uttar Pradesh.
2019 and 2022: Alliance and the unfinished bargain
The BJP and Nishad Party continued their alliance into the 2022 Uttar Pradesh assembly election.The BJP won 255 seats, while the Nishad Party won six. The NDA retained power with 273 seats in the 403-member assembly.For the BJP, the alliance helped reinforce its eastern Uttar Pradesh coalition.For Sanjay Nishad, however, being part of the government brought a different problem: once an ally enters government, its demands are increasingly judged against what it can actually secure from that government.The biggest unresolved issue remained the demand for Scheduled Caste status for sections of the Nishad community.Sanjay Nishad has repeatedly pressed the BJP government on the demand.On August 18, 2026, just months before the 2027 elections, he escalated the issue again, saying he was prepared to give up his ministerial position if necessary.His friction with the BJP had also become visible after the 2024 Lok Sabha election, when he blamed BJP leaders for his son Praveen Nishad's defeat in Sant Kabir Nagar.Praveen, who contested the seat on a BJP ticket, lost to the Samajwadi Party's Laxmikant Pappu Nishad.The result was another reminder that a BJP-Nishad Party alliance does not necessarily translate into a uniform Nishad vote.
SP and Congress try to prise open BJP's base
That fluidity is what the opposition is trying to exploit ahead of 2027.In March 2026, it appointed Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti as chairperson of the Uttar Pradesh Backward Classes Commission. The move came alongside the BJP's continuing alliance with the Nishad Party.The SP responded by appointing Phoolan Devi's sister, 67-year-old Rukmini Devi, as president of the party's Uttar Pradesh women's wing. The appointment was seen as part of Akhilesh Yadav's PDA — Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak — outreach ahead of the 2027 election.Rukmini Devi subsequently attacked Sanjay Nishad, questioning what he had delivered for the community while being part of the government.The appointments show that the competition for the Nishad vote is not merely about alliances. It is a contest over who represents the community's political memory.Congress, on the other hand, has a more difficult task because its organisational presence among Nishads is weaker.Its August outreach in Tarun was therefore significant. Ajay Rai's visit to the Nishad community programme was an attempt to establish a direct connection with the community.The party's subsequent defence of the event, that the hosts were Nishads with their own food traditions, also allowed Congress to frame the controversy around community identity and traditional livelihoods rather than solely religious conduct.For the SP and Congress, the broader argument is that the Nishad vote is not synonymous with the Nishad Party.
The VIP factor
The Vikassheel Insaan Party (VIP), led by Bihar-based Nishad leader Mukesh Sahani, adds another layer to this contest.VIP entered Uttar Pradesh politics in the 2022 assembly election, seeking support among Nishads and other Extremely Backward Classes, particularly in Purvanchal.The party did not emerge as a major electoral force, but its campaign showed how smaller caste-based parties can complicate a close contest.VIP contested more than 100 seats, primarily in eastern Uttar Pradesh, and said its candidates polled more votes than Congress candidates in 15 constituencies, including Bairia, Bansdih, Phephna, Alapur, Jalalpur, Ghanghata, Balha, Shahganj and Kerakat.Its relationship with the BJP has been politically fluid rather than a straightforward alliance in Uttar Pradesh.Sahani has been a vocal critic of the BJP at various points. However, in neighbouring Bihar where the Nishads remain relevant across the seats in the Ganga area, his political trajectory has repeatedly shifted. VIP contested as part of the opposition Mahagathbandhan in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, switched to the NDA for the 2020 Bihar assembly election (winning 4 seats and entering the cabinet), but was dropped from the NDA in 2022 after contesting against the BJP in UP. In last year's Bihar polls, his party failed to secure any seat.However, in upcoming polls in UP, a few thousand votes in its favour can alter the results in close constituencies.
The 2027 question
The fish controversy may fade, but the political question it has exposed is unlikely to disappear.The BJP has the advantage of a long association with the Ram movement, an established organisational network and an alliance with the Nishad Party.
The SP is seeking to revive the community's social-justice connection through Phoolan Devi's political legacy and the PDA framework.Congress is attempting to build a direct relationship with Nishad voters, while smaller parties such as VIP can potentially fragment the vote.For the Nishads themselves, however, the choice is unlikely to be framed around a single issue.Their political history has moved from the epic memory of Nishadraj and Ekalavya, to participation in the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, to the social-justice politics associated with Phoolan Devi, to the rise of the Nishad Party, its alliance with the BJP and subsequent friction over representation and reservation.The lesson from that history is clear: the Nishad vote has never been permanently owned by one party.In 2027, the contest will be over whether Ram and the BJP's organisational alliance can outweigh demands for reservation, representation and livelihoods - and whether the opposition can convert those demands into votes.

PALAU, Micronesia — The ride out to sea was, in a word, unpleasant. The coastal waters of Palau, an island nation in the western Pacific, are typically calm and electric blue, like what you might see on a screensaver or postcard. The country has put in place some of the world’s most rigorous protections to keep its marine environment pristine.
These scientists are super-charging evolution to save coral reefs
A low-tech solution just might save these animals around the world.
But on this particular morning in July, a super typhoon named Bavi was churning north of us in the Philippine Sea. Clouds darkened the water and battered us with rain as our boat seesawed through the swell toward the horizon.
Our destination was what you might call a coral garden — a patch of coral, about two miles from shore, that scientists had planted over the past couple of years in an effort to rebuild a damaged reef.
I was wet, cold, and nauseated when we arrived. So naturally, I strapped on a mask and jumped in.
Below me, I could see dozens of star-shaped metal structures that researchers had attached to the seafloor. They were studded with corals in all forms and colors: neon blue antlers, fluffy green mittens, baseball-sized brains. Some of the corals looked like a collection of human vertebrae. Others resembled miniature pine forests.
In the past two decades, governments, nonprofits, and even hotels around the world have dedicated hundreds of millions of dollars to replanting coral reefs like this one. Reefs are among the planet’s most endangered ecosystems: Rising ocean temperatures, pollution, and other threats have killed off an estimated 50 percent of live coral globally since the 1950s.
Those steep losses erode the irreplaceable benefits that coral reefs provide. They go far beyond tourism. Healthy reefs lessen coastal flooding from storms like Bavi. They also serve as nurseries and homes for larger animal species, such as endangered sea turtles and valuable fish like snappers and groupers that people eat.
That’s why so much time and money has gone into restoring these ecosystems globally. Including here in Palau. A different typhoon and warming waters had destroyed some of the region’s coral many years ago, which caused the local fishery to decline, according to Sharp Sakuma, the governor of Ngaraard, a Palauan state where the coral garden is located. “It’s our food,” Sakuma said of fisheries. So a few years ago, he asked local researchers to help bring the reef back.
But reef restoration has a fatal flaw.
Rising global temperatures are heating up the ocean and fueling marine heat waves, which kill reefs. That means that much of the coral that people painstakingly plant often ends up dying months or years later — simply because the ocean is too hot. It’s like planting trees to restore a forest that will soon burn in a wildfire. And this raises serious doubts about the role reef restoration can play in the recovery, and ultimate survival, of these iconic ecosystems.
The colorful antlers, mittens, and brains below me, however, were not your typical planted corals.
They were different.
And they may offer a new reason for hope.
These corals had all gone through what you might call a fitness test. In a lab on shore, marine scientists exposed them to extreme heat and scored them for their ability to tolerate warming. Corals on some of the metal stars here got top marks — they appeared resistant to heat. Those individuals may have more of a fighting chance at surviving as ocean temperatures rise.
These sorts of fitness tests for corals are inexpensive and unexpectedly low-tech: They take place in cheap, store-bought picnic coolers, like what you might bring to the park. But by helping researchers identify the hardiest corals, these tests could help overcome one of reef restoration’s greatest challenges.
Subjecting corals to hot water in a plastic cooler may sound ridiculous. Until you consider the stakes and the circumstances: As the planet warms, simply protecting our beloved, life-supporting places is no longer enough to save them. Neither is restoring them to some former state.
To truly help coral reefs endure, we may actually need to reengineer them.
Scattered across a remote stretch of the Pacific is a collection of more than 300 islands, which, together, form the nation of Palau. Many of those islands are no larger than a small house. And because they’re eroding at the base, they look as though they’re floating above the ocean. When you’re out at sea, it’s easy to pretend that you’re flying through the floating mountains of Avatar’s Pandora.
But the real magic is, without a doubt, underwater.
Palau is surrounded by a vast network of coral reefs, many of which are in near-perfect condition. The region has more than 400 coral species — for comparison, the Caribbean has about 70 — which form the base of a thriving marine ecosystem. On just one weekend of diving there, I encountered close to 100 sharks, more than a dozen sea turtles, and three enormous manta rays. (In my more than 20 years of diving, I’ve rarely seen such an abundance of sea life.)
In the last two decades, Palau has become an epicenter for research on how warming affects coral reefs. Part of that is practical: The country’s abundant corals allow scientists to study how different species and populations respond to rising temperatures. It’s also home to a well-equipped marine lab, the Palau International Coral Reef Center.
But there’s also an urgent local need. Palau is deeply dependent on its coral reefs: Its fisheries and tourism make up more than a quarter of the country’s GDP. And while Palau is home to one of the world’s largest marine protected areas — which bans commercial fishing across 80 percent of its national waters — that does little to protect the reefs here from the existential global threat of ocean warming.
Why is heat such a dire problem?
One “coral” is not a single animal but a colony of hundreds or thousands of individual animals, known as polyps. Those polyps are all nearly genetically identical. They grow the colony — the coral structure that you see on a reef — by cloning themselves over and over again.
Polyps fuel themselves, in part, by grabbing particles out of the water with tentacles (up close, polyps look a bit like sea anemones). But most of their food, and much of their color, comes from a kind of algae that lives within their cells. Like plants, that algae photosynthesizes. And it passes the solar energy it generates onto the coral, in return for nutrients and a place to live.
This partnership fails under extreme heat.
When the ocean is too warm, the algae malfunction, and the polyps kick them out. As a result, the corals lose their primary source of food and their iconic color. That’s bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead but starving, and it will die unless the water cools back down.
Yet there’s another key detail here: Some corals seem to resist this heat-fueled bleaching. They appear naturally more tolerant to warming than their peers. And you can actually see this when you’re snorkeling during a heat wave: Some corals will be bone white, whereas other colonies of the same species nearby will appear fully saturated. Heat tolerance is a trait with natural variation, like height or eye color in humans.
It’s this detail that underpins efforts to make reef restoration less futile in a warming world. If scientists can find local corals that can tolerate warming, they can use them to regrow native reefs that might endure some degree of climate change, here and anywhere coral reefs can be found.
What scientists in Palau are trying to demonstrate is how — absent a naturally occurring heat wave — you can identify those heat-tolerant colonies.
On a mostly clear afternoon in July, days before the typhoon grazed Palau, I boated out to a shallow reef with Steve Palumbi, a marine ecologist at Stanford University. He’s tall and thin and has white hair that he often pulls back into a short ponytail.
Once the boat dropped its anchor in the sand, Palumbi and I jumped in, along with three researchers from the Palau International Coral Reef Center (PICRC). I felt like I was swimming in a tropical fish tank. The water was clear and full of silvery fish. A carpet of colorful coral coated the seafloor. Every hole and crevice was occupied — by a giant clam, a spiky starfish, a sea cucumber, a furry crab. The reef was a giant apartment building with a cast of unusual tenants.
I followed Palumbi and the PICRC researchers over to metal structures on the reef that his team had built. They looked like sunken bed frames, and like those metal stars, they were covered in pieces of coral.
These corals are some of Palumbi’s guinea pigs.
Over the last two years, researchers in his lab at Stanford have been subjecting them to a variety of different heat tests and scoring their performance. The concept is simple: Put the corals in a tank, crank up the temperature, and measure how quickly each one bleaches. The colonies that stay colorful as the temperature soars — the “winners” — may be more tolerant to warming.
Why are some corals more heat-tolerant than others?
For years, scientists have been chipping away at this question. We now know, for example, that a polyp’s genetics has something to do with it; like height in humans, heat-tolerance is partly heritable and can be passed on from parents to their kids. The specific kind of algae living in the coral tissue — its solar power-plant partner — matters, too.
Yet there are still big unknowns. Scientists still don’t know exactly how the genes of polyps and algae may combine in some way to influence tolerance. In search of answers, a researcher in Palumbi’s lab, Brendan Cornwell, is running corals through heat tests, and then examining the genomes of the winners and losers in search of clues.
There are several different ways to measure a coral’s tolerance to warming in a lab. Some tests expose corals to moderately high temperatures over weeks, whereas others blast them with extreme heat over days, or even hours. Longer-lasting tests tend to better represent a natural heat wave — what corals will actually face in the years to come. But they’re expensive, time-consuming, and require expertise. That’s a problem for people who are racing to rebuild damaged reefs, especially in poor regions that lack fancy marine labs and funding.
Working with PICRC, the Nature Conservancy, and other partners, Palumbi’s lab has been trying to demonstrate that the quick and cheap version of these heat tests — using picnic coolers to pressure-test corals over a few days — works well enough. They can help identify heat-tolerant corals and, thus, improve reef restoration, all within one work week, and on a low budget.
That afternoon, Palumbi was collecting corals from those metal frames to test at PICRC. Using wire cutters, Palumbi and the other researchers snapped off branches of coral from the individual colonies. Breaking fragments of coral off a colony is not unlike taking clippings from plants — the “donor” colony continues to grow, even as parts of it are removed.
After filling plastic bins with dozens of coral fragments across three species, the researchers brought them to the boat, loaded them into a large container full of seawater, and then we headed back to shore.
It is hard to put a price tag on coral reefs, but those who have tried say it is quite a lot.
The authors of one study published in 2024 estimated that reefs in the Asia Pacific, which includes Palau, Australia, and Indonesia, among other countries, contribute about $25 billion a year on average to the region’s economies for their role in supporting fisheries and tourism alone.
That doesn’t include the damage that reefs offset during tropical storms. Coral reefs are self-regenerating seawalls that can reduce wave energy — dulling the fiercest brunt of a hurricane making landfall, for example — by an average of 97 percent. In the US, economists estimate that reefs save the country more than $1.8 billion a year just in avoided flood damage. Globally, the cost savings from coral reefs are far higher.
So it’s no surprise that people are so eager to rebuild reefs when they collapse.
To restore these ecosystems, people typically harvest fragments of coral from the wild and grow them in a tank on land or in a “nursery” in the ocean. Then they plant them, one piece at a time, on the seafloor, often using an adhesive putty.
Reef restoration has grown into a global project of enormous scale: A network called the Coral Restoration Consortium counts more than 900 reef restoration efforts worldwide led by more than 350 organizations. By one estimate, groups have spent more than $250 million on reef restoration over roughly the last decade.
But as important as those efforts may be, many of them haven’t worked — they haven’t actually helped coral reefs grow back. “Show me a square mile of reef that has been [successfully] restored,” Palumbi said. “There isn’t one.”
At the heart of that failure is climate change: Prolonged bleaching kills off much of the planted coral, undoing a tremendous amount of effort.
One of the most extreme examples of this is in Florida. In the last three decades, organizations have planted tens of thousands of corals in the Florida Keys, which is home to the world’s third-largest barrier reef. I visited in 2022 and saw the progress of restoration firsthand — there were beautiful fields of planted staghorn and elkhorn, two federally threatened coral species. Some colonies were more than a meter wide. I wrote a story about how it was reviving Florida’s reef.
Then in summer 2023, a record-breaking heat wave struck. The reefs turned a ghostly white. And eventually, nearly all of the staghorn and elkhorn coral in the Florida Keys — including the vast swaths of replanted corals — died, becoming functionally extinct. It was one of the more devastating things I’ve seen in my time covering the biodiversity crisis.
There are similar examples from around the world — in Colombia and Costa Rica, for example, along with Indonesia and the Seychelles.
It’s not that restoration groups are unaware of this problem. Scientists have been studying bleaching for many years in search of solutions. In Florida, researchers are testing out what happens if you cross-breed corals from South Florida with colonies from a warm reef in Honduras, which have a natural ability to withstand higher temperatures. Perhaps their hybrid babies will be more likely to survive the next heat wave. But most of these approaches are time-intensive, costly, run by teams of PhDs, or stuck in the lab.
“The lab science is cool,” Palumbi told me. “But it’s going too slowly. We don’t have time to wait.”
The outdoor research space at PICRC looked like a typical marine lab — a labyrinth of pipes and pumps and, of course, tanks full of sea creatures, which in this case included corals, urchins, and giant clams that would abruptly close if you got too close. It looked appropriately science-y. With the exception of one wooden shelf. On it were eight blue and red plastic picnic coolers, in which Palumbi’s team is doing the bulk of its heat testing.
After returning to shore with bins full of coral fragments, Palumbi put some of them into the coolers, which were fitted with small heaters and pumps. The water inside was around 30 degrees C (86 degrees F). That’s the average high temperature for waters in this region, and the baseline for the test he was about to run.
Then Palumbi, rather unceremoniously, cranked up the dial.
Over each of the next four days, the water in half of the coolers would hit a higher temperature, before returning to the baseline of 30 degrees. On day one, for example, it would reach 34; on day two, it would hit 35; and so on. And each morning, Palumbi would assess the fragments for bleaching. Although these tests run for only a few days, they’re meant to mimic what some corals might experience at low tide during a heat wave, Palumbi said.
I visited the lab early one morning, after just one day of heat stress — after the coolers had reached 34 degrees. Palumbi laid the fragments out on a white grid to evaluate their color, ranking them from one (no bleaching) to five (fully bleached). They were shaped like twigs and still had their normal orangy brown color. No bleaching yet. By the next morning, however, the corals appeared more varied: Some were starting to pale and others remained saturated.
On the last morning of the test — after the coolers had reached 37 degrees, or close to 100 degrees F — nearly all the fragments were white, resembling cauliflower florets. They had expelled their algae. And yet a handful of the fragments still appeared mostly brown. Even after getting blasted by extreme heat, they hadn’t bleached.
“Those are the champions,” Palumbi said.
Palumbi believes that quick heat tests like this stand to benefit restoration projects across the tropics. The equipment, including four coolers, costs less than $1,000, according to Courtney Klepac, a researcher in Palumbi’s lab, who studies heat testing. Groups that are rebuilding reefs can essentially run the corals they harvest through these tests, and then only plant the champions.
That’s precisely the idea behind a project Klepac leads called the Coral Futures Academy. She’s been helping environmental groups across the Pacific integrate these low-overhead heat tests into local reef restoration efforts. And these actually include the coral garden I snorkeled during the typhoon: All the pieces of coral there had gone through similar heat tests.
As promising as this approach sounds, however, there is an important caveat: These tests are only useful if they actually predict which corals are more likely to survive under real-world warming. And so far, scientists haven’t proven that.
Previous studies comparing short heat tests to those that are longer and more faithfully replicate a real heat wave show mixed results; the winners of one are often not the winners of the other. It suggests that surviving a short blast of heat requires different skills than withstanding warmth that lasts for weeks.
Some researchers have also measured what happens to corals that went through an even faster one-day test after they were put in the ocean and then experienced a real heat wave. The champions in those rapid tests were not always more heat-tolerant in the wild.
Ilan Bubb, a marine biologist at the University of Amsterdam who’s studied heat tests, says it’s like trying to predict a person’s marathon time based on how well they perform in a sprint. “We know there’s some correlation there, but how good is that correlation?” he said. “How much information you can get about that marathon from a hundred-meter sprint is still just undetermined.”
Palumbi, Klepac, and their colleagues have been exploring this question, too. They’ve compared bleaching scores from heat tests that last for three or four days to those that last for roughly two weeks. The results appear to be similar, Klepac said: On average, the same corals resisted or succumbed to bleaching in both experiments.
Klepac has also studied what happens to heat-tested corals when an actual marine heat wave hits. At the coral garden I visited with those metal stars, PICRC researchers planted the heat-test winners as well as the poorer performers, as a point of comparison. And as Klepac’s unpublished research shows, the winners of the short heat tests survived better during a bleaching event in Palau in 2024, compared to the losers.
“I am probably one of the few people that you will talk to that kind of low-key gets a little excited for bleaching events,” Klepac told me. “It is a very true test of what we’ve been doing. If we’re trying to market this approach, I want to feel confident that what we’re prescribing actually works.”
There are other drawbacks to this testing approach. For one, it relies on a visible trait — whether a coral resists bleaching or not. That trait, however, doesn’t always indicate whether the coral has the genes to resist bleaching. The colony may have just been healthier going into the test than its peers. Two runners, for example, might get different times in a 100-meter sprint, not just because of their genes but because of how much rest they got the night before.
This matters when you’re trying to rebuild a reef: Typically, you want the coral colonies you plant to eventually reproduce and create heat-tolerant babies. That only happens if the parents have heat-tolerant genes.
And there are other traits that corals need to survive, beyond the ability to withstand warming.
“It’s not just about heat tolerance,” said Liam Lachs, a coral researcher at University of Queensland in Australia who has extensively studied the value of different heat tests.

By only planting the corals that perform well on these heat tests, you might miss colonies that have other important strengths, such as the ability to withstand disease. In fact, future research may reveal that testing corals for one of these other traits may ultimately be a better predictor of their survival in the era of climate change, says James Guest, a reef ecologist at Newcastle University in England.
Palumbi readily admits that the short picnic cooler tests are not perfect. But the important question, he says, is whether they are good enough — good enough to start using them now to help reefs as the science around fitness testing gradually improves.
That much is clear, he says, and several other researchers I spoke to agreed. While the utility and accuracy of short heat tests is not yet proven, people who want to rebuild reefs should still use them, they said. For restoration, there simply aren’t many better alternatives.
“It’s quick, it’s easy to do, people can apply it relatively straightforwardly, and it offers some kind of test,” Guest told me. “Coming up with these practical approaches makes sense.”
The sun was still low in the sky as Palumbi and I strapped on our tanks and weights and plunged into the ocean near one of Palau’s floating islands.
Sinking down felt like descending onto an alien planet. There were rolling hills of branching coral and stacks of plate coral the size of merry-go-rounds. Schools of colorful fish flew over them, like flocks of birds across a woodland.
Toward the end of the dive, we came across a single coral colony as large as a suburban home. The surface was lumpy and covered in what looked like large bulbous fingers. Given its size, the coral was likely at least three hundred years old.
When we were back on the boat, I asked Palumbi what he thought of the reef. “It doesn’t get better than this,” he said.
Isn’t it arrogant to think we can recreate, or even fortify, something as complex as a coral reef?
There could have been 200 species of coral on this one reef alone, Palumbi said, some of which may still be unknown to science. If this is what coral reefs are supposed to look like, even our best science probably can’t recreate them.
It seems like our time would be far better spent trying to prevent reefs like this from dying in the first place. “We all know that we have to solve the bigger problem,” Guest said. “If we don’t reduce carbon emissions and we don’t deal with climate change, nothing we do is going to help corals.”
But the way Guest and other scientists see it, restoration — and the science to improve it — is not about recreating thriving coral reefs. The goal is much more humble, and much more depressing: to prevent as many species and reefs as possible from disappearing altogether so that, if and when the planet cools back down, there’s still something left to regrow.
Reef restoration encompasses a broad range of approaches, Guest said, meant to “stop species and populations from going off into an extinction vortex.” It would seem anything that might help that cause even a little bit — including a handful of plastic picnic coolers — is worth a try.

Liverpool's midfield is fragile - will they act in the window?

A little over four minutes had passed at St James' Park on Sunday and Liverpool had started encouragingly, keeping the ball well and with urgency in their play.
Ryan Gravenberch created space with a brilliant touch to get past Lewis Miley but instead of shooting from the edge of the box or playing Dominik Szoboszlai through, the Netherlands international lost possession.
Just 11 seconds later, Newcastle were ahead through Anthony Elanga after a devastating counter that required one pass after Amar Dedic's initial clearance.
Liverpool simply had no structure when out of possession. It was schoolboy stuff and a nightmare start for Andoni Iraola.
It was a similar story in the second half when Gravenberch was dispossessed after trying a back heel on the edge of the Newcastle box.
This time, Yoane Wissa went on a brilliant run through the centre - evading an array of Liverpool players - and played the ball to Joe Willock, who finished in style.
As Iraola alluded to after, perhaps one of his players should have had the know how to commit a foul in that situation but Liverpool were punished again.
Looking back on both goals, Gravenberch's decision-making should have been better and perhaps the centre-back pairing of Virgil van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet could have engaged quicker rather than holding off.
But having a defensive midfielder stationed accordingly would, in all likelihood, have nullified the threat.
Liverpool have not had an out-and-out number six since Fabinho, who left in 2023, and as it stands Iraola's preference is a two-man pivot in midfield with Florian Wirtz playing as a number 10.
Both of those two midfielders, Gravenberch and Szoboszlai, were in the Newcastle box when Liverpool lost possession before Elanga's opener.
If Liverpool are to be taken seriously, they simply cannot concede goals like that regularly.
'It's just not personnel' - Iraola
Iraola tends to avoid major debriefs in the dressing room after a game, with his personal preference to speak to the players a day later.
Asked in his post-match news conference about what could be done to prevent the kind of goals his side conceded, the Liverpool head coach suggested that it was not due to the type or identity of midfielders he had selected.
"I think it's just not personnel," said Iraola. "I understand you are telling me basically that Ryan Gravenberch is the six and he is on the edge of the box - but if he shoots and he scores we are saying what a play from Ryan Gravenberch."
It was an interesting point, given that Gravenberch produced the assist for Cody Gakpo's equaliser.
But shortly after Newcastle went 2-1 up, Iraola reacted by bringing on Alexis Mac Allister for Wirtz and Liverpool did seem more stable defensively - even if the Argentina international prefers to play as an eight.
Szoboszlai made zero tackles and won three of his 10 duels (30%) while Gravenberch similarly failed to make a tackle and won four of his 10 duels (40%).
When Mac Allister came on, he made two tackles and won four of his five duels (80%).
"We have to adapt as a team to these situations and we have to know that these situations can happen," added Iraola.
"I think the second goal, we probably did better in terms of having the numbers to defend - we don't make the foul, or go to the first challenge or probably reduce the distance with the ball carrier, so it's an incredible goal.
"Situations [are] just not because one person is playing there, [it] is something that we have to correct between a lot of players."
At full-time, the xG was 1.43 to Newcastle and 2.73 to Liverpool - indicating Newcastle had ruthlessly seized their opportunities against Iraola's side.
Will Liverpool act before the window ends?
On Sky Sports, former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge did not hold back in his criticism.
"Liverpool do not have that profile of player right now." said Sturridge. "The team has needed a defensive midfielder for three years. If you analyse the midfield, they are all naturally attacking players."
At Liverpool, the focus in the remaining days of the transfer window is clear. Their stance is unchanged in that the priority remains wide attacking players rather than midfield, even after the exit of Curtis Jones.
As always, if an opportunity presents itself in the market then Liverpool will consider it but Iraola is understood to be satisfied with his depth in midfield - with Wataru Endo, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell as the back-up options.
Liverpool have previously enquired about Adam Wharton but Crystal Palace's stance is that the 22-year-old is not for sale.
Under Jurgen Klopp, Liverpool tried to get Moises Caicedo in 2023 and when Arne Slot arrived in 2024, Liverpool were keen on signing Martin Zubimendi from Real Sociedad.
But that fell through when the now-Arsenal midfielder turned the move down.
Gravenberch had a brilliant season under Slot as Liverpool cruised their way to the Premier League title, perhaps masking the issues temporarily by covering over emerging cracks.
Liverpool's summer window 12 months ago then became about super-charging their attack with Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike, rather than reinforcing the middle of the pitch.
Those fault lines are much clearer now and Iraola will know that his midfield must become harder to break down or else his side will keep on conceding.

No lead poisoning in children linked to infant formula scare: health authorities
Officials say all 237 children are healthy after consuming Friso batch flagged by Macau authorities
Hong Kong health authorities have confirmed that no child showed signs of poisoning after drinking a batch of infant formula found to contain excessive levels of lead.
The Department of Health gave an update on Wednesday, a month after Macau authorities alerted the public that a batch of Frisolac Prestige Stage 1 infant formula, manufactured by the Dutch company Royal FrieslandCampina, might contain lead levels exceeding permissible limits.
The department said its dedicated hotline and the maternal and child health centres had received 762 relevant inquiries.
Health officers provided advice on switching infant formula and referred 446 babies and young children to public hospitals for assessment and follow-up. Among them, 237 had undergone clinical assessments.
“Results indicated that their overall health is good and that none have shown signs of lead poisoning,” the department said.
The rest are either pending assessment or the parents have decided not to proceed with check-ups, it added.

A former Armenian president is detained in a corruption investigation
Armenia's Anti-Corruption Committee says former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son have been detained after law enforcement officers raided businesses linked to the family
YEREVAN, Armenia -- Former Armenian President Robert Kocharyan and his eldest son were detained Tuesday after law enforcement officers raided businesses linked to the family, the country’s Anti-Corruption Committee said.
A case was opened against Kocharyan, 71, who leads parliament’s second-largest opposition bloc, on charges of abuse of authority, bribery and large-scale money laundering, according to Armenia’s Prosecutor General’s Office.
Besides Kocharyan and his eldest son, Sedrak, four other people were detained as part of the investigation, the office said.
The raids came less than 24 hours after Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan clashed with Kocharyan’s younger son, Levon, in a fiery exchange in parliament.
Armenia’s Anti-Corruption Committee said it was investigating allegations that state assets had been illegally sold to private companies for under market value during Kocharyan’s time in office from 1998 to 2008.
His successor, former President Serzh Sargsyan, also was summoned to the Anti-Corruption Committee headquarters, Armenian media outlets reported.
Bagrat Mikoyan, who heads his office, described the detentions as “yet another attack on President Kocharyan and his family” by authorities. He added that Kocharyan felt ill after his detention and was taken to a hospital.
During a parliamentary question-and-answer session, Levon Kocharyan accused Pashinyan of pressuring the courts and law enforcement agencies to open investigations against individuals.
Pashinyan responded by asking Levon Kocharyan the source of his family’s wealth, saying that any assets acquired at public expense should be returned to the state.
In a social media post Tuesday, Robert Kocharyan's Armenia Alliance said the case was one of personal vengeance and “another cynical manifestation of a regime that has lost its legitimacy."
"This is not a legal process; this is the open subjugation of the state apparatus," it said.
Robert Kocharyan went on trial in 2019, accused of ordering the illegal use of force by security officers against demonstrators protesting alleged fraud in the 2008 presidential election. At least 10 people were killed in the clashes. The charges were later dropped, and the legal proceedings ended in 2021.
Analyst Alexander Iskandaryan, director of the Caucasus Institute in Yerevan, told The Associated Press that critics have long accused Kocharyan of corruption while in power.
He said the case will intensify the conflict between the pro-Russian opposition, where Kocharyan is a key figure, and Pashinyan's government, which is pursuing a pro-Western course and prioritizing closer ties with the European Union.
“Of course, this is a signal to the Kremlin," Iskandaryan said. “Kocharyan effectively positions himself as a Russian proxy, and we see a trend where the authorities have begun to fight — intensively and by all possible means — against political forces aligned with Russia.”

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.

Thousands of people in northern Japan joined forces on Wednesday to help return a 400-tonne castle tower to its original location, pulling it along with ropes while chanting together. The main tower of Hirosaki Castle was moved 80 metres (262 feet) in 2015 to enable repairs to the stone walls beneath it.
Rather than dismantling the three-storey wooden structure, engineers lifted it intact and moved it along metal rails to a temporary platform.
Since Saturday, thousands have taken turns pulling the tower forward by just a few centimetres at a time. Local authorities estimate that roughly 4,000 people, including participants from overseas, have taken part in the operation so far.
Their combined efforts have shifted the structure by almost five metres.
"It's like trying to move a mountain," said 56-year-old Hirosaki resident Takahiro Kogawa, speaking to AFP after spending several minutes pulling the heavy structure in the heat.
Among those who joined the effort was Azusa Nimiya, a 46-year-old history and castle enthusiast who travelled from Shimane, located on the opposite side of Japan's main island.
"It's the experience of a lifetime, a precious and unique memory," she said.
The municipality plans to bring in heavy machinery in September to finish moving the tower. Officials are targeting November for its permanent installation at the site.
Further restoration will then be carried out on the castle's copper roof and facades. The landmark, which dates back to the Edo period (1603-1868), is expected to fully reopen to visitors in 2033.
The restoration project has deliberately involved members of the public in the traditional moving process.
"By involving the public, "we wanted everyone to be able to experience history physically," said Kensuke Hayasaka, who heads the restoration project.
"It's extremely significant for passing on the history of Hirosaki to future generations," he told AFP.
The castle tower has a long history of being moved. Lightning destroyed the structure in the 17th century, after which it was rebuilt in the early 19th century.
Several decades later, concerns over the stability of its stone foundations led authorities to move the tower again, this time using human strength. It was eventually returned to its original location in 1915.
The latest operation is being carried out using a traditional Japanese method known as "hikiya", which involves moving buildings and other structures using human power.
"This large-scale, human-powered operation, known as "hikiya", "is a traditional technique for moving structures that has existed in Japan since ancient times," Hayasaka explained.
He said the project aims to protect the historic structure while ensuring that the main tower is firmly secured to its foundations before heavy snowfall arrives in the region during winter.
"Our goal is to preserve this unique heritage, while ensuring that the main tower is securely fixed to its base before the first snowfall," he said.
Hayasaka also described the completion of the project as an emotional moment after years of planning and work.
"Seeing all these discussions and the methods devised by our predecessors and our teams finally come to fruition this year is extremely moving. We feel a profound sense of accomplishment," he added.
Among the most enthusiastic participants was 82-year-old Katsumi Terada, who joined the effort with two Japanese flags tucked into his headband.
Terada had also taken part in the castle's previous relocation 11 years ago. He recalled wondering at the time whether he would live long enough to see the historic tower returned to its original position.
"I wondered then, with some anxiety, if I would still be around to see it return to its base. But look, I persevered. I'm alive and well."
(With inputs from news agency AFP)

VC firm Lightspeed Venture Partners has exited edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW), minting ₹549.7 Cr from the sale of 4.67 Cr shares via block and bulk deals today. According to market data, the firm, via its holding entity Lightspeed Opportunity Fund II sold the shares at weighted average trade price of ₹117.72 apiece, a 6.7% discount to the stock’s closing price today. The investor held 1.61% stake or 4,66,98,120 shares in PW as of June 30, 2026. With the offloading today, Lightspeed has completely exited from the edtech bet. ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund emerged as the largest buyer, acquiring 2.2 Cr shares worth ₹259 Cr, or nearly half of the volume sold. Among the other buyers, Goldman Sachs picked up 89 Lakh shares across five different entities, while Ghisallo Master Fund, Societe Generale and Morgan Stanley Asia also lapped up chunks of stake in the company. Lightspeed first invested in PW during its $210 Mn Series B funding round in September 2024. It owned 1.79% stake in the company at the time of its public listing in November. Although Lightspeed, like PW’s other institutional investors WestBridge Capital, Hornbill Capital and GSV Ventures, didn’t partake in the OFS component of the IPO, it lowered its stake slightly since then. PW’s other major backer WestBridge Capital’s nominee director, Sandeep Singhal, resigned earlier last week “due to his other professional and personal commitments”. The edtech major raised up to ₹3,100 Cr while promoters Alakh Pandey and Prateek Maheshwari sold shares worth ₹380 Cr via the IPO. After making a stellar public markets debut, the company’s stock hasn’t had a smooth sailing. While the scrip is currently trading 12% lower than its opening price of ₹143.10, the stock has gone as low as ₹77.75. The performance could be attributed to the fact that the company hasn’t been able to turn profitable till now, despite reducing its net loss significantly since listing. For the full FY26, the edtech company cut its net loss by 90% to ₹24.2 Cr from ₹243.3 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue surged 35% YoY to ₹3,899.5 Cr. The company continued to be in the red, reporting a net loss of ₹88.3 Cr in Q1 FY27. While it managed to trim its net loss by 30% YoY, PW turned EBITDA positive during the quarter, posting an EBITDA of ₹52 Cr and a margin of 4.9%. Its operating revenue crossed the ₹1,000 Cr mark, jumping 24.4% YoY and 15% QoQ to ₹1,054 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company also noted that its results were impacted by the postponement and subsequent re-examination of NEET UG, which resulted in a 28% plunge in online NEET collections. Shares of PhysicsWallah ended the day 3.91% higher at ₹126.10 apiece on the BSE.

We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built
Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences crave honest voices like hers.
Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character.
Parton’s self-construction project began in her childhood. She was born the fourth of 12 kids in a tiny cabin in Pittman Center, Tennessee. Her parents were so poor that they paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. As a girl, she sang songs on her porch into a fake mic fashioned from a tin can and a tobacco stick, envisioning herself at the Grand Ole Opry. Her talent drew attention from local radio and TV personalities, and by age 13, she was singing on the real Opry stage.
The craftiness and self-consciousness that came from growing up impoverished shaped her outlook for life. As she’d sing in her 1971 song “Coat of Many Colors”—her signature (and favorite) hit—her mother used to sew rags into garments that the young Parton would flaunt at school. Mockery from other kids taught her the lesson in self-determination that she’d turn into one of her defining lyrics: “One is only poor only if they choose to be.” As a young woman, she modeled her fashion off a “town tramp”—as she later put it—whom she’d grown up around. Her preacher grandfather whipped her for dressing that way, but to her, women with heels and push-up bras weren’t trashy; they were glamorous and confident.
A fascination with stereotypes—with fulfilling them and subverting them—gave her an edge when she moved to Nashville. In 1966, her first solo hit, “Dumb Blonde” (written by Curly Putman), saw her singing that despite her looks, she “ain’t nobody’s fool.” On the TV variety series The Porter Wagoner Show, she played the aw-shucks second fiddle to the titular star even as she wrote songs that outcompeted Wagoner’s music. Her 1970 hit “Joshua” spun a tale in which the narrator approaches a mean-looking backwoods hermit, someone whom the rest of the town fears, only to realize that he has a heart of gold. It was an example of how her penchant for social criticism and her interest in flipping expectations made her songwriting stand out.
She left Wagoner behind in 1974 to court an audience that transcended country music. Her songs sparkled with fun production touches, clever lyrical twists, and melodies that seemed at once as winding as a lazy river and as smartly constructed as good Levi’s. For 1980’s “9 to 5,” the sound of her fingernail clicks did as much work as the lyrics—and the movie the song accompanied—in celebrating the hustle of women at work. “Jolene,” her enduring ballad of jealousy, built itself around a chorus so plaintive that it seemed surely scraped from a harrowing chapter of Parton’s own life—but she was quick, in interviews, to say that the song’s story was more or less fiction.
As she settled into icon status, she seemed to revel in the franchisability of her image: Dolly Parton was an idea that everyone could benefit from. She founded a theme park in her home state, selling a blend of rustic realness and fun kitsch. She only ever seemed tickled that Whitney Houston’s cover of “I Will Always Love You” eclipsed Parton’s original in eminence. She made childhood literacy the central focus of her philanthropic efforts—another subversion of the “dumb blonde” image (and one that channeled her upbringing by a father who couldn’t read).
In recent years, Parton’s persona has come to take on political significance. She was, as my colleague David Graham has written, the rare public figure who seemed beloved by both red and blue America. She maintained that status through careful circumspection regarding partisan politics. But when it came to questions about sexuality and identity, she took a stand by repeatedly supporting gay, trans, and gender-nonconforming people. After all, she once told RuPaul, she herself was a drag queen.
Many of the most important stories in music this decade owe a lot to Parton. Sabrina Carpenter has brought Dolly-style humor (and hair) back to the charts; Beyoncé enlisted Parton to play emcee on her 2024 album, Cowboy Carter; Ella Langley is blending backwoods scenery with wry, shrugging wisdom that recalls Parton’s catalog. But Parton set an example bigger than music—by showing how to take the scraps you were given and stitch them into something bright and new.

'To avoid scandal': Unearthed letters show how N.L. bishop handled allegations in Baie Verte
Insurance company believes therapy records can show who knew what, and when
The first letter is dated March 31, 1970.
Father Leonard Joseph Kelly was told to leave his parish in a hurry. The bishop could see no other option.
“It seems that you have been committing these acts over a long period,” reads the letter from John Michael O’Neill, then the bishop of Grand Falls. “You should make immediate preparations to leave Baie Verte permanently. To avoid scandal, you can say that you have not been feeling well and need medical care.”
The wording is ambiguous. The bishop never spells out exactly what the priest has done. He refers to it only as a “problem” far more “deep-seated” than was previously known.
O’Neill asks Kelly for frankness and honesty — and underscores his desire for secrecy.
“I thought of calling a meeting of the consultors but decided against it for fear that something might [get] out,” O’Neill wrote.
Rather than alert authorities, newly unearthed letters show the bishop referred the priest to the Southdown Institute — a controversial therapy centre near Toronto, where priests have been treated for a range of issues from alcoholism and depression to pedophilia for decades.
These letters, discovered in Kelly’s personnel file at the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls, are now at the centre of an uncommon legal action in central Newfoundland.
The church's own insurance provider is seeking a Norwich order — an exceptional move compelling a third party to hand over vital documents that could lead to a lawsuit against another entity.
In this case, Guardian Insurance is asking a judge to compel the Southdown Institute to turn over its files on Kelly to find out exactly why he was admitted there in 1970.
Guardian believes the records could show the church knew Kelly was a risk to children before entering into an insurance policy in the 1980s. Those records could lead to another court action, in which Guardian would seek to avoid covering the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls for Kelly’s abuses during its policy period due to material non-disclosure or misrepresentation.
I cannot be expected to condone the seriousness of his betrayal of confidence and the terrible scandal which, but for the discretion of the family involved, could have blighted the whole life of the church in this small province.- Bishop John Michael O'Neill
The church is currently facing a lawsuit, filed in 2022, accusing Kelly of sexual abuse in Gander.
The plaintiff alleged he was “subjected to regular and frequent forced oral sex and occasionally other invasive sexual touching by Kelly” between 1977 and 1983, when he was between the ages of six and 12.
Kelly was also convicted of sexually assaulting a pair of 12-year-old boys in the mid-1980s. A provincial court judge sentenced him to two years of probation, contingent on him returning to the Southdown Institute for treatment.
The province’s court of appeal found that to be inappropriate, and instead sent Kelly to jail on a four-month sentence in 1988.
Bishop credited family’s ‘discretion’ in avoiding scandal
The Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls is the church’s corporate body overseeing larger centres such as Grand Falls-Windsor and Gander, while also serving dozens of smaller churches dotting rural outports throughout the island.
Father Kelly — who hailed from Windsor — was ordained in 1955. He was welcomed to the priesthood by Bishop O’Neill at a ceremony in his hometown in front of 500 people “eager to honour the young cleric,” according to an article published by the Advertiser on June 9, 1955.
It’s not clear when he moved to Baie Verte.
Three months after being told to leave the parish, Bishop O’Neill began exchanging letters with the Southdown Institute about Kelly’s progress. The first letter quotes from a psychiatric evaluation conducted after his admission, referring to his actions as “rather pathetic homosexual adventures” fuelled by alcoholism.
“I do not feel the sexual episodes will cause any future difficulties if this priest is successful in his attempt to separate himself from alcohol,” it reads.
The person evaluating Kelly recommended he return to the priesthood in the Diocese of Grand Falls.
“It is felt that when returned to the ministry, Father Kelly should not be removed from the diocese since sexual problems play only a small role in his total inability to adjust. Rather than being removed from the home diocese, he should be given considerable support in his attempt to attack his central alcoholic difficulties.”
Bishop O’Neill responded two weeks later, pushing back on the idea.
“It must be obvious to him, as it is to me, that he was lucky to get out of Baie Verte with his name unsullied,” O’Neill wrote. “There could well have been a court case with all its ugly implications. Even he should realize that it is not merely a case of taking up where he left off.”
Father Kelly letters (PDF KB)
Father Kelly letters (Text KB)CBC is not responsible for 3rd party content
The bishop suggested Kelly should be moved to Halifax on a temporary basis.
“While my sympathy goes out to Father Kelly, as it would to any poor priest in trouble, I cannot be expected to condone the seriousness of his betrayal of confidence and the terrible scandal which, but for the discretion of the family involved, could have blighted the whole life of the church in this small province.”
The response — authored by Southdown’s executive director, John Kelly — came close to spelling out the nature of the complaint against the priest, without explicitly stating it.
“I am keenly aware that his conduct could have created wide-spread scandal and I am grateful that this was avoided,” the director wrote. “The more we see of Father Kelly, the more we become convinced that he can make a good recovery. His motivation is good and it becomes increasingly apparent that prolonged drinking had removed, as it frequently does, the restraints which normally he would have exercised in his relationships with the boys in question.”
He goes on to suggest they find Father Kelly an assignment close to the Southdown Institute in Ontario, so they can keep an eye on him before returning to Newfoundland.
O’Neill obliged, and conveyed the message to Father Kelly on July 30, 1970. They’d start him in Ontario, he said, before moving him to Halifax with the goal of working his way back to Newfoundland.
“It is apparent you were a very sick and mixed up priest,” O’Neill wrote. “As it is, we are all fortunate that the situation did not become public with irreparable damage to the Church and the priesthood. Now, fortunately, all that is past and I am happy to forget the whole thing and look forward to your future work in the holy Priesthood.”
Kelly’s personnel file shows he took up a pastoral assignment in Gander in 1977, before moving home to Grand Falls-Windsor in 1983.
O’Neill died in 1974. He didn’t live to see the consequences of his decision to “forget the whole thing.”
Court filing seeks to uncover Winter Commission mystery
Kelly was part of the first wave of Catholic clergy and Christian Brothers to face criminal charges in the late 1980s. What began as a trickle turned into a flood of allegations, prompting the Archbishop of St. John’s, Alphonsus Penney, to call for a commission of inquiry.
"It's a great mystery to me how such a thing could go on for so long without somebody blowing the whistle,” Penney told CBC News in 1989.
The Winter Commission report was released in 1990, and found allegations of sexual misconduct spanned back as far as at least 1975 — when Penney himself sent a priest from the Diocese of Grand Falls to the Southdown Institute over allegations of pedophilia. Penney did not report the priest to authorities, and the Winter Commission did not uncover the priest’s name.
Guardian Insurance is now asking the court to compel Southdown to turn over its records on the unnamed priest, as well as Father Leonard Joseph Kelly.
“Guardian has a reasonable basis to believe that the offending priest was Kelly, or alternatively another Grand Falls priest whose attendance at Southdown was precipitated by inappropriate interactions with a child, thus the priests’ identification in the Southdown records would be material to Guardian’s coverage investigation,” the company’s application reads.
The Winter Commission found church officials in Newfoundland and Labrador relied on Southdown for a range of reasons, starting with the unnamed priest in 1975.
The letters unearthed by Guardian Insurance show that reliance existed at least five years earlier than previously known.
In total, the Winter Commission report referenced five Newfoundland priests who were sent to Southdown, including four who were accused of inappropriate relationships with minors.
“The Southdown facility seems to have been seen as a quick fix for nearly any kind of behavioural problem,” the report reads.
The Southdown Institute still operates today, offering psychotherapy, counselling and spiritual direction to clergy, lay pastoral ministers and “all adults who consider faith and spirituality to be integral to their lives.”
Lawyers for Guardian Insurance, Southdown and the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Grand Falls were in court earlier this month for a brief appearance. A hearing on the application will be held on Jan. 26, 2027.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
