Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday (August 22, 2026) spoke about the growing tendency among people to turn to the internet and ChatGPT to diagnose their ailments, and, on a lighter note, narrated how patients in rural areas often describe symptoms to doctors in ways that can make diagnosis challenging.
Addressing the inauguration of a Mahajan Imaging and Labs facility here, Mr. Singh said people now often search their symptoms online before visiting a doctor.
"Now ChatGPT has also come. Whatever happens, the first thing people do is to search online," he said, adding that increased awareness about one's health was a positive development but also posed a challenge.
Mr. Singh said a person experiencing mild chest pain could search the symptom online and soon conclude that he was suffering from a "serious" heart disease, although such pain could also result from anxiety or muscle-related problems.
He said patients sometimes reached doctors not merely with their symptoms but with the diagnosis they had arrived at through internet searches.
"Instead of telling the doctor about the symptoms, the patient comes with his internet research and tells the doctor the name of the disease," Singh said.
Speaking on a lighter note, Singh said patients also sometimes described their problems to doctors in colloquial terms, particularly in rural areas.
He gave the example of a villager telling a doctor that he was experiencing "dhuk dhuk" in his chest.
"In the entire medical education, the doctor has never heard or studied about a symptom called 'dhuk dhuk'," Singh said, explaining that patients could find it difficult to accurately express what they were experiencing.
He said such situations made proper diagnostic testing even more important.
Singh also narrated another lighter moment involving a patient who had gone to a doctor after reading about his symptoms on the internet and said he believed he had "claustrophobia". The doctor then suggested "MRI scan" to begin the treatment and the patient instantly agreed.
The doctor responded that if he really had claustrophobia, he would not have agreed to undergo an MRI scan, Singh said.
The Defence Minister said these examples showed why "technology and medical expertise needed to work together".
He said modern machines could help doctors understand what was happening inside the human body, but there was still no machine that could understand what was going on in a patient's mind.
"Machines make diagnosis better, but understanding the patient, giving him confidence and courage can only be done by medical professionals," Singh said.
"Technology and emotion together make the medical profession unique," he said, stressing that doctors had to use their experience, sensitivity and compassion while treating patients.
Singh also underlined the growing responsibility of healthcare professionals as technology, AI and digital diagnostics expand.
He said diagnostic data was highly sensitive and protecting patients' health information and privacy was a primary responsibility.
He also called for transparency in the use of artificial intelligence, avoidance of bias and priority to patient safety.
"When a person comes for a test, he brings his anxiety, fear and hope. Protecting that trust is the biggest responsibility of everyone in healthcare," Singh said.
He stressed that there should be no unnecessary tests, wrong reports or incorrect diagnoses and patients should never feel that they were being treated merely as "a number".

Pakistan’s jailed former prime minister Imran Khan was briefly taken to a hospital in the country’s capital on supreme court orders after weeks of uproar about his deteriorating health.
Khan, 73, was transferred to the hospital in the early hours of Friday, but then moved back to Adiala prison in Rawalpindi after a few hours, a spokesperson for his party said on Friday.
Khan’s lawyers say his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye. The government has said medical reports disclosed no condition requiring immediate treatment.
Pakistan’s information minister said Khan was returned to prison after a “team of qualified doctors … declared him medically fit.”
In its order on Tuesday, after weeks of uproar about his worsening health, the supreme court told authorities to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within 48 hours and allow him access to a medical panel that includes his personal physician.
Security was beefed up in Islamabad, and hundreds of security personnel were posted around the hospital before Khan was taken there.
For months Khan’s party and family has been demanding he has access to specialist medical care.
In February, officials at Khan’s party said he was facing severe eye damage and had only 15% eyesight, and was being kept in solitary confinement. He was also being denied basic medical care and meetings with family and lawyers. The family eventually took the case to the supreme court.
For months, Adiala jail has been a protest site, where Khan’s family and dozens of protesters would gather to demand medical care for him and for him to be allowed to meet his sisters.
On Tuesday the judges said that they would involve an eye specialist for Khan’s treatment. The order read: “We are mindful of the constitutional and legal obligation … to safeguard the life, health, dignity and security of the prisoner.”
Khan’s party assured the judges that his supporters would not gather in front of the hospital and would allow treatment to go smoothly. In the early hours of Friday, Asad Qaiser, the former speaker of the national assembly and a close aide of Khan, wrote on X that it had been decided by the party that no worker would gather in front of the hospital after Khan is taken to Shifa.
He wrote “if anyone attempts to gather in front of the hospital and violating the party’s decision, he would have no affiliation with the party.”
Khan was arrested in 2023 and sentenced to three years in jail on corruption charges and disqualified from politics for five years.
Khan, who is facing more than 100 cases, was sentenced to 14 years in 2025 on corruption charges and accused of obtaining lucrative plots of land worth billions of rupees through a corrupt deal with a Pakistani property tycoon when he was the prime minister. Khan and his party denied the charges and said cases were politically motivated.
He was Pakistan’s cricket captain before becoming a politician, and served as the prime minister of Pakistan from 2018 to 2022. He was ousted in a vote of no confidence. Khan had enjoyed good relations with Pakistan’s powerful military before he came to power.
Once he was removed from office in 2022, he blamed the US for his removal initially and then Pakistan’s then army chief Gen Bajwa. Both have denied his accusations. After his brief arrest and release in May 2023, Khan in an interview with the Guardian accused Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir of harbouring a “personal grudge” against him and ordering his arrest and a crackdown on his party.

Gao Zhen, a prominent Chinese artist known for provocative sculptures of the former leader Mao Zedong, has been sentenced to three years in prison after being found guilty of slandering China’s “heroes and martyrs”. The sentencing came two years after he was detained while visiting the country with his family, according to his wife and human rights groups.
The case has attracted international condemnation, largely because the artworks at the centre of the case were created more than 10 years before China created the law under which Gao was charged.
The law, which bans defamation of China’s heroes and martyrs, came into force in March 2018. Courts have previously used the law to charge people who challenge official accounts of Chinese history.
Gao, 70, a Chinese citizen and US permanent resident, was detained on 26 August 2024 after returning to China with his wife and son. Police later raided his studio near Beijing.
In one of Gao’s most famous works, he depicts Mao kneeling. In another he portrays a firing squad made up of seven Mao statues pointing rifles at Jesus.
Gao’s wife, Zhao Yaliang, told the Guardian that the two years since her husband’s detention had been a painful ordeal for the family.
“His arrest and trial should never have happened. We have had no choice but to wait in anguish … I am very sad that it’s going to be this long,” she said after the verdict.
According to his wife, two of Gao’s relatives were allowed to enter the Sanhe city people’s court in Hebei province for the verdict, while she waited with their son and several friends outside.
“For two years he has suffered in the detention centre, while my son, our closest family members and I have also endured this torment,” she said.
Gao’s family said he had fainted in detention and was afflicted with back, knee and respiratory problems. His wife said Gao had sustained heatstroke during the summer and described experiencing a feeling of “being close to death”.
Weiquanwang, a human rights monitoring network, said Gao had been sentenced for “infringing the reputation and honour of heroes and martyrs”. The rights network said Gao’s studio and property had been sealed and that friends and supporters had been silenced.
Artworks made by Gao during his time in detention and seen by the Guardian include a series of colourful paper cuttings.
“A body can be confined, but clarity of mind is harder to take away. Mentally he remains remarkably sharp and unbroken,” said Gao’s younger brother Gao Qiang, who spent decades producing art with him as the Gao brothers.
“Art should never be a crime scene waiting to be discovered,” he said.
In a handwritten letter sent from detention to his young son, Gao wrote: “Dad’s eyesight isn’t very good, and I don’t have my glasses, so my handwriting isn’t very good.
“I hope I can finish my work as soon as possible and return to you and Mum,” he wrote. “Son, remember: Dad will always love you!”
Sophie Richardson, a longtime China human rights campaigner, said: “Gao has been prosecuted for conduct that has never been criminal, and his family has endured collective punishment at the hands of the authorities, and that is criminal.”
Sarah Brooks, the China director for Amnesty International, said the decision to sentence Gao to a maximum three-year prison term illustrated “the authorities’ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression”.
Gao’s wife and their young son have been unable to leave China since his detention. Human rights campaigners said his wife was stopped from travelling abroad based on national security grounds. His young son is a US citizen but has been unable to leave without his parents.
The Chinese foreign ministry was approached for comment.
Yu-chen Li contributed to reporting.

So, another Test match in Australia has finished within two days. This has happened four times there in the last few years. And we are yet to hear any criticism of the trampoline-bounce pitches that produce such results. The excuses will come thick and fast. ‘Oh, the groundsman, sorry, turf executive, got it wrong. He went by the weather forecast, which predicted some hot weather, so he left a little more grass, and that led to the excessive bounce.’ Or the other cricketing excuse that the batters didn’t have the technique to cope with the bounce and it wasn’t the fault of the pitch. This last excuse could be faintly accepted if the home team batters had batted well, but when even the home batters can’t stitch a run or a decent partnership together, then what does it tell you about the pitch?
The pitch in Mackay was no surprise. After the Aussies were humiliated by the Bangladeshis in the first Test, they were going to prepare a pitch that would be fast and bouncy. And, of course, claim that the groundsman had done it on his own and there were zero instructions from the team management. We all know what really happens. It’s just that the Indian management is open about wanting pitches to suit its bowling strength while those from the old powers will do the little whispering and nudging and get a surface that they need.
Bangladesh got Test status way back in the year 2000, but it was only after 23 years that Australia deemed it fit to invite them for a second Test series, and that too at their non-regular Test venues. India also had to wait for 20 years after its inaugural tour in 1947-48 for its second tour in 1967-68 and then another 10 years for its next tour Down Under. Thereafter, tours have been every four or five years, but now, with the TV revenues depending on whether India is touring the country or not, the old powers would love India to tour there every year if possible. That’s why there are split tours too, where there’s the red-ball series one year and the white-ball limited-overs series the following year. So, in a broadcast rights cycle of four years, there are two India tours, which bumps up the value of their broadcast rights manifold.
It will be interesting to see the report and rating for the Mackay pitch by the match referee. There’s generally been a desire among the referees to get brownie points from the media of the old powers, so it won’t be a surprise if there’s no adverse rating for the Mackay pitch just as we have seen for similar two-day finishes in recent years. But lo and behold, if a game finishes in three days in India, there will be all kinds of derogatory reports and insinuations made about the pitches, BCCI and Indian cricket. The hypocrisy is so brazen that it is simply mind-boggling. The usual excuse of ineptitude against fast bowling will be brought out. Nobody says the same when the overseas batters can’t play the spinning ball. Then there’s no lack of ability but hidden devils in the pitch.
Even today, that brainwashed thinking that a batter has to be judged by how he bats on fast, bouncy pitches prevails, while nobody even asks why lack of footwork, which is such an essential skill requirement to play spin bowling, is not considered a negative and all blame for lack of runs is put on the surface. Playing spin is a real test of batting skill, as it requires deft footwork and soft hands, while playing fast bowling basically has just two movements, either front foot or back foot. Yet lots of players with ordinary records in the subcontinent are called great by those from the old powers. Amazingly, their fast bowlers are never judged by their failure to take wickets on the so-called slow surfaces of the subcontinent. Batters not scoring runs on fast pitches are not rated, but their fast bowlers not getting wickets on slow surfaces still are called great.
Like I said earlier, the double standards are simply staggering. Let’s see what rating the match referee gives the Mackay pitch. But Indian fans, don’t hold your breath. The Aussies are breathing comfortably already, knowing there’s absolutely nothing for them to worry about.

Indian versions of Nestlé’s KitKat contain 4.5% cocoa solids, while the milk chocolate used in the Australian variant has at least 22% cocoa, according to a Reuters report. It also highlighted differences in Nestlé’s Maggi noodles, stating that all Maggi variants sold in India use palm oil, while several versions available in the UK are made with the more expensive sunflower oil. Despite many UK-sold Maggi packets being manufactured in India, they feature red front-of-pack labels indicating high salt levels, as per the Reuters investigation. According to the report, Revant Himatsingka, 34, a former McKinsey management consultant, has posted videos comparing the ingredients used in Nestlé’s KitKat sold in India with versions available in Europe and Australia, arguing that the Indian variants are less favourable. Himatsingka has amassed an audience of more than 5 million followers across YouTube and Instagram. The content creator is popularly known online as “Food Pharmer”. Himatsingka stated that many Indian consumers believe they are being offered lower-quality products. The Reuters report said growing consumer preferences are also prompting companies to rethink their products. In 2024, Nestlé announced plans to introduce a sugar-free version of Cerelac in India after activists, including Himatsingka, raised concerns that the company had sold only the sugar-containing variant in the country for five decades. Nestlé has been offering sugar-free Cerelac in other markets for years. Himatsingka’s content has also led to legal challenges. In 2023, he posted a video questioning the levels of sugar and artificial sweeteners in PepsiCo’s Sting caffeinated beverage, which is sold as an energy drink and has a significant following among young Indian consumers. PepsiCo later obtained a Delhi court order directing the removal of the video, arguing that the allegations were untrue and could fuel a campaign against the drink. In July, Indian regulators directed PepsiCo and other companies to stop marketing such products under the “energy drink” category within 90 days. PepsiCo did not respond to its queries seeking comment. Industry estimates suggest that around 80% of products in India’s packaged food and beverage market, valued at more than $100 billion, could be classified as high in fat, sugar or salt. Deepak Jolly of the India Food & Beverage Association (IFBA) said at a meeting with regulators in March that introducing colour-coded warning labels could result in red markings appearing across a large portion of packaged products, as per the report. The IFBA, which counts companies such as PepsiCo among its members, told Reuters that the industry is seeking greater clarity from regulators. It said the proposals could potentially result in products such as coconut water carrying “high sugar” warnings despite the sugar being naturally occurring. Indian regulators have considered measures including prominent colour-coded health warnings and star ratings to indicate the nutritional value of packaged foods since 2017. However, manufacturers are currently required only to provide ingredient lists and basic nutritional information on the back of their packaging. Health activists campaigning for greater transparency over packaged food products approached the Supreme Court, which in February asked regulators to examine the introduction of warning labels. The court also suggested studying Israel’s use of red-and-green nutritional indicators. However, following its March meeting with industry representatives, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) moved away from interpretive front-of-pack labelling. In August, the regulator told the Supreme Court that aligning India’s packaging rules with international standards was “difficult”, a position that mirrored concerns raised by the industry. At least 75 killed and hundreds missing after flash floods in Nepal and China
UDIN DHUNGA, Nepal — Massive flash floods in a border area of Nepal and China on Wednesday killed at least 75 people and left hundreds of tourists, workers and others missing after sweeping through communities and bringing travel in parts of the Himalayan country to a halt.
Officials in Nepal said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals were reported missing. Sunil Sharma, a Nepal Tourism Board spokesperson, said 133 missing were from India on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in China's autonomous region of Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing were 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from the Britain and 24 from Canada, he said, adding that people from at least 26 countries had been present in the affected area.
At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in the Gosaikunda lake in Rasuwa, coinciding with the Nepali festival of Janai Purnima on Friday, Sharma added.
China's state broadcaster CCTV said a mudslide in Tibet's Gyirong County near Nepal killed at least three people and left 265 missing, based on a preliminary count.
Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle, who gave the local death toll, also told The Associated Press that at least 28 police officials were among the missing.
Officials warned residents in several of Nepal's districts to stay away from the banks of the Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. The Bhotekoshi flooded around 9 a.m. Wednesday, destroying several villages, roads and hydropower projects, officials said.
"We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts," said Sasmit Pokharel, a Nepali government spokesperson.
Nepal's steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors but precarious ones when disaster strikes. Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in hard-hit Nuwakot district slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and stunned survivors were caked in mud.
The U.S. Geological Survey reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake early Wednesday, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) north of Kathmandu, near the border with China's autonomous region of Tibet.
Though the current monsoon season is less favorable for trekking in Nepal, it's a major season for Kailash trekking in Tibet, which follows the route in Nepal's Rasuwa district bordering Tibet's Gyirong.
Countries express alarm over missing citizens
South Korean government officials said citizens working on building a hydropower plant in Nepal were among those reported missing.
Malaysia's foreign ministry said its embassy in Kathmandu received reports from travel agencies that they had lost contact with 11 Malaysians believed to be in the Rasuwa district, also hit hard by floods.
Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up the efforts, state news agency Xinhua reported.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah and offered help. "India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts," Modi said on social media.
In a joint statement, Australia, Britain, the European Union, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland expressed solidarity with the affected people in Nepal., adding: "We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve."
The same region saw flash floods last year
The same regions saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.
Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood.
The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, had maximum flooding Wednesday, they said.
"The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream," said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.
He noted the importance of early warnings in "a warming Himalaya."
The Himalayan region, which spans several countries including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because it is warming faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research shows that extreme weather events, including heat waves, rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent.
Researchers in Kathmandu found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000, primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.

Root shows off-field leadership - now for on-field
- Published
At the back of the Compton Stand at Lord's is an enormous picture of Ben Stokes.
In the snap, Stokes unleashes a bouncer to a flinching Mohammed Siraj, the India tailender. It was taken during England's heart-stopping 22-run win on this ground last summer.
England's defeat of India was all about Stokes. He made contributions with the bat in both innings, ran out Rishabh Pant with a direct hit and put in a trademark marathon bowling spell on the final day. Stokes came to the post-match media conference with blood seeping through his sock.
Throughout Stokes' tenure as England captain, the question loomed of how anyone would eventually go about succeeding him.
For better or worse, Stokes became the all-encompassing figure in the team, for his performances on the field and what he said or did off it. It was hard to imagine how anyone could emerge from his shadow without having their leadership compared to the talismanic all-rounder.
England are little more than a week into the post-Stokes era and there is already no doubt about the strength of leadership at the helm. This is Joe Root's team now.
The last thing Root would have wanted at the beginning of his second reign as skipper was the Brydon Carse controversy.
Yet, the Yorkshireman has shown himself to be the captain English cricket needs, yet probably does not deserve.
Root's measured, assured and honest address to the media at Lord's on Tuesday was the most impressive display of leadership from anyone connected with the England team in a long time.
Perhaps Root is helped by the circumstances. If Brendon McCullum was still around, he would have been pushed in front of cameras, but McCullum has gone and his replacement Stephen Fleming is yet to arrive. It leaves Root as unquestionably the man in charge.

In terms of Root's second coming as skipper, the off-field part might be the easy bit. It is on the field where he now has a point to prove.
He said as much last week before the Headingley Test - that the biggest challenge in resuming the captaincy was overcoming the perceptions others have of his leadership.
It is not that Root was an awful captain first time around - far from it. It is just the abiding memory is an awful ending of only one win from 17 matches, a horror run that left Root and his team broken.
Leeds was a dream restart, an innings win over Pakistan wrapped up inside three days.
But the one-sided nature of that victory did not give Root room to show what kind of on-field captain he will be this time around. His best act at Headingley was to win the toss and, after Ollie Robinson took a wicket with the first ball of the match, England were on top.
There have been glimpses of what the New Root could become.
Stokes' preference for naming an England team two days before a Test has gone, at least for now. England are likely to be unchanged at Lord's, though that will not be confirmed until the toss.
Root has removed himself from first slip and now fields at mid-off. It may only be a temporary move, but it puts him closer to his bowlers. On the first morning at Headingley, Root yanked a wayward Jofra Archer from the attack after only two overs. It is hard to imagine he would have done the same to either Stuart Broad or James Anderson.
There was a hint of funkiness in the field, albeit an overhang from Root's first spell as captain. The dismissal of Azan Awais in Pakistan's second innings was the eighth time a seamer under Root has had a catch taken at leg slip - the most of any captain since such data began being collected in 2006.
Asked what the difference was between the captaincy of Stokes and Root, fast bowler Josh Tongue said: "It's very chilled out there." Tongue probably did not mean to imply Root brings a greater calmness than Stokes, yet few would argue he has taken the intensity down a notch or two.
For all the impressive media conferences, bowling changes and leg slips, Root will be judged on results, and a win this week would give England their first series triumph since 2024.
There will be plenty of attention on the Lord's pitch, so heavily criticised after England's win against New Zealand. On Wednesday, Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) chairman Mark Nicholas and director of cricket Rob Lynch were seen taking a good look at the surface.
Pakistan should be better than their showing at Headingley, mainly because they cannot get much worse. They are boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam from a hand injury and have won the previous two Tests they have played here.
England will want to build on the green shoots of recovery that sprouted in Leeds.
Jordan Cox impressed at number three and is highly rated by the management. There could be a logjam in the top order when Jacob Bethell returns to fitness, so all of Cox, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence and Jamie Smith will want to ensure they are not squeezed out.
Root said his quartet of fast bowlers "do not know how good they can be". That foursome now have the opportunity to show they can be England's first-choice attack in a range of conditions. It is a bad time for Carse to put himself out of the picture.
As for Root, no man has more runs or hundreds on this ground. Now he returns as the captain, already leading by example this week.
"When you have the privilege of being a leader within a team, you want to build something bigger than just winning," he said. "I feel like I didn't do that very well first time around.
"There's a lot to look forward to, there's a lot to work hard towards. I guess that's the fun side of it."
For Root and his players, following the past few days, the fun side will simply be returning to playing cricket.

The FIA has confirmed findings from the first two periods of performance review; Red Bull were adjudged to have the strongest engine in the first period, giving the other manufacturers upgrades; watch the Italian Grand Prix at Monza live on Sky Sports F1 on September 4-6
Wednesday 26 August 2026 17:26, UK
The FIA has confirmed that Mercedes have been granted the opportunity to make upgrades to their engine despite protestations from rival teams.
Following the introduction of all-new engines for the 2026 season, Formula 1's governing body implemented an Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) system, designed to allow manufacturers to catch up to the performance of the leading power unit during the rules cycle.
It was revealed in June after the first round of performance assessment, which included the first five rounds of the season, that the FIA had adjudged Red Bull to have the strongest engine and had granted upgrades to Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi and Honda.

The FIA never revealed their findings to the media, but teams and drivers confirmed the outcome publicly, while a document revealing the results was also leaked.
The ruling was seen as controversial because the consensus in the paddock was that Mercedes, whose works team had won the first six grands prix of the season, were being given an upgrade, while Red Bull, who had managed just a single podium in that time, would potentially lose more ground to their rivals.
Red Bull driver Max Verstappen spoke out against the findings, while Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff raised further questions over the FIA's processes when he said in July that his team have "the most powerful power unit".
The FIA refrained from publicly confirming the results while a review was carried out, but now, following the second round of assessment, which concluded with the Hungarian Grand Prix ahead of the sport's summer break, the findings from both periods have been announced.
An FIA statement said: "For the first period: Mercedes were determined to be in the two to four per cent window, and will thus be allowed one additional homologation in 2026 and an additional one in 2027, together with corresponding cost cap and dyno testing increases.
"Audi, Ferrari and Honda were determined to be above four per cent, and will thus be allowed two additional homologations in 2026 and two in 2027, together with corresponding cost cap and dyno testing increases."
While this part of the FIA's statement was confirmation of information that had been leaked in June, their findings for the second period provided a further blow for Red Bull.
Had upgrades made by any of the other teams since June been adjudged to have propelled their performance beyond Red Bull's, the Milton Keynes squad could have been granted their own upgrade opportunity.
However, the statement said: "For the second period, no additional homologations were granted to any of the Power Unit Manufacturers."
That means that Red Bull are at the very least seen to be performing within two per cent of the best engine, and may well still be adjudged to have the strongest power unit.
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli leads his team-mate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton by 59 points at the top of the drivers' standings, while Verstappen is 130 points back from the Italian in sixth.
Mercedes are 87 points clear of Ferrari at the top of the constructors' standings, while third-placed McLaren, who use a Mercedes engine, have found form with reigning world champion Lando Norris winning the last two races.
Mercedes have been free to use their 2026 upgrade since the first-round results were communicated in June, but are not thought to have done so yet. Ferrari, Audi and Honda are thought to have each introduced one of their two upgrades for 2026.
FIA director of single seater Nikolas Tombazis said: "The FIA has undertaken thorough and exhaustive analysis as part of our ADUO review process.
"With the release of the findings of period two, we are confident that, based on the quality of the data, its analysis is incredibly robust, giving us a high level of confidence in our findings.
"We also have to respect the confidentiality and intellectual property of the teams and their Power Unit Manufacturers in disseminating any details from the findings.
"This is the first year of ADUO so naturally there are areas which we may evolve over time, in discussion with all the PU Manufacturers"
The third ADUO review period commenced with the Dutch Grand Prix over the weekend, and runs until the Mexico City Grand Prix on November 1.

Indonesians brave choking smoke to pray for rain as country battles wildfires
PALEMBANG, Indonesia — Authorities in Indonesia's South Sumatra, the province with the highest number of wildfire hot spots, turned to spiritual measures on Tuesday as huge blazes in central and western regions scorched wide areas of forests and peatland, creating a choking haze that blanketed some cities in the world's most populous Muslim-majority country.
The prayer gathering initiative comes as the province faces prolonged dry weather that has heightened the risk of forest and peatland fires.
The latest satellite data from the Environment Ministry showed South Sumatra recorded the highest number of hot spots nationwide with 1,429, followed by West Kalimantan with 1,226 and Central Kalimantan with 811. Forestry Ministry data indicated that nearly 940 square kilometers (363 square miles) were burned in July alone, including over 20 square kilometers (8 square miles) in South Sumatra province.
About 3,000 residents gathered in Palembang, the capital of South Sumatra province, to perform a special Islamic prayer for rain, known as "salat istisqa." They prayed shoulder to shoulder in the courtyard of the governor's office as thick smoke shrouded roads, buildings and public facilities, reducing visibility and forcing motorists to drive with their headlights on during the day.
"We have done everything we can and worked closely with all relevant parties," South Sumatra Gov. Herman Deru said before the prayer. "As people of faith, we are also praying to God to send rain so that life can return to normal."
He also said the public prayer would complement ongoing firefighting and drought-mitigation measures and serve as a moment for residents to unite in confronting the environmental challenges facing the province.
Emergency services have been battling fires driven by an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season, generating dense smoke that crossed into Malaysia and Brunei, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.
Indonesia is actively intensifying weather-modification operations to help firefighters combat wildfires by inducing rainfall through the dispersal of salt particles into suitable clouds, with 30 aircraft for cloud-seeding and water-bombing operations over Kalimantan, and another 22 helicopters covering Sumatra.
Indonesian police have arrested 72 people suspected of starting some of the forest and peatland fires, while four companies are under investigation for allegedly using fire to clear land at low cost.
Plantation owners and traditional farmers often start fires to clear land for farming, triggering hazardous haze that reduces visibility, disrupts land and air transportation and threatens public health.
Fires are a regular problem during the dry season in Indonesia, and the haze they generate has periodically drawn diplomatic complaints from neighboring countries in Southeast Asia.

- The claim that the Trump administration uses a legal loophole to sell protected wild horses to slaughterhouses is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from reporting by The New York Times in August 2026 and was backed by research by animal rights groups that suggested buyers of wild horses sold through the Bureau of Land Management's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter.
- According to its website, it is BLM policy "not to sell or send any wild horses or burros to slaughter," and buyers from the sale program sign a bill of sale saying they will not slaughter or sell for slaughter the animals they buy.
- The Times' reporting brought to light a long-standing issue within the BLM about what to do with excess wild horses and burros. The bureau is bound by law to regulate populations but has historically avoided euthanizing healthy animals due to concerns about public perception.
- Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses.
- Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that more recent buyers have purchased horses from the BLM and sold them for slaughter, the article did not include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administration. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- We contacted the Times journalist who wrote the article and an animal rights group that provided research to ask for additional evidence and await replies to our queries.
In August 2026, The New York Times published an investigation into the Bureau of Land Management's sale of wild horses, titled "Under Trump, Protected Wild Horses Are Going to Slaughter."
Synopses of the Times' findings circulated widely online. For example, one Facebook page wrote (archived):
A heartbreaking investigation revealed that Trump's Bureau of Land Management is systematically rounding up thousands of America's wild horses, then quietly selling them off to buyers who are shipping them to slaughterhouses abroad. Before, the U.S. government rarely sold wild horses. But since Trump took office, government sales have more than doubled.
Versions of the claim also circulated on Threads (archived), Instagram (archived), X (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to learn more about it. One reader wrote, "Is Trump really rounding up horses to sell to slaughterhouses?"
The Times article reported how the U.S. government, faced with the ballooning costs of taking care of more than 50,000 wild horses it has rounded up to control herd sizes, sold thousands every year to buyers who purchased the animals for as little as $25 to sell at auction to other buyers that shipped them to slaughterhouses. This was allowed to happen, the Times reported, because selling a wild horse removes its statutory protection from "capture, branding, harassment, or death."
Though the Times provided very strong circumstantial evidence to suggest that some buyers of wild horses sold through the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Sale Program were transporting the animals overseas for slaughter, the article didn't include primary evidence, such as ownership documents, pictures or videos, of the alleged transfers happening during the Trump administrations.
Government investigations in 2008 and 2015 documented instances of wild horses and burros sold by the BLM ending up at slaughterhouses after being sold to private buyers before the start of the Trump administrations.
Snopes contacted Skydog Ranch and Sanctuary, an animal rescue organization that said it tracked animals from BLM ownership to auctions attended by slaughterhouse buyers to ask for additional evidence of the process the Times article described. We also contacted Dave Phillips, who wrote the Times article, to ask what primary evidence he used for his reporting. We await replies to our queries.
In the meantime, we leave this claim unrated.
A BLM spokesperson said in an emailed statement on Aug. 24, 2026:
The Bureau of Land Management does not sell or send wild horses or burros to slaughter, and allegations that individuals are violating federal law or the terms governing the sale of these animals are taken seriously.
The Times article suggested the BLM had found a way to offload its large off-range holding population of wild horses and burros that was effectively sending the animals to slaughter without incriminating the bureau.
The Wild Horse and Burro Program allows the BLM to sell animals that are more than 10 years old or that it has unsuccessfully listed for adoption at least three times. However, the Times reported, "Livestock inspection records show mustangs sold by the government soon ended up on trucks bound for slaughter plants in Canada."
The article focused on one reported buyer from Ohio, who the Times said had bought 500 horses from the BLM in a matter of years. Some of those horses, the article said, later showed up for sale at "an auction in Tennessee frequented by slaughter buyers."
The article also alleged that a week after the Ohio buyer received a shipment of 97 formerly wild mares, an Ohio exporter of animals for slaughter shipped two trucks of horses across the Canadian border. The Times said that, according to one image its reporter had viewed, at least one of those horses had a BLM freeze mark.
The Ohio buyer reportedly spoke to the Times reporter for two hours but "refused to say specifically what had happened to the horses he purchased from the government, other than to insist that none had gone to slaughter." He declined having worked with the Ohio exporter that shipped the two trucks across the Canadian border. The exporter would not comment to the Times on whether he had purchased horses from the buyer.
Without primary evidence — meaning sales documents tracking individual animals from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the auction in Tennessee or from the BLM to the Ohio buyer to the Ohio exporter to a slaughterhouse — it was not possible for Snopes to independently verify the claims in the Times article.
Holding costs tie up BLM program budget
The Times article highlighted an issue that the BLM has grappled with for years: how to legally, effectively and tastefully control wild horse populations. According to the bureau's data, wild horse and burro populations exceed the BLM's Appropriate Management Level, meaning the number of animals that can thrive in balance with other public land resources and uses, in nearly all the states where the bureau tracks populations.
The BLM is required by The Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971 — the same act that protects wild horses and burros from "capture, branding, harassment, or death" — to uphold the AML for the populations it tracks (Sec. 1333b1). Under the Act, the BLM is allowed to euthanize excess animals "in the most humane and cost efficient manner possible" (Sec. 1333b2C). However, a 2008 report by the Government Accountability Office on the BLM's management of "unadoptable" horses found that the bureau hesitated to do this because it was thought to be "unacceptable to the public" (Page 56).
The BLM estimates that wild horse and burro populations, if left unregulated, would double every four years. Therefore, the bureau rounds up and removes thousands of animals from the wild to control populations. Those animals end up in the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program's off-range corrals and pastures. By May 2026, the program reported that it held 58,025 formerly wild horses and burros and that its total capacity for off-range holding was 78,751 animals. According to the program's figures it spent $101 million — 66% of its budget — on off-range holding costs in fiscal year 2024.
A long-standing problem
According to the 2008 GAO report, the BLM's Wild Horse and Burro Program faced the same challenges then that the Times article highlighted 18 years later. The report said the cost of caring for off-range animals was already overwhelming the program in 2008, and that the program had "limited" options for "dealing with" animals it could not adopt out because it feared the public would not support humanely euthanizing healthy animals (Page 9).
The program had reportedly sold animals since 2005, though at that point also faced issues with animals ending up at slaughterhouses after the sale (Page 43). As a result, the bureau implemented a mandatory "statement of intent" at purchase, which required the buyer to say that they did not intend to sell the animals they bought for slaughter. BLM bills of sale for wild horses and burros still included such a clause in 2026.
The effectiveness of the clause was unclear because the BLM also said on its website about its sales program that it did not track animals after it sold them. The 2008 report noted that the introduction of a "statement of intent" was part of the reason the BLM sold fewer horses than before.
The existence of the "statement of intent" did not deter one buyer, who admitted in a 2015 investigation carried out by the Office of the Inspector General that "most of" the 1,700 wild horses he bought through the BLM between 2008 and 2012 had gone to slaughter.
The GAO and OIG reports suggest that the issue of wild horses and burros ending up at slaughterhouses after BLM sales is documented and predates the Trump administration.
Aside from adoption, sale or euthanasia, the BLM has been pursuing fertility treatment as a way to control populations since 1992 (Page 69). However, the BLM itself and peer-reviewed research have found it comes with its own challenges around finding and accessing animals and keeping up with treatment. According to the BLM, it delivered 921 fertility treatments to wild horses and burros in fiscal year 2025. That same year, it removed 7,853 horses and burros from the wild.
The Times report said that although government experts did recommend wider use of fertility treatment to control populations the recommendation was hard for the BLM to act on because its funds were largely tied up in the removal, holding and care of excess animals.
In sum, while it was not possible to verify the exact elements of the Times' reporting, the article brought to light a complicated issue for the BLM that predated both Trump administrations but nonetheless had lethal consequences for the horses and burros the U.S. government is bound to protect.

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry this past week tightened controls on all fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) containing chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine hydrochloride, requiring manufacturers to carry a clear warning that they must not be used in children below four years of age.
What are these two drugs?
Chlorpheniramine is an antihistamine. It can reduce allergy symptoms such as a runny nose and sneezing. Phenylephrine is a decongestant, intended to relieve a blocked nose.
An FDC puts both ingredients into one medicine. Such combinations are commonly encountered in cold/allergy preparations.
The government’s action does not mean every medicine containing either ingredient individually has been banned. The specific regulatory action concerns FDCs containing the two ingredients together.
What has changed now is the rule where manufacturers must put the warning. “Fixed Dose Combination shall not be used in children below four years of age” — on the label, package insert and promotional literature. The restriction covers manufacture, sale and distribution of these FDCs.
This expands an earlier action. In 2023, India’s Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) had already directed manufacturers of a particular chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine formulation to warn against use below four.
In April 2025, restrictions were imposed on certain FDCs. The August 2026 notification extends the warning requirement to all such formulations.
Why are children under four the focus?
Young children are more vulnerable to medication-related adverse effects because their bodies process medicines differently from adults and because dosing errors can have proportionally larger consequences.
The government’s Expert Committee and Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) concluded that these combinations could pose risks to children below four and that safer alternatives are available.
There is also a broader international concern around giving young children multi-ingredient cough-and-cold medicines. The US FDA, for example, warns that decongestant- or antihistamine-containing cough/cold products can cause serious adverse effects in very young children and notes the risk of accidental overdose when several ingredients are combined.
Does this mean cold medicines don’t work?
Not necessarily. These drugs can relieve symptoms, but they don’t cure the underlying viral infection. Most childhood colds resolve on their own. What doctors have been saying is that while parents may understandably want to make a congested or coughing child comfortable, but more medication isn’t automatically better.
For nasal congestion, relatively simple measures such as saline nasal drops/spray, fluids and a cool-mist humidifiercan help.
The key message is don’t self-medicate a child under four with a chlorpheniramine + phenylephrine combination, even if the product is marketed as a children’s cold medicine.
Check the active ingredients, not just the brand name. Many cold preparations contain several ingredients, creating a risk of accidentally giving the same drug twice through different products.
For fever or discomfort, parents should use medicines such as paracetamol/acetaminophen or ibuprofen only according to age/weight-appropriate instructions and medical advice.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

Google has updated Gemini Audio with some new Gemini 3.5 models, introducing new transcription capabilities that automatically detect specialized jargon and more than 85 languages. Gemini 3.5 Live, 3.5 Live Experimental, and 3.5 Transcribe are designed to provide better precision for Google’s voice-controlled AI features, without struggling with background noise or when your speech is interrupted.
Google’s new AI transcription edits out your ‘ums’ and ‘ahs’
We got Gemini Audio models while we’re still waiting for the overdue Gemini 3.5 Pro launch.
Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is a completely new addition to the Gemini family, and its introduction comes as we’re still waiting for Google to release the Gemini 3.5 Pro model that it promised to roll out in June. Google says that 3.5 Transcribe “represents a major advancement from our previous transcription model, Chirp 3,” especially regarding multilingual performance and wording error rates.
The transcription model allows users to “edit naturally with just your voice,” according to Google, and can automatically format text and remove filler words like “um” and “uh.” Users can provide a customized vocabulary to the model, allowing 3.5 Transcribe to automatically adapt transcription to unique spelling requirements and specialized jargon to prevent those words from being edited manually. It can also attribute speech for up to three speakers in pre-recorded audio, alongside providing word-level timestamps.
Transcribe is launching alongside 3.5 Live and 3.5 Live Experimental, which build on the existing speech recognition tech that powers Gemini’s voice chat mode. Gemini 3.5 Live is better at handling mid-sentence interruptions, language recognition, and live visual processing, while Gemini 3.5 Live Experimental goes further by narrating its progress step by step in real time while it tackles reasoning on more complex tasks.
These Gemini Audio updates are rolling out starting today in English for all macOS Gemini app users, and the Rambler dictation feature on Android in select countries and languages. It’s also available for developers in public preview in the Gemini API via AI Studio and Antigravity. Google says that Chrome support is coming soon.

Story so far: The Supreme Court on August 20, 2026, has ruled that the police cannot independently investigate offences relating to illegal prenatal sex determination under the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994. The responsibility lies primarily with the Appropriate Authority, a specialised body constituted under the law. In a judgment authored by a Bench of Justice Sanjay Karol and Justice Nongmeikapam Kotiswar Singh, it settles a long-standing disagreement among High Courts over whether the police could register FIRs and investigate such offences because they are classified as “cognisable” and “non-bailable”.
What was the case about?
The case arose from an allegation of illegal sex determination of a foetus at a hospital in Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh.
The District Magistrate, who was the Appropriate Authority under the Act, received information about the alleged practice. A Tehsildar was authorised to conduct a decoy operation. Following the operation, a raid was conducted at the hospital, and an FIR was registered against the doctor and others.
The FIR included offences under the Indian Penal Code as well as the sex-determination law. The accused approached the Allahabad High Court seeking to quash the chargesheet.
The High Court noticed that courts had taken different views on the role of the police in such cases and referred the issue to the Supreme Court.
There were essentially three questions before the Supreme Court: Can the police register an FIR for an offence under the Act? Can they investigate it? And can a Magistrate take cognisance of the offence on the basis of a police chargesheet?
Who is the Appropriate Authority?
The Appropriate Authority is the specialised authority created under the law to enforce the ban on sex selection and regulate the use of prenatal diagnostic techniques.
Section 17 of the Act specifically gives it the responsibility of investigating complaints of violations and taking action.
According to the section, when appointed for the whole of the State or the Union territory, it should consist of the following three members i) an officer of or above the rank of the Joint Director of Health and Family Welfare Chairperson; ii) an eminent woman representing women’s organisation; and iii) an officer of Law Department of the State or the Union territory concerned.
The functions of the appropriate authority includes to grant, suspend or cancel registration of a Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory or Genetic Clinic; to enforce standards prescribed for the Genetic Counselling Centre, Genetic Laboratory and Genetic Clinic; to investigate complaints of breach of the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder and take immediate action and to seek and consider the advice of the Advisory Committee.
The Supreme Court therefore held that the law has deliberately placed the investigation of such offences with this specialised authority.
So, can the police register an FIR?
Not for the purpose of independently investigating a violation of the Act.
The complication came from Section 27 of the law, which says that every offence under it is “cognisable, non-bailable and non-compoundable.” A cognisable offence ordinarily allows the police to investigate without first obtaining permission from a court.
But the Supreme Court said that Section 27 cannot be read on its own. It has to be read along with the provisions that specifically give the Appropriate Authority the power to investigate and Section 28, which lays down how a court can take up an offence under the Act.
The Court said, “The language of the statute, more particularly Sections 27 and 28 of the Act when read together, in light of the other provisions and the socially beneficial nature of the Act as also the requirement of sensitivity along with medical and technical know-how, indicates that the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act. This is further made clear by the fact that an FIR once registered cannot be taken to its logical conclusion as per the procedures of this Act. The restriction applies only to offences under this Act and does not restrict the police’s power to investigate or prosecute independent offences disclosed under substantive criminal law (IPC/BNS)”.
The Court held that allowing the police to independently investigate would undermine this specialised system.
It said, “the police are not meant to be the investigators for the purpose of this Act.”
The police can, however, assist the Appropriate Authority when their help is necessary. Rule 18A(3)(iv) says that police involvement should be avoided “as far as possible”. The Court held that this rule has statutory force.
The phrase does leave room for police assistance, but not for an independent police investigation. The Court said that, when involved, the police would have to act “strictly in a supplemental or aiding capacity.”
What happens if there is also another crime?
The Supreme Court has not said that the police have no role whenever a suspected sex-determination offence is involved. The police can investigate a separate offence under the IPC, BNS or another criminal law, even if it arises from the same incident.
For example, if the facts disclose both a violation of the sex-determination law and an independently constituted offence under general criminal law, the two investigations can proceed separately.
The Appropriate Authority would investigate the offence under the special law. The police would investigate the independent criminal offence.
But the police cannot use the existence of another offence as a way of taking over the sex-determination investigation. The Court’s concurring opinion makes the distinction clear: the police cannot use a general criminal offence “as a gateway to take over the PC & PNDT inquiry.”
Similarly, the special law cannot be used to prevent the police from investigating a genuinely separate criminal offence.
Can a Magistrate act on a police chargesheet?
No. This was the third question before the Supreme Court, and the Court’s answer was categorical.
Section 28 says that a court cannot take cognizance of an offence under the Act except through the complaint mechanism specified in the provision. A police chargesheet therefore cannot, by itself, give the Magistrate jurisdiction to take cognizance of a PC &PNDT offence.
The Appropriate Authority has to follow the procedure prescribed under the Act.
The Court concluded that there is a “complete statutory embargo” on taking cognizance except in the situations provided under Section 28.
What is the takeaway?
The immediate impact is on how a suspected illegal sex-determination case moves through the criminal justice system.
If information received by a police station discloses only a violation under the Act, the police should record the information and send it, along with the relevant material, to the Appropriate Authority. They should not independently investigate the offence.
If the information also reveals an independent cognizable offence under the IPC, BNS or another general criminal law, the police can investigate that offence while sending the sex-determination component to the Appropriate Authority.
The Supreme Court has also made clear that a police investigation cannot simply end with a chargesheet for the offence under the Act. Section 28 creates a separate route for bringing such a case before a court.
The ruling does not weaken the prohibition on prenatal sex determination. Instead, it clarifies who is responsible for enforcing it.

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

Doctors from a private health facility in West Bengal have successfully treated a seven- year-old boy suffering from thalassaemia using an advanced Haplo Cord transplant process.
The parents of the 7-year-old child diagnosed with HbE Beta thalassemia, who needs monthly blood transfusions, were counseled to register under the “Save the Sibling” programme. They underwent IVF (in vitro fertilization) and pre-implantation genetic testing to produce a matched thalassemia-free sibling with compatible HLA (human leukocyte antigen), which is critical for bone marrow transplantation.
A haplo-cord transplant was performed using the cord blood from the patient’s sibling and some stem cells from his father. The transplant was conducted by Narayana Health. During the transplant period, the child developed complications such as infections, mucositis, liver derangement, and persistent low blood counts, which were effectively managed. The patient has recovered well and is now transfusion-free, the doctors said.
In another feat, the team treated a 62-year-old male patient from Myanmar with brain cancer after a successful CAR T-cell therapy (an advanced type of immunotherapy). The patient was initially found to be having gait disturbance (an unusual change in the way a person walks). He was then diagnosed to have primary CNS lymphoma, a rare, aggressive type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma where cancer cells form in the brain, spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, or eyes.
After receiving four cycles of high-dose chemotherapy yielding unsatisfactory results, the doctors decided to have him undergo CAR T-cell therapy. He underwent lymphocyte collection, bridging with radiation and other medications, before receiving a dual CAR targeting CD19 and CD22 on the cancer cells.
Speaking about these two rare recoveries, Joydeep Chakrabartty, Senior Consultant, Hemato Oncology & Clinical Lead - BMT Programme (East), Narayana Health, said that the recoveries are landmark achievements with both facing potential fatalities.
“Using the Haplo-cord technology for the child and the CAR T-cell therapy for the aged patient, the expert team of doctors attending them have been able to turn their lives around for the better. Narayana Health has always been at the forefront in breaking new grounds in medical science, and these two cases clearly reflect that,” Dr. Chakrabartty said.
Also read: Evidence of CAR T-cell therapy against cancers presented at US conference
Prasanta Chowdhury, Laboratory Director, Cord Life Sciences India Pvt. Limited, said that cord blood banking is a complex issue involving medical, financial, ethical, and scientific debates. “The core dilemma centres on choosing between private storage for family use and public donation for general use, weighed against high costs and low statistical odds of personal use. In these two cases, we have successfully addressed every single concern with absolute compassion and clarity,” Dr. Chowdhury said.
