New Delhi, Aug 26: The Embassy of India in Kathmandu is closely coordinating with government of Nepal for the early rescue and relief of Indian nationals affected by flash floods in the Himalayan nation on Wednesday, the Ministry of External Affairs said.
The embassy earlier in the day issued emergency phone numbers for those seeking assistance and information related to Indian nationals affected by the calamity.
"Embassy of India in Nepal is closely coordinating with Government of Nepal for the early rescue and relief of Indian nationals affected by today's flash floods in Nepal," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal posted on X.
At least 46 people have died and nearly 500 others, including 105 Indians, are missing after a massive flash flood originating in Tibet swept through central Nepal districts on Wednesday.
So far, 46 bodies have been recovered from the flash flood hit areas, security officials said.
According to an earlier statement by Nepal Tourism Board (NTB), a total of 384 travellers, 291 foreigners and 93 Nepalese nationals, have gone missing due to the Rasuwa floods.
These travellers include 105 Indian tourists, 37 NRIs and remaining tourists from USA, Malaysia, UK, South Africa, Australia and Netherlands.
The Embassy of India in Nepal in a separate post said, it has "remained engaged with the relevant authorities of Government of Nepal for early rescue and relief for Indian nationals affected by the flash floods that took place in Nepal today. Rescue and relief efforts continue to be strengthened in coordination with the Government of Nepal. @MEAIndia".

Mumbai, Aug 26: A 26-year-old woman was dramatically rescued by the Mumbai Fire Brigade after she allegedly jumped from the 10th floor of a building in suburban Bhandup on Wednesday morning, only to get caught in a tree.
The woman, identified as Pratiksha Hiwrale, landed in an adjacent tree after she allegedly plunged from the window of a flat in Sunshine Building on Lake Road. She was found hanging about 20-25 feet above the ground. The fire brigade was alerted at around 9.32 am.
Fire brigade personnel rushed to the spot and used a hook ladder to bring Hiwrale to safety. She was then taken to a private hospital in a private ambulance.
Doctors said she suffered an injury to her left leg. She was later shifted to Sion Hospital for surgery, a civic official said.

Portrait of the Artist as a Movie Star
Rachel Cusk’s latest novel is about the life of a famous actress—or is it?
A few months ago, I traveled to a new city in a foreign country to talk about a book I’d written. At lunch one day, my host told me about a publishing acquaintance of hers who’d hosted the writer Rachel Cusk some years back, only to find herself seemingly replicated later, in cartoonish and (she felt) unflattering form, within one of the books in Cusk’s Outline trilogy. The woman was apparently devastated; although Cusk had withheld some details, the portrait, according to its presumptive subject, was specific and precise enough that anyone who knew her and read the book would immediately recognize the person being portrayed.
“Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is indefensible,” Janet Malcolm wrote in her classic 1990 book, The Journalist and the Murderer, about a nonfiction writer who used ethically questionable means to get close to a subject. Does the same theory hold true for autofiction? The license that art allows is generous, which Cusk has learned to make use of. On the occasions when she’s written openly autobiographical works, she’s been pilloried, or even sued: Her 2001 book about motherhood, A Life’s Work, was lambasted in the British press for its frank portrait of maternal self-abnegation, and her 2009 book The Last Supper sparked a libel lawsuit from a man who took issue with her depiction of him. (The publisher settled the suit and printed a revised version of the book.)
But it was Cusk’s 2012 memoir about her divorce, Aftermath, and the excoriation she received for its exposure of supposed private family matters, that seemed to bring her to a breaking point. “Without wishing to sound melodramatic, it was creative death after Aftermath,” she told The Guardian two years after publication. “That was the end. I was heading into total silence—an interesting place to find yourself when you are quite developed as an artist.”
Instead of retreating, she turned that silence into its own ingenious form. Outline, published in 2014, is about a writer named Faye who’s traveling to Greece to teach creative writing, and its conceit is that Faye is an almost entirely passive vehicle for other people’s stories, which different characters spill out to her with unguarded enthusiasm. The book and two following installments, Transit and Kudos, were categorized as novels, which offered more protection than Cusk had previously been allowed. Still, Cusk made clear that what she was really interested in as a writer was truth—the resonance of pure reality. “I’m certain autobiography is increasingly the only form in all the arts,” she said in that same Guardian interview, which is an unusual thing to declare on a promotional tour for a work of ostensible fiction.
Life of M, Cusk’s newest book, takes autofiction’s familiar dance of authorial ambiguity and shakes it into something odd and unsettling. “A little while ago I told the actor M that I was thinking of writing her autobiography,” it begins. M, as has been widely reported, is believed to be either based on or inspired by the actor Natalie Portman, who has praised Cusk’s writing and featured it in her book club. Both women live in Paris, where Life of M seems to be set. M is described as having first become famous as a child, and two of her roles—playing a ballerina and a performer who survives a school shooting—seem easily recognizable as Portman’s roles in Black Swan and Vox Lux. M, like Portman, is an avid reader, a mother, and a star of such renown that the world bends itself to accommodate her. When the narrator proposes writing about M to her, the actor initially likes the idea, asking wryly, “Would you just make it up?”
For most of the book, like M, we’re left to wonder what the answer to that question is. Cusk has long blown up form and genre in her attempts to capture the authenticity of female experience. Her pursuit is relentless and uncompromising; it’s also bound by a logic that only Cusk herself seems to really understand. (You cannot write an autobiography of another person, any more than you can write a fictionalized portrait of one of the most recognizable women alive and expect most people to understand what about it is or isn’t true.) Life of M is a strange book, written with cold formality. But in its final pages, it performs an astonishing rug pull that makes you wonder whether the book actually has been an autobiography all along, interested in exposing not M but the knotty and unpalatable process of Cusk’s art.
In the first pages of Life of M, the author meets M at a bookstore. We are told that M is “interested in books,” that she is small and her house is large, and that “her smile had a sweetness that almost seemed to reproach those who look at it for their dim and suspicious view of life.” The author finds it “hard not to feel ugly next to M”—the words ugly and ugliness appear almost 30 separate times over the book’s 180 or so pages—but seems drawn to the contours of their difference. M is portrayed as kind and thoughtful; the author comes across—intentionally, I am presuming—as surly and paranoid. “I had never learned how to make experience easier for myself,” she writes. “For M it was the reverse. Her difficulty lay in her distance from the random violence of insignificance.”
After this short introductory section, we do not hear directly from the author again until the end of the book, when she goes to meet M to discuss what she’s written. The chapters in the middle toggle between scenes describing M’s life and more elliptical sections written in the first-person plural, which seem to interrogate experiences shared by the author and M. “We live in the same city but millions of other people live here too,” the first of those first-person-plural installments begins. That city is beautiful yet unstable, full of sidewalk cafés and cultural venues and tourists, but also of “angry people, people who shout and rail in the streets.” Cusk, in these sections, has the wafty portentousness of a stoned philosopher. “Often we don’t know what to do, how to occupy ourselves,” she writes. “Then at other times, we’re very busy and the idea of creating ourselves seems less important. But suddenly we find it is there, the question: Who are we? Yet everyone else seems to know who we are.”
These interludes are, however, brief; the majority of the book comprises the descriptions of M engaged in the day-to-day business of her life: She reads Marcus Aurelius in a hotel room, she conducts research for a role by visiting an archive related to a historical figure, she meets a friend for coffee. Cusk begins many of these scenes with the same French-inflected sentence structure: “It is a hotel room in a foreign city.” “It is an office, square and high-ceilinged, with walls of paneled wood.” “It is the interior of a limousine. The air inside it is scentless and almost without temperature.”
The descriptions sometimes go on for several pages, as though Cusk is writing stage directions or action lines in a screenplay. But inevitably, we end up in M’s inner thoughts. She struggles to relate to a friend’s depression. Returning home after an acting job, she feels strangely like she needs to get into character as herself. At a dinner party one night, as a pie is cut up and served at the communal table, she senses “a great chasm of loneliness and terror yawn inside her, as though this knife were intended for her. She would be split open and made to come out.”
Some authorial projection here seems likely, given the precision with which Cusk describes M’s emotions, the “sensation of ground glass running in her veins instead of blood” when she has to meet with a man with whom she formerly had a relationship, who once “relished her fame” but now “sees it as a limitless series of opportunities for contempt.” But the descriptions of M sitting on a terrace above an olive grove, or meeting with her creative team, or participating in a book event sponsored by a fashion house feel distinctly real. They have the chilly detachment and careful texture of observation. They’re also laced with what feels like judgment: While reading on her terrace, M “lifts her eyes to the horizon with its primitive blue-grey shapes of islands washed in milky light, for the book is in French and does not entirely hold her attention.”
Several times, Cusk refers to M as having projects: She makes a point of befriending interesting people, for instance, or tries to mentor “younger female actors” to help them “avoid some of her own errors and misconceptions.” What is Cusk’s project? Toward the end of the book, the author returns, showing M “some of what only I was referring to as our project. She didn’t seem to like it very much. She said we needed to talk.” The author goes to see M in her big house, taking care to describe the scrolled mantelpiece of the fireplace, the polished herringbone parquet of the floor. M doesn’t like how she’s been portrayed. “It’s hurtful,” she says. “But it isn’t you,” the author explains. “It isn’t anyone.”
M points out that “she had never been to any of the places I described, nor done the things I had narrated.” The author struggles to communicate how none of that matters—that what she’s written isn’t a portrait of M but a rendering of the author’s own “private interior world” refracted through someone else. But all M can see are deficiencies—or, rather, the author’s projections of them—made real on the page. “You’ve made it seem like I lack humanity,” she says. “But you’re just playing a character,” the author replies. “The character was invented by me. So if that’s true, then it’s me it’s true of.”
Is Life of M about Portman, or Cusk, or neither, or both? Cusk’s “we” seems to seek out points of commonality between the two, despite their many differences: Both are well known, though to different degrees; both have seemingly difficult or tense relationships with their parents; both have had intimate relationships end under public scrutiny; both work in creative realms, although M insists that she is not a creator but “merely an element in the creations of others,” a statement that bears extra weight by the end of the book. And yet in its final pages, the author finds her power as a writer—the capricious and godlike influence of the storyteller—bludgeoned by M’s authority, her look of “mechanical power, a power that seemed to erase what it looked on.”
That final scene is freighted with tension. M is cold and angry; she feels betrayed. She forbids the author from using her name. More significant, everything we’ve read in the book thus far (the descriptions, the interiority, the endless self-scrutiny) is seemingly revealed to be false. M is just one more person left offended by the author’s excavation of her. The author, for her part, doesn’t seem to care about the truth of who M is—“I haven’t even googled you,” she says—so much as how she can manipulate the idea of M to make sense of her own life. During a year when the author had been preoccupied with her partner’s grave illness, she says, her focus on M “had enabled me to leave and go and live in someone else.”
To be a writer in this way is to be parasitic—to latch onto someone real and to try to draw out their life force to make art. It isn’t exactly defensible, but for Cusk to expose that practice is deeply fascinating, particularly in a book that some were always going to see as ethically fraught—and that many readers will be reading anyway in hopes of revelation and insight. Which is, Cusk might argue, the whole point of literature: that even, or especially, in its most uncomfortable form, it offers us moments of authentic humanity that thrum with recognition.
“I don’t really believe in character,” Cusk once told the author Sheila Heti. “I believe in moments of truth.” There is, Heti said in response, “a darkness in how far away we are from truth, how all the forces in life sort of conspire to keep one away from it.” But there’s also a darkness in seeking to uncover it, especially when the truth at hand isn’t your own. I can’t decide whether Cusk’s willingness to delineate and accept this paradox in Life of M is admirably resolute or absolutely merciless. Or both.

Soon after his appointment as the BJP’s national social media co-convenor, Arun Yadav made his X account private and then deleted more than 60,000 posts before making it public again. When the account was locked, it showed around 65,500 posts. By August 22, only 2,794 remained — a deletion exercise that wiped out virtually his entire publicly visible posting history.
At present, the oldest post that can be traced on Yadav’s timeline dates to August 19, 2026. All posts preceding it have been deleted. Many of those posts included abusive and racist remarks, attacks on women’s character, and content directly targeting Muslims in communally provocative terms.
On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced a new social media cell where Deepak Mhaskey replaced Amit Malviya a the party’s IT cell chief. One of the newly inducted members of the social media cell was Yadav, who had previously been removed from his position as head of the Haryana BJP IT Cell.
When attention turned to Yadav’s old social media record following his new appointment, he locked his X account, @BeingArun28. Yadav has now made his account public again, but not before deleting the posts on a massive scale. The sequence of events indicates that making the account private might have given him the opportunity to remove his old controversial posts and wipe his social media record clean.
A review of Arun Yadav’s social media activity over the past several years reveals a clear pattern: abusive and racist remarks against opposition leaders, attacks on women’s character, and several explicit instances of directly targeting Muslim minorities and making communally provocative statements.
The Post that Led to his Ouster in 2022
Arun Yadav’s history of controversial remarks goes back several years. In 2017, he shared an image of the Kaaba in Mecca alongside a glass of whisky and wrote in an objectionable post that he could see “the Prophet in a peg of alcohol”. Questions continued to be raised over the remark for years. Finally, amid mounting pressure, Haryana BJP removed Arun Yadav from his post as state IT Cell chief on July 8, 2022.
The timing of the action taken against him was particularly significant. It came just a month after then BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma’s derogatory remarks about prophet Muhammad of Islam had sparked a massive controversy in India and abroad. During a television debate, the BJP spokesperson had made offensive remarks about the prophet, triggering an international backlash.
Amid intense international pressure, the BJP had termed its spokesperson a “fringe element” and expelled her from the party. The following month, a screenshot of Arun Yadav’s old objectionable post went viral on social media. In this sensitive environment, Yadav’s removal was, in a sense, a tacit acknowledgement that his post had crossed a line the party was not prepared to publicly defend at the time.
The significant new responsibility handed to Arun Yadav within the party sends a serious political message: the conduct for which his own party had once sacked him has not stood in the way of his appointment to a higher position with greater responsibility.
“The Digging will Continue until God leaves India, Keep Digging”
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another objectionable remark about Islam, writing: “The digging will continue until God leaves India, keep digging.”
The post was made at a time when the Gyanvapi Mosque dispute was before the Supreme Court. The Hindu side had claimed that a “Shivling” was present within the mosque complex. Given the sensitivity of the case, the Supreme Court transferred the suit filed by the Hindu side from the trial court to a more senior and experienced district judge.
In this tense legal and social environment, Yadav’s statement was not merely an inflammatory post or an insult directed at a particular religion. It also sought to frame the “digging” of sites containing mosques across the country as a coordinated campaign.
Attack on Rahul Gandhi
Political opponents have also been among Arun Yadav’s targets. In a post from January 2023, he shared a video of Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s speech and used the phrase “the harvest of the brown aunty” for him.
The remark was not merely a deeply insulting personal attack but also reflected a clearly racist mindset. It was a direct reference to Rahul Gandhi’s mother, Sonia Gandhi, and her Italian origins. However, this is not an exception among BJP leaders. They have often been seen using such derogatory language targeting Sonia Gandhi’s foreign origins in the name of political opposition.
“…They Aren’t as Afraid Even when Their Wives Undergo Halala with other Men”
In a May 2022 post, Arun Yadav targeted Muslim women who were opposing surveys and excavations of mosques, making an obscene remark about them. Referring to the sensitive subject of “halala”, Yadav wrote: “As afraid as they are of the excavation of mosques, their wives aren’t even when they undergo halala with other men.”
In India, “halala” has long been the subject of an intense public debate. In Yadav’s post, the term was not merely used as part of a comment, but as a weapon to demean Muslim women.
More Islamophobia
In May 2022, Arun Yadav made another highly provocative post directly targeting Islam and the Muslim community. He wrote: “What kind of an ignorant community must those be whose Allah lives in temples stolen and looted from others?”
This was not simply a comment on the temple-mosque dispute. It was a direct attack on the Muslim community as a whole, using the dispute as a pretext. Yadav’s post was widely circulated.
“Who Got a Nine-month Recharge for Rs 500?”
One of the most shameful instances of Arun Yadav’s repeated targeting of Muslim women and making demeaning remarks about them emerged in May 2020. The case involved Jamia Millia Islamia student and activist Safoora Zargar.
Safoora was pregnant at the time and was imprisoned under the UAPA in connection with the 2020 Delhi riots case. While the detention of a pregnant woman was drawing criticism in India and abroad, Arun Yadav mocked Safoora’s pregnancy by comparing it to a mobile recharge plan.
Making a direct insinuation about her character, Yadav posted: “Who got a nine-month recharge for Rs 500?”
The matter did not end with the derogatory post. Yadav also actively endorsed other obscene and abusive comments posted under it. Arun Yadav was not the only BJP leader to make such remarks about Safoora’s pregnancy; several BJP leaders had also made demeaning comments about it.
The BJP’s IT Cell has long faced criticism over the spread of misinformation, targeting of minorities, promotion of regressive attitudes, circulation of controversial content and trolling. Its significance goes beyond the party’s own messaging: As one of the country’s most powerful political social media operations, it plays a significant role in shaping the information ecosystem — what millions of users see, discuss and believe online. Against that backdrop, Arun Yadav’s elevation is striking. A party that once disciplined him over communal posts has now entrusted him with a larger role in its national social media machinery. What was once grounds for his sacking has, years later, not come in the way of promotion.

At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals.
The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.
A statement by the hospital administration confirmed that 14 newborn babies had died in the fire.
Hospital spokesperson Dr Aneeza Jalil told Dawn newspaper that 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that “one baby was saved by a doctor”. Women who had just given birth were forced to run down several flights of stairs to evacuate.
The health minister, Mustafa Kamal, said many of the babies had been in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters had exacerbated the fire.
Kamal suggested that the blaze had been caused by an air conditioner but investigators were still at the scene and authorities have not confirmed the cause. Repair works and construction were ongoing at the hospital.
Sohail Ashraf, the Islamabad chief commissioner, said the emergency call was made just before 7am, with rescue and police teams quickly reaching the scene.
“The fire was immediately brought under control and the children were immediately shifted to the intensive care unit,” said the hospital administration’s statement.
The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation into the incident, which was one of the deadliest hospital fires in years.
“Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” said Sharif. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken.”
Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, expressed condolences to the families of the newborn babies. In a statement, he said that the loss of lives was “heartbreaking”.
Fires in large buildings such as factories and shopping malls are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and lax enforcement of building codes.

Washington, Aug 26:President Trump has submitted to Congress for review an agreement with Saudi Arabia aimed at bolstering the kingdom's civilian nuclear program, but continues to insist that it won't move forward if Saudi Arabia doesn't normalise relations with IsraelPresident Trump has submitted to Congress for review an agreement with Saudi Arabia aimed at bolstering the kingdom's civilian nuclear program, but continues to insist that it won't move forward if Saudi Arabia doesn't normalise relations with Israel.
The classified document was submitted to Capitol Hill on Monday as required by the Atomic Energy Act, according to the administration official, a congressional aide, and two others familiar with the matter. All four spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly on the classified matter.
The agreement was signed last month in Washington by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart. But the next day, Trump announced he was requiring the Saudis to normalise relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords as part of the pact, raising doubts that the agreement would come to fruition.
Neither the administration official nor the others familiar with the matter would comment on whether Trump's call for the Saudis to join the accords is detailed in the classified document submitted for the congressional review.
Under law, Congress has 90 days while in session to review the agreement. Unless Congress passes a joint resolution rejecting the agreement during the review period, the agreement can take effect without a vote by either chamber.
It is unusual for the entire contents of such agreements to be classified at such a high level. Previous civil nuclear pacts with other countries -- known as 123 agreements -- have been made public, although some of them have contained classified annexes that were not released.
The Saudi embassy in Washington did not have any immediate comment on the matter.
But Trump's continued insistence on the Saudis joining the accords could complicate the path to final approval. The accords approved in 2020 expanded the number of Arab and Muslim-majority nations with diplomatic ties with Israel.
The Saudis were taken by surprise by Trump's announcement that the completion of the civil nuclear deal would hinge on Riyadh's agreement to join the accords.
Trump faced fierce criticism from some lawmakers, including some who are concerned it could potentially help the Saudis fulfil their long-standing desire to enrich their own uranium and, in the process, spur new rounds of nuclear proliferation and competition.
The Saudis, meanwhile, have made clear that normalising relations with Israel would first require the establishment of a clear path for Palestinian statehood. And Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the idea of Palestinian statehood as being untenable for his country's security.
The deal, if approved, is expected to last 30 years and is also expected to involve US firms in developing the program following a joint US-Saudi study.
The formal submission of the agreement to Congress for review was reported earlier on Tuesday by the Wall Street Journal.

The countertop kitchen composter is a lovely thought. Instead of a smelly bucket of vegetable scraps and coffee grounds breeding fruit flies on your counter or attracting rats to your backyard, you could just put it all into a nifty electric gadget, and at some undetermined point in the future you'll have a bountiful supply of nutrient-rich compost to use in your garden.
Unfortunately, none of the more popular electric kitchen composters do exactly this. Even though some of these devices are marketed as “composters” and have instruction booklets and apps detailing all the ways in which one can use compost, the vast majority of kitchen composters are just going to grind up and dry your food scraps. You will greatly reduce your food waste output, and it will no longer smell, but if you’re hoping to put eggshells and banana peels into a machine and magically scoop out the kind of compost you’d buy at the garden center, that’s just not going to happen.
That said, you can mix small amounts of these grounds into potting soil in tiny ratios or use them as a feeder for a “real” compost pile. But again, most of these machines are meant for reducing the volume of household food waste. This is, itself, a legitimate goal, as cast-off food makes up 24 percent of municipal solid waste, resulting in the release of methane, a destructive greenhouse gas, as it breaks down in the landfill.
Or maybe you'd just like your food grounds to be odor-free and shelf-stable before adding them to your green waste bin for municipal composting or your backyard compost. In any case, despite critics’ cries of greenwashing and corporate astroturfing, there is indeed value to these devices. They make people more aware of their food waste. They don't use a huge amount of power (around 1 kilowatt-hour was typical in my testing). And my top pick, the Reencle Prime (8/10, WIRED Recommends), even produces something close to compost.
Also, be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems and Best Smart Bird Feeders.
Updated August 2026: I’ve added a section on the bokashi method, including testing notes on Bokashi Living’s signature bucket; more general buyer and user information; and a comparison table. Links and prices have also been updated.
Best Overall
As I mentioned above, none of these machines makes truly ready-to-use, biologically stable, fully decomposed compost, but Reencle comes the closest to creating what you'd scoop out of a traditional compost bin or pile. Popular in South Korea years before it appeared in the US, the Reencle arrives with a starter bag of Reencle Compost Starter 1.0 (which you can purchase separately for $65) containing activated carbon, wood pellets, glucose, and a trio of patented thermophilic microbes ready to chow down. There's also a prefilled charcoal filter that slots into the back.
The Prime is too large for a kitchen counter, but it conveniently operates much like a heated trash can. The lid opens via a sensor at the bottom or a button on the control panel, and it goes into your organic matter. That's it. There are no cycles, tablets, or auxiliary buckets to worry about. Even the app is totally optional. Within hours to days, depending on the item, the scraps break down into a material resembling a cross between dirt and sawdust.
The smell isn't always pleasant, but you can usually mitigate this with the control panel's Dry and Purify buttons or by adding what, in composting lexicon, is called “browns”—dry, carbon-rich materials, like bread or shredded paper.
The Reencle also tends not to stink when you feed it its preferred diet of 1.5 pounds of scraps per day. Unlike other machines, it can also accept meat and dairy. For larger households, there's the Reencle Gravity ($649), which is a couple of inches taller and can accept 3.3 pounds of waste a day. I also tested this and found it to be significantly quieter than the Prime—not that the Prime is noticeably loud, only about 30 decibels. The Gravity is nearly silent, which is a nice bonus. I did, however, find that over time, the Gravity contents went anaerobic (read: smelly) much faster than with the Prime. The increased volume seemed to retain more moisture. If you go with a Gravity, I recommend keeping plenty of browns (old bread, shredded paper) on hand to maintain microbial balance or adding in an additional few sessions of manual stirring per day with the included shovel.
When the volume reaches the fill line on each model, it’s time to scoop out the grounds. At this point, you can mix the grounds with potting soil at a 1:4 ratio and leave it to cure for three weeks (I used a large tub in my garage). Afterward, you can use it for both outdoor and indoor plants. I’ve used the resultant mix to positive effect both indoors and outdoors.
Eighteen-Month Update: For years, I’ve read about people experiencing the stainless steel stirring paddles breaking off in the Reencle Prime. And after a year and a half of using the device, the same fate has finally found me. I contacted Reencle to ask what customers should do in this situation. I learned that if the Reencle is within the warranty period (two years for units purchased on or after May 13, 2026; one year for units purchased previously), they can contact customer service to receive a paddle repair kit at no charge. If the unit is outside the warranty period, a kit runs $35. I don't love that this has happened, but Reencle's models are still the best of these devices, and I've found the company's customer service to be responsive and easy to work with, so it remains my top pick.

Most kitchen “composters" simply grind and dry your food scraps, but the Lomi 3 countertop composter does the best job of this of the bunch. I'm always impressed when companies listen to feedback and adapt, and Lomi's new model solves a couple of the quirks found on the now-discontinued Lomi 2. Gone are the multiple modes, the annoying twist-off lid, and the need to put scraps right into the machine. Now there's a convenient 3-liter, 7.5-inch-tall countertop bucket, just like the FoodCycler below; an easy push-button lid; and Grow and Express modes. The Lomi 3 is also smaller and supposedly quieter than the Lomi 2, but my decibel meter found the difference to be negligible. One feature I did like on Lomi 2 that's missing from the 3, however, is Lomi mode, which could break down a list of approved bioplastics, including Lomi's own packaging. Lomi confirms the new model cannot accept bioplastics.
Like with the Lomi 2, an app exists for basic management, but I enjoyed not having to use it; simply press a button, and the Lomi turns on. When it's done (cycle lengths vary from three to 16 hours, depending on amount and moisture of contents), it will play a little chime, and you can either put the processed grounds, which are very fine and look like Folgers, in your outdoor compost pile, top-dress your lawn with them, or add them to soil at a 1:10 ratio (1:15 if using meat or dairy). I also like that the Lomi 3 has a clear lid, so you can see exactly where it is in its cycle.
It's a lot to pay for what's essentially a grinder-and-dryer, which is why I generally recommend the Reencle above, especially if you want to generate something close to compost. However, if you're simply looking to reduce the volume of waste in your trash, or if you live in an area that's subject to composting fines, the Lomi 3 is a thoughtfully engineered, easy-to-use option most people would be happy to use.

Launched in 2024, the Eco 3 is a smaller version of the Vitamix FoodCycler FC-50 (7/10 WIRED Recommends), sporting a larger 3.5-liter capacity and, according to FoodCycler, better grinding capability. At 11 by 9 by 13 inches, it is small enough to sit on a counter or tabletop, though the real convenience with this machine is its auxiliary pail. Fill the sleek, 8-inch-tall lidded container with scraps (in my household of three people, this took about three days), and once it's full, swap out the lids, seat it in the machine, and press a button.
A few hours later, you'll have a handful of “Foodilizer,” a "homemade soil amendment” that looks like finely ground dirt. In fact, the output is one of the most finely ground of any of these machines. There's no assembly (other than filling a filter with carbon granules), no app, no making an account, no pods or tablets or choosing various cycles—you don't even have to plug it in until you're ready to use it.
The cycle runs from four to nine hours, depending on the water content of the scraps. All of these machines do a great job breaking down food scraps in some way or another, but none fully address what to do with them, absent a yard or compost pile. Adding them at a 1:10 (or 1:15!) ratio to potting soil is kind of a pain, and many people don't have the space to store all this dirt. The Mill is the only device that solves for this issue by allowing users to ship their grounds in a box via USPS to a farm in Washington state that repurposes the broken-down scraps for chicken feed (for an extra fee).
When I first tested the Mill in 2024 (6/10 WIRED Recommends), I didn't care for this idea, which seemed inefficient at best and canceled out the benefit of recycling the food waste at worst. I also didn't love the coarse texture of the grounds, having tried to use them in my garden and finding them too easily rehydrated. The price also seemed over the top for what's essentially an oversize Lomi. But if you're looking to reduce the amount of food waste leaving your house, the Mill has the best ease of use, requiring the least amount of work on a user's part.
Like the Reencle, it acts as a big trash can—you can throw in whatever you'd like at any time, and you can program a cycle any time you'd like via the app, which is exceedingly complete and user-friendly. There's an almost encyclopedic directory of what can and can't go in the machine, as well as a tracker that shows how many pounds of waste you've diverted over time. The Mill also has such a massive capacity that it only needs to be emptied about once a month, a claim I found to be accurate during my testing period. It's on the louder side at around 60 dB, so I highly recommend scheduling its processing cycle to run at night.
There are now two versions of the Mill: the Plus, which is the 27-inch version with a stylish wood-veneer top and lid-opening foot pedal that I tested, and the Essential, which is $200 cheaper, 4 inches shorter, and lacks the convenient foot pedal and wood-veneer finish. The Analog OG
To truly understand what problems these electric composters are solving for, one first needs to understand the original indoor home composting method: the bokashi bin. Unlike traditional outdoor composting, which is straightforward anaerobic decomposition, the bokashi method, invented in Japan in the 1980s, is instead anaerobic fermentation. This alternative method is a bit like quick-pickling your food waste to prep it for the decomposition process. The food scraps will still need to decompose, but this gets it part of the way there with the least amount of hassle and time. In fact, some gardeners even prefer bokashi to compost, as the output retains nitrogen, a critical plant nutrient.
To start, put your food scraps in the included bucket, and once you have about a 1-inch layer of waste, add a sprinkling of microbe-infused bran (a 2-pound bag of bran with a little spouted measuring cup is included with the Bokashi Living kit). The instruction booklet for my Bokashi Bin also recommended putting a plate inside the bucket to push down the contents. Compost “tea,” or liquid byproduct of the fermentation process, can be drained off the bottom through a spigot every couple of days and added to your outdoor plants. The smell is reminiscent of kombucha brewed in a hot dumpster with diapers and stale beer, so be sure to rinse out the cup each time.
Once your bin is full, let it sit for two weeks, and your food waste will have broken down enough to be able to bury in your garden or add to your backyard compost. I admit I struggled with this part—after two weeks, my scraps looked much the same, only stinkier and slimier. Bokashi Living says on its website that this is normal: If it has a pickle-like smell and produces bokashi tea, it's a success.
I’ll admit it was refreshing at first to have a device that didn’t make noise, need maintenance, or use electricity, but after a few weeks, I found myself sorely missing my Reencle. I didn’t keep a separate scrap bin on the countertop, so every time I needed to add refuse to the bucket, I had to peel the lid off with my dirty hands and remove the plate, which then made my hands even dirtier. The smell of fermenting food waste would then immediately—and as time went on, almost violently—permeate the kitchen and vicinity. I certainly prefer any of the above options, but bokashi has its devoted adherents. If what I've explained above doesn't sound bothersome to you, it may be worth a try.

Other Kitchen Composters I Tried
Clear Drop Organics Collector (OC) for $450: New from the makers of the innovative Soft Plastic Compactor, this simple white box does not claim to grind, process, or compost your food scraps; it simply stores up to 3.5 gallons' worth of them in an enclosed container with a fan and carbon filter for odor control. For its part, it did this well. I also appreciated the included paper-bag liners, which made it easy to drop off the scraps at a nearby collection bin, as my town does not have municipal compost. I also loved the sensor-activated lid that slides back and forth. Clear Drop posits that municipal composting is the best option overall for reducing waste via compost, because the process can be standardized for quality and is easy for everyone to do. I agree, but let's be real: You can get a carbon-filter compost canister for less than $30. If taking the compost out every couple of days instead of every seven days is a chore you're willing to pay $450 to avoid, then knock yourself out. But you should know that the OC makes a loud fan noise—40 dB on my decibel meter—which annoyed everyone in my household so much that I didn't even make it through the full test period.
Vego Countertop Kitchen Composter for $360: This grind-and-dry processor is roughly the same size as the Lomi 2, with many of the same operational features, but it is significantly less expensive. However, there are definitely some inconveniences that come with the lower price point. For one, you need to add scraps into the bucket while it’s seated in the machine. You can remove the bucket, but unlike with the FoodCycler, there's no separate lid for the bucket, and the metal mechanism underneath is exposed. Further, the machine’s lid is a bona fide pain to get on and off, requiring precise alignment of notches and two hands to wrench it open or closed. Needless to say, this is no easy feat with fists full of scraps. Vego claims its Vego mode does create a biologically active soil amendment when processed with one of the included VegoTabs (packet of 30, $30 if purchased separately). In all modes, but Vego mode especially, the barrel turns every couple of minutes, emitting a loud whirring. Because the sound isn't constant, it's more noticeable. Even from 10 feet away, I found it obtrusive enough to want to turn up the TV volume.
GEME Terra II for $649: Billed as the first “AI-powered kitchen appliance that uses industrial-grade microbes to turn waste into living soil,” this machine was the largest and bulkiest one I've tested (12 inches long, 22 inches high) and operates much like the Reencle, with a heated, enclosed container and a bag of proprietary starter microbes. Instead of a replaceable carbon filter, it uses a metal-ion purification system. Also like the Reencle, it does not make ready-to-use compost but, rather, pre-compost that can be mixed with dirt. What role AI plays in this process is unclear: I couldn’t find an explanation on the website, on the machine itself, or in the instruction booklet. (GEME says it is working on an improved description.) The Terra II's signature feature is that its industrial-grade microbes can withstand the supposed high heat of the breakdown process. However, when I put a temperature probe into the Terra II's pre-compost, it was 97 degrees Fahrenheit—nowhere near hot enough to kill pathogens. Further, during my testing period, this machine emitted a constant fan noise, like a range hood on medium speed—46 dB on my decibel meter, which was loud enough to be disruptive.
FoodCycler Eco 5 for $549: Like the Eco 3 above, this is a food recycler and doesn’t claim to create true compost. It’s a large, quiet machine; my 3-year-old likes to turn it on when I’m not looking, and I don’t notice until I see that the blue light is on. The result doesn’t look like compost, but it does get ground down to some bare-bones food bits after several extra cycles initiated by my son and his sneaky button-pushing. Each cycle runs between four and nine hours. It hasn’t been stinky, and I’ve found it handy to have nearby in the kitchen for food waste. It is quite large, though—nearly as bulky as my robot vacuum station due to its 5-liter capacity. The cheaper Eco 3 is likely a more efficient use of space in the kitchen, unless you have a ton of food scraps on a regular basis and really need the larger-capacity bin. —Nena Farrell
How I Tested
I cook daily for my family of three, and I've been processing our kitchen scraps in these composters in my home kitchen since summer 2024. Each was tested under typical household use for a minimum of four weeks each, and in several cases, six weeks or longer. I tested all cycles offered, with all manner of foods allowed, according to each manual. I even attempted to use the finished product in my yard and potted plants (to varying effect).

In July, an Alt News post about the upcoming Bollywood film ‘Chauhaan’ was removed twice by Instagram. The post survived when we shared it the third time, but only after two references to Burhan Wani were removed. The episode offers a glimpse into the opaque manner in which content restrictions are being enforced on Instagram in India, and raises key questions amid growing concerns over censorship on the platform.
The original post was a carousel based on an Alt News analysis of the teaser of ‘Chauhaan’ starring Ajay Devgn. The 2.24-minute video shows its protagonist dismissing pellet guns as an ineffective crowd-control measure causing only “limited damage”. This stands in stark contrast to the documented reality in Kashmir, where pellet guns have killed scores, and blinded or permanently disabled thousands. The teaser sparked an online backlash for trivialising violence as entertainment, pairing it with upbeat music. The story can be read here.
Alt News first uploaded the carousel on July 1. Instagram restricted the post within minutes. Since the carousel contained visuals of pellet injuries, Alt News initially suspected that these images might have triggered the removal. The carousel was therefore modified, with some of the visuals changed, and uploaded again.
Instagram removed the second version as well.
Alt News then removed two references to Burhan Wani on two slides in the carousel and uploaded it for a third time. This version was allowed to remain online.
The sequence raises the possibility that the use of Burhan Wani’s name itself may be restricted on Instagram in India — an apparent moderation measure that has not been publicly announced by either Meta or the Indian government.
A search for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram currently yields no results.
What makes the episode particularly striking is that Instagram never explicitly told Alt News why the post was being removed. The platform’s notifications stated that the action had been carried out “through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements” and cited India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
The notification did not identify the specific legal requirement behind the action, the government order on the basis of which the post had been restricted, or the particular element of the post that had triggered the removal — a point that multiple users affected by the government-ordered censorship frenzy has flagged over the past weeks.
An Opaque Moderation System that Leaves Users Guessing
As for us, Alt News had to figure it out through trial and error. This raises the question — Why should a user have to go through this process to find out why their post has been restricted? If a particular name, word or image is prohibited under a legal order, why does the notification not clearly state so? A user should not have to repeatedly alter and repost content, guessing what may have triggered a platform’s moderation system.
The opacity is particularly concerning because the platform appears to know what triggered the restriction. Its automated system identified the content and removed it within minutes, yet the user is given no meaningful explanation for the action. Instead, the notification offers only a generic reference to an automated system and “legal requirements”.
Besides, a blanket restriction on a name such as “Burhan Wani” makes little sense because names can occur in entirely unrelated contexts. Other people may share the same name, while legitimate references, including news reports, historical discussions or fact checks, could be caught by the same restriction.
Alt News emailed Meta spokespersons asking when the apparent moderation rule relating to Burhan Wani was implemented, why it was enforced without public notification, why users were not clearly informed about the reason for the restriction, and what other names or keywords may be subject to similar restrictions. The company has not responded.
Interestingly, we found that a similar restriction may be in place for ‘Monu Manesar’ was well. A search with these terms throws up the same response. Mohit Yadav alias Monu Manesar, a controversial ‘gau rakshak’ associated with the Bajrang Dal, has been accused in several cases linked to vigilantism and communal violence. He was arrested in 2023 in connection with the alleged abduction and murder of Nasir and Junaid, two Muslim men from Haryana. He has denied the allegations against him.
The apparent restriction comes amid a wider and increasingly opaque censorship controversy surrounding Instagram in India. A recent investigation by The Indian Express found that from March to July 2026, the government sent 1.95 lakh blocking orders to Meta, or one every minute on an average. Over 1 lakh of these were for Instagram.
The Burhan Wani episode illustrates another dimension of this opacity. If the name is itself subject to an undisclosed moderation rule, users have no way of knowing this in advance, or of understanding why content that merely mentions him is being restricted.
And even though the sequence strongly suggests that the references to Burhan Wani triggered the removals, this remains an inference. Instagram has not confirmed that this was the reason.
Fact-Check Posts Restricted
Posts related to an Alt News fact check were restricted in July 2026 on both Faecebook and Instagram.
The report looked at false claims about an old video that showed armed Nihangs clashing with police and breaching barricades. It was being circulated as ‘Khalistanis’ joining the Cockroach Janta Party protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. In reality, the video was from June 25, 2026, nearly a month before the CJP protests, and showed Nihangs from Punjab marching toward Uttarakhand during a protest. The story can be read here.
Our social media posts on the fact check were restricted in India by both the platforms. And we do not know why.
Readers should note that a click on the ‘How we made this decision’ tab does not bring about any clarity. The response only states, “We are legally required to restrict access to your post in certain locations. We have taken this action based on a local legal requirement.”

A video showing a submarine launch is being shared with the claim that it shows Iran unveiling its first locally made nuclear submarine (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows Iran unveiling its first locally made nuclear submarine.
Fact: This video shows a Japanese Taigei-class diesel-electric submarine from 2023. Iran is not publicly known to possess nuclear-powered or nuclear-armed submarines. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
On performing a relevant keyword search regarding the viral claim, we found no credible news reports about Iran unveiling a nuclear-powered submarine. By conducting a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video, we found a similar video posted on X on 26 June 2023. The caption of the post stated, “Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force 4th Taigei-class Attack Submarine Raigei (SS-516).”
Based on this clue, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found a YouTube video uploaded by a channel called “Military Coverage” on 17 October 2023. The video featured a longer version of the same footage and also identified the vessel as Japan’s fourth Taigei-class submarine, Raigei (JS-516). The video did not mention Iran.
Further investigation led us to the official website of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force, which confirms that the naming and launch ceremony of the FY2020-planned submarine Raigei was held at Kawasaki Heavy Industries’ Kobe Plant on 17 October 2023. The JMSDF identifies Raigei as the fourth Taigei-class submarine, with the hull number 516, and states that it uses diesel-electric propulsion.
The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force issued a press release on 28 February 2025, stating that the handover ceremony of the submarine would be held on 6 March 2025, in Kobe, Japan.
As of August 2026, Iran is not publicly known to possess nuclear-powered or nuclear-armed submarines. Its indigenous Ghadir, Nahangand Fateh-class submarines use conventional diesel-electric propulsion.
To sum up, an old video of a Japanese submarine’s launch is falsely shared as showing Iran’s first domestically built nuclear submarine.

Following the attacks on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) workers in Rajasthan, several social media users claimed that CJP convenor Ashutosh Ranka was accompanied by a man who had earlier been found calling for demolishing the Parliament and provoking Nepal-like violence during the July 20 protest in Delhi.
As part of its ‘School Thik Karo’ initiative, a CJP team visited a government school operating from a buffalo shed at Rampura in Kanwarpura area of Jaipur district in Rajasthan when they were allegedly attacked. They reported being beaten with sticks and pelted with stones. CJP later accused the attackers of being affiliated with the BJP.
On August 21, X user Office of Vijay Patel (@VijayGajeraO) claimed that Ranka had arrived with “goons” who wanted to attack Parliament and trigger Nepal-style mass violence in India. The post featured a collage comparing a man accompanying Ranka with another man seen in a viral video from the CJP protest. The latter had allegedly said that Parliament would be attacked and a Nepal-like situation created if Dharmendra Pradhan did not resign. (Archive)
Ashutosh Ranka came with the goons who wanted to attack the parliament and wanted to cause Nepal-style mass violence in India. pic.twitter.com/yoKV2KnetZ
— Office Of Vijay Patel (@VijayGajeraO) August 21, 2026
The handle is run by Right-wing influencer Vijay Patel who claims to be an investigative journalist. The post has garnered over 850,000 views.
Abhijit Iyer Mitra (@Iyervval), another Right-wing influencer, shared and amplified the claim. (Archive)
The most important part of this video isn’t what happened today. It’s the fact that this video captured a stated intent to commit violence on 20th July outside parliament. Also that far from being “outsiders”, the rioters were in fact core CJP members. https://t.co/r0VbwXGEfU
— Abhijit Iyer-Mitra (@Iyervval) August 21, 2026
The post amassed over 150,000 views.
Another pro-BJP handle user, Raushan Sinha (@Mrsinha), also shared a similar comparison, claiming that the man who once threatened to turn India into a Nepal-like situation during the protest is now a CJP volunteer. His post read, “From threatening Parliament to becoming a ‘volunteer’ for CJP, quite a journey for the champions of democracy.”
The post gained around 100,000 views, and thereafter it was deleted.
This is not the first time that such comparisons have been made. Immediately after the July 20 protest, it was claimed that the man who called for Nepal-like violence had been seen sitting with Abhijeet Dipke, and was a CJP core member.
Fact Check
A closer examination of the two visuals — the Rajasthan video and the Jantar Mantar footage — reveals that the comparison is flawed, as they are two different people.
The man seen with Ashutosh Ranka and the CJP team is Vijay Sherawat, who hails from Jaipur, Rajasthan.
Alt News found a video that Sherawat had shared in response to the older claim, in which he defends himself against false accusations. He clarifies that he was not the same person who remarked that a Nepal-like situation would be created in India and the Parliament would be set afire if Pradhan did not resign.
In the video uploaded on July 31, Sherawat stated, “It is the IT cell people who are engaging in this low-level politics to defame the CJP team. I am not that person.” He also strongly condemned the remarks made by the other individual during the protest and called for appropriate punishment for those comments.
अंधभक्तों से सावधान🚨#cockroachjantaparty #abhijeetdipke pic.twitter.com/rYrYDxhjKA
— Vijay Sherawat🇮🇳 (@vijaysherawat5) July 31, 2026
The individual whose video went viral during the ‘Chalo Sansad’ march has also been identified as Saurav Singh, who claims to be a physiotherapist by profession.
View this post on Instagram
Below is a comparison between the a screengrab from the viral threat video and a close-up shot of Singh from a reel he shared on Instagram:
To sum up, the individual who provoked violence and threatened to set the Parliament ablaze is not the same one as the one seen with Ashutosh Ranka during the CJP team’s visit to Rajasthan or with Abhijeet Dipke in an older video. The individual seen with the CJP leaders is Vijay Sherawat. The man who issued threats at Jantar Mantar is Saurav Singh.
After the post by @VijayGajeraO was called out as false, the user reshared it with a corrigendum acknowledging the mistake. However, the false claim has not been taken down.

He staggered rather than sprang out of the lake but it wasn’t surprising.
Neil Gilson, a former international athlete, could be forgiven for feeling a little wobbly, having become the first person to swim the 10 largest lakes in Switzerland, a total of about 230 miles (370km).
Over the last two summers, Gilson, a father of three from Devon in the English West Country, has ticked the lakes off and on Wednesday he finished swimming the 45-mile length of Lac Léman (Lake Geneva), taking just over 22 hours.
His 12-year-old daughter, Lily, and 10-year-old son, Jack, were in the water waiting as he neared the end to accompany him across the finishing line.
“They swam the last 200m with me,” Gilson said. “There were tears in my goggles. For the whole challenge, I was envisioning that moment. It kept me going through some difficult times – lovely.”
Gilson, 40, was once ranked second in Britain for the 1500-metre freestyle and after finishing race swimming, turned to endurance challenges. In 2024, he swam across Lac Léman in 22 hours and nine minutes, a world record. But it wasn’t enough. He decided to tackle 10 Swiss lakes.
Gilson put in countless hours in the pool at a leisure centre, the sea off the north Devon coast and the gym to prepare.
There have been blips. Gilson admits that a swim of about 40 miles in Lake Maggiore this summer almost broke him. It was colder than he anticipated and he had to swim more quickly to get his core temperature up, which meant he used more energy than planned. He had “nothing left” for the last few miles.
Lake Thun proved surprisingly difficult as the pressure to complete the challenge – and the physical effort – caught up with him. After clambering out of the lake, he said: “My arms don’t like me and I feel shattered.”
Gilson said he found swimming in lakes more demanding than the sea. “They’re more unpredictable. You can get some really choppy conditions because of the wind and you can hit walls of cold water.”
He began Léman on Tuesday morning and finished on Wednesday lunchtime. He admitted that 18 hours into the swim, he thought of giving up. “It was so tough in the night – the current was strong. I felt really close to stopping but what kept me going was my family waiting there.”
Gilson said his support team, which accompanied him in a boat, helped by giving him coffee – and saying “the right things”.
He just missed out on beating his own world record for Léman, but is confident Guinness World Records will recognise him as the first to complete what has been billed the Legend of the Lakes challenge – and in subsequent years, that other ultra-swimmers may try to do it more quickly.
As well as doing the swim as an extraordinary challenge, Gilson is seeking to draw attention to a neuropsychiatric condition, Pandas, that affected his son at 18 months old. People with Pans or Pandas experience a variety of symptoms ranging from mental health symptoms to changes in behaviour and difficulties with movement.
Jack was diagnosed with Pandas after catching tonsillitis. “He went to bed a happy, healthy little boy, and woke up as someone we didn’t recognise, gripped by aggression, OCD [obsessive-compulsive disorder], tics and intense fear; he refused to eat, wouldn’t leave the house or even speak. It was terrifying,” Gilson said.
Jack is doing well – as shown by his joining his dad for the last leg of his swim – but Gilson said: “The challenge has always been about more than swimming. Every lake, every kilometre and every difficult moment has been about raising awareness of Pans and Pandas.
“It’s a condition that isn’t rare but is rarely diagnosed. Raising awareness of it means more than anything.”

Consumer appliances brand Atomberg filed its draft IPO papers with market regulator SEBI, for a proposed public issue comprising a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 7.65 Cr equity shares. Institutional investors A91 Partners, Temasek Holdings, Inflexor Ventures, and Steadview Capital intend to dilute their stake in the company via the IPO. Including the selling shareholders, the company has a total of 69 shareholders till date. A91 Partners holds the highest stake of 21.02% in the company via holding entity A91 Emerging Fund I. The investor first backed the startup in 2019, as part of its Series A funding round of $10 Mn, along with Whiteboard Capital and Survam Partners, back then. Following A91, cofounders Manoj Kumar Meena and Sibabrata Das own 17.73% and 10.02%, respectively. Meena and Das are not selling any shares in the IPO. Meanwhile, Temasek, via its holding entity V-Sciences Investments, commands 11.8% ownership in Atomberg. While Jungle Ventures (JV4) holds 10.03%, Steadview Capital Mauritius and Jongsong Investments own 7% and 6.98% in the company, respectively, Further, Inflexor Ventures, via Inflexor Opportunities Fund I and Inflexor Technology Fund, holds 6.08% ownership in Atomberg. Founded in 2012 by Meena and Das, Atomberg initially focused on selling energy-efficient brushless direct current (BLDC) fans to businesses before entering the consumer market in 2016. It has since then expanded beyond fans into categories such as mixer grinders, water purifiers, and cold-pressed juicers. However, fans continue to be its largest revenue-generating product category. Atomberg now sells its products through offline retailers, online marketplaces, and its own website. The company obtained the board approval for its public listing, about a week ago. Additionally, the board also approved the raise of up to ₹90 Cr via a pre-IPO placement of equity shares. On the financial front, the consumer appliances company saw its consolidated net loss widen 26.8% to ₹148.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹117.4 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue jumped 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the year under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. A Break Down Of Atomberg’s Leadership Deck Board of Directors Manoj Kumar Meena Meena is the managing director and chairman of the company. He founded Atomberg and headed the company as its chief executive for the first 14 years. Sibabrata Das Das is the CEO and executive director of Atomberg. He cofounded the company along with Meena and headed as the chief operating officer till 2025. Prior to that, he was the CEO for almost a year of online personal care brand 24x7 Styles. Abhay Kumar Pandey A91 Partners’ general partner Pandey is the nominee director on Atomberg’s board. While he has been a general partner at A91 Partners for nearly eight years, he previously worked with Peak XV Partners for over 11 years. He has been part of the boards of companies like Awfis, Bira 91, curatio, among others. Anand Kantilal Vora United Phosphorus Ltd’s CFO Vora is an independent director on Atomberg’s board. Over a finance career spanning nearly four decades, Vora has worked with companies like Dow Chemical & Dow AgroSciences, Ranbaxy Brazil and HTMT Global Solutions. Suman Gopalan Gopalan, who has been the managing partner at Rivendell Advisory for over two years, has been on the board of Atomberg for about four months as an independent director. Previously, she has also worked with Freshworks as chief HR officer for about five years. Subhasis Chaudhuri Chaudhur, also an independent director at Atomberg, has been a full time professor at IIT Bombay since 1990. Besides, he is currently the chairperson of BSE’s board, a position he has held for nearly two years. Key Managerial Personnel Manish Kumar Bansal Bansal is the chief financial officer of the company for nearly four years. Prior to this stint, he was working with L’Oreal for more than six years. Holding an overall experience of 20 years, he previously worked with Marico and kaya skin care. Priti Baria Joined on November 11, 2024 as manager of legal function, Baria is now the lead of legal, company secretary and compliance officer at Atomberg. Prior to this, she worked with WestRock Company as India legal and company secretary for over a year. She holds an overall experience of 15 years, working with companies like Bajaj Consumer Care, Knight Frank India and Parker Hannifin, among others.

The main drug that has been in use for decades to combat malaria in sub-Saharan Africa is running into a problem: In recent years, researchers have become increasingly concerned that parasites are becoming less sensitive to treatment. Identifying the underlying genetic factors has become an urgent priority.
In an attempt to identify the reason for drug-resistant malaria, a team led by Brown University researchers conducted whole-genome analysis of 157 malaria parasite samples selected from specimens collected in Uganda between 2016 and 2024. The work, published in Nature Medicine this week, shows evidence that mutations in a gene that encodes a protein called px1, which had previously received little attention, is likely responsible for the rise in drug resistance.
“Malaria still is a major killer, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa,” Jeffrey Bailey, an associate professor at Brown University specializing in pathology, says in a press release. “As drug resistance continues to emerge, we worry it will undermine control of its spread and result in even more deaths for a large number of people there and beyond.”
When Bailey’s research team examined the px1 gene in detail, they found that a set consisting of three amino acid mutations and two deletions—the loss of a portion of a chromosome or DNA sequence—was being passed down through generations. The researchers named this cluster of mutations PIN.
Genes undergo recombination with each generation, causing their sequences to gradually break down. However, malaria parasites carrying the PIN mutation were found to have passed on a large region surrounding the px1 gene to multiple individuals almost entirely intact. This suggests that not enough time has elapsed since the PIN mutation emerged for genetic recombination to occur, indicating that it has spread rapidly in recent years.
To pinpoint when the PIN mutation first appeared, the research team examined historical samples and confirmed the presence of the PIN mutation for the first time in a sample from 2008. Since then, the PIN mutation has spread at an astonishing rate. By 2016, half of the samples from northern Uganda showed evidence of the mutation, and as of 2023, the same was true for eastern Uganda. By 2024, the prevalence had reached 84 percent in the north and 55 percent in the east.
Furthermore, the research team compared the response to common antimalarial drugs between malaria parasites carrying the PIN mutation and those that did not. The results of the experiment showed that malaria parasites carrying the PIN mutation exhibited reduced sensitivity to lumefantrine—one component of the combination drug artemether-lumefantrine that’s commonly used to treat the parasite—as well as other antimalarials.
To confirm whether these results were truly due to the px1 gene itself, the researchers used malaria parasites created in a previous study by intentionally disrupting the px1 gene and examined their response to the drugs in the same manner. They found that the parasites lacking the px1 gene responded more strongly to these treatments. In a separate test examining resistance to artemisinin, no clear differences were observed due to the PIN mutation.
Previous research has pointed to mutations in a gene called Kelch13 (K13) being associated with artemisinin resistance. However, for lumefantrine, no verified marker mutations had been identified.
“We didn’t have any validated molecular marker of lumefantrine resistance,” Karamoko Niare, the paper’s lead author, says in a press release. “We knew that there was a gene involved in partial resistance to artemisinin but couldn’t explain changes observed for lumefantrine.” He noted that this new mutation should be incorporated into surveillance systems and further studied.
When the research team examined historical global genetic databases collected between 2001 and 2015, it found that the PIN mutation was still extremely rare at that time, with only five samples identified in the neighboring countries of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Kenya. Notably, the mutation was not detected in 13 samples from Uganda collected in 2010 that were included in this dataset. The extent to which this mutation has spread across borders remains unclear due to a lack of up-to-date data.
This study merely demonstrated changes in drug susceptibility at the laboratory level; the extent to which this affects clinical outcomes in actual malaria patients remains unclear. The researchers point out that, in order to continue providing effective malaria treatment, it is urgent to establish systems for predicting when drugs will become ineffective and to develop new treatments.

Spirit Airlines may have declared bankruptcy this spring, but the budget airline is still worth something—to AI giants, at least. In mid-August, Google won a $10 million bid to purchase some 34 years of the airline’s data, from invoices and flight operations information to Wi-Fi sales, employee records, and crew pairings.
In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge.
If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems.
The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!”
The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI.
But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say.
“There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.”
In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions. Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals, cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them.
The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records.
The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9.
One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment.
The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says.
In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information.
Though the flight attendants’ objections are just a small part of the larger Spirit Airlines bankruptcy proceeding, the outcome could have a major effect on how labor unions and companies think about employee data going forward, says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine, who studies privacy and technology.
“In a world where billions and trillions are being spent on [large language models], anything where words are used is subject to its own profit-making purpose,” he says. “If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.”
The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value. “All workers bring an immense amount of knowledge,” Patel says. “Now artificial intelligence has given us the ability to process all different kinds of data.”
More value, meanwhile, is one of the former Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ goals. Separately, the union has also intervened in the bankruptcy to demand roughly $68 million in unpaid vacation, health care, and back pay.
“We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.
