3 Telangana students killed in Florida after car veers off highway, catches fire
Three Telangana students were killed in a crash on Interstate 95 in Florida while travelling to work. The driver and the front-seat passenger died at the scene.
Three students from Telangana were killed in a road accident in Brevard County, Florida, on Tuesday. The crash occurred on Interstate 95 near mile marker 172 in Palm Bay. According to preliminary information, the vehicle carrying the students veered off the highway, hit a tree and caught fire. The victims were travelling to their part-time workplace when the accident occurred.
One of the deceased has been identified as N. Rahul, a native of Navipet in Nizamabad district, Telangana. Rahul had travelled to the United States around three months ago for higher studies. He had completed his master's degree and had enrolled for a PhD at the University of South Florida while also looking for employment.
The driver and the front-seat passenger reportedly died at the scene, while Rahul was taken to a hospital where he later succumbed to his injuries. The identities of the other two victims have not yet been officially disclosed.
Rahul's family has appealed to the Telangana and Central governments for assistance in bringing his mortal remains back to India. The Telugu Association of North America (TANA) is reportedly coordinating with authorities regarding the necessary formalities and repatriation.
The family said they received information about the tragedy early Wednesday morning. Rahul had reportedly spoken to his mother shortly before his friends arrived to pick him up for work.
Further details are awaited as authorities continue their investigation into the accident.

Less than two months after the Supreme Court ruled against President Donald Trump’s attempt to fire a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors — a move that would have allowed him to seize control over the nation’s central bank if it had succeeded — Trump is once again trying to fire the very same member.
Trump’s new attempt to seize control of the Federal Reserve, explained
This completely unnecessary showdown was brought to you by an incompetent Supreme Court.
Earlier this month, Trump sent a letter to Lisa Cook, a Joe Biden appointee to the Federal Reserve, demanding that she respond to exceedingly flimsy allegations that she committed mortgage fraud. This is the first step in a process that is likely to end in Trump attempting to remove her from the Federal Reserve’s board a second time — which means that the courts will inevitably have to get involved once again.
Cook has until Wednesday to respond to Trump’s allegations.
It’s tempting to blame this bout of déjà vu on Trump, but the Supreme Court is at least as responsible for his actions as the president itself. If the Court didn’t want Trump to thumb its nose at their decision in Trump v. Cook (2026), they should have written that decision clearly enough that lawyers could actually figure out what the president is and is not allowed to do.
This is a perennial issue with the Court’s current majority, which is unusually bad at explaining themselves. They invent bold new doctrines that give them a near-complete veto power over the executive branch, then only apply this doctrine to Democratic presidents. They once handed down an anti-abortion decision that, if taken seriously, would allow any state to nullify literally any constitutional right. Every single one of their Second Amendment decisions are so incoherent that it is impossible for lower court judges to figure out how to apply them.
The Cook decision, which involved Trump’s first attempt to fire Cook, is similarly incomprehensible. It was handed down the same morning as Trump v. Slaughter (2026), which seems to hold that Trump can fire anyone who leads a federal agency. But Cook does not even cite the Slaughter decision, much less explain why the two cases are different.
Slaughter was grounded in the “unitary executive,” a theory shared by all six of the Court’s Republicans which claims that the president must have full control over federal agencies, including the power to fire their leaders — and thus agencies that have some ability to act independently of the president, such as the Federal Reserve, are unconstitutional. Cook suggests that there’s a Federal Reserve exception to this theory, although the opinion does not offer a clear explanation of why this exception exists.
There are very good policy reasons why Trump should not be able to fire Cook, or any other member of the Federal Reserve’s board. The Fed has the power to inject cocaine into the US economy, temporarily giving it a boost at the price of much greater turmoil and higher inflation down the road. If presidents are allowed to fire the Fed’s leaders, they can remove anyone who refuses to give the economy a bump during an election year — boosting the president or his party’s reelection chances, and triggering consequences that won’t be felt until after the election is over.
But the fact that preserving the Fed’s independence from the president is a good idea does not mean that the Constitution permits it. And, in Slaughter and several related cases, the Court’s Republican majority endorsed an interpretation of the Constitution that is completely incompatible with the idea of an independent Federal Reserve.
That means that, until the Court resolves this tension between Slaughter and Cook, there’s likely to be a great deal of confusion about who really controls the Fed — Trump or its current board — and whether Trump may effectively order the Fed to take actions that benefit him, but that could cause lasting harm to the US economy.
The unitary executive, briefly explained
The issue at the heart of Cook was whether the president is able to fire a member of the Federal Reserve.
Federal law provides that the Federal Reserve’s governors may only be fired “for cause,” and not simply because the president does not like them or disagrees with their policy views. The Republican justices have also long argued that Congress is forbidden from limiting the president’s power to fire federal agency leaders, because this would give the president less than full control over the federal government’s executive branch.
These justices point to a line in the Constitution that states that “the executive power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America.” According to the Court’s Republican majority, this means that the president must have full control over any federal agency that wields power that is “executive” in nature, including the power to fire that agency’s leaders for any reason whatsoever. As Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in an influential 1988 dissenting opinion, this constitutional provision “does not mean some of the executive power, but all of the executive power” is held by the president.
There are numerous problems with this unitary executive theory. The biggest one is that, while the Constitution does say that there is something called the “executive power” that belongs to the president, it does not define what this power is, and the Court’s decisions embracing the idea of a unitary executive often rely on dubious historical claims.
But, regardless of whether the unitary executive rests on a sound reading of the Constitution, it is now the law. And Slaughter suggests that this Court’s definition of the term “executive power” is quite expansive. In that case, the Court indicated that any agency leader who “enforces and administers” a federal statute wields “executive” power, and thus must be fireable at will by the president.
But then, almost immediately after the Court handed down Slaughter, it ruled in Cook that Trump could not fire one of the Fed’s leaders — or, at least, that he could not do so right away.
The Cook decision is word salad
Under the Republican justices’ definition of which officials wield executive power, and thus must be fireable at will by the president, Cook clearly should qualify. But five justices, the three Democrats plus Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh, joined a majority opinion by Roberts that, at least, temporarily delayed Trump’s ability to fire Cook. Three other justices took the coward’s way out, arguing in dissent that Trump should win on narrow procedural grounds that would have allowed him to fire Cook, but that also might permit a court to reinstate her at some point in the future.
Only Justice Clarence Thomas seemed to fully embrace the unitary executive theory, in Cook, and with it the idea that firing Cook is well within Trump’s power.
As Thomas wrote in his dissent, the Federal Reserve enforces or administers numerous federal statutes. It can “change the fees on consumer debit-card transactions,” or “impose monetary penalties, levy assessments, and examine private books and records.” Its power to set interest rates flows from federal statutes requiring it to “promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.”
Thus, if Slaughter is correct that an agency leader who “enforces and administers” a federal statute must be fireable at will by the president, Trump should have the power to fire Cook.
Roberts’s majority opinion doesn’t really make a legal argument. But it does make a couple of historical and policy claims that point in the direction of allowing an independent Federal Reserve to exist. Roberts begins his opinion with a history of nationally chartered banks, noting that the first such bank “predates even our Constitution “And he alludes to a “‘long tradition’ of ‘monetary policy … exercised independent of … executive influence.’”
But it’s hard to tell why this tradition matters, at least in a world where every other federal agency is subject to the unitary executive. The Republican justices have previously claimed, for example, that the president must have full control over all federal prosecutions. But historical evidence suggests that, at the founding, prosecutions were often led by private attorneys or by judicial appointees — that is, not by the president or his appointees. So why doesn’t this historical evidence exempt the Justice Department from the unitary executive?
And, if the legal reasoning in Cook is thin, the decision’s actual holding is largely toothless. After laying out his half-baked argument for why the Federal Reserve is unlike any other federal agency, Roberts doesn’t actually write that Trump may not fire Cook. He simply says that “Cook was entitled to notice and some opportunity to respond prior to her termination” — although Roberts also writes that, once Cook has a chance to respond to the allegations against her, “only then can the courts assess the validity and sufficiency of such charges.”
So, by sending a letter to Cook informing her of the allegations against her and giving her a little bit of time to respond, Trump has complied with the Supreme Court’s decision. He will likely then attempt to fire her no matter what she says in response, and then there will be another round of litigation where some poor trial judge will have to “assess the validity and sufficiency” of the allegations against Cook without any guidance from the Supreme Court regarding how strong those allegations must be.
That said, it is likely that when Cook does respond to Trump’s allegations, those allegations will prove quite flimsy indeed. Trump alleges that Cook committed mortgage fraud by claiming two separate properties as her principal residence in bank documents. But Reuters examined those bank documents and discovered that she disclosed to the lender that one of those properties would be used as a vacation home. So it appears that no fraud actually occurred.
Will that be enough for Cook to keep her job? The short answer is “probably” — why would the Supreme Court have handed down such an incoherent opinion in Cook if it intended to apply the unitary executive to her anyway? But the Cook opinion itself offers little guidance to the judges who will need to sort through this mess.

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Prince Harry and Meghan arrive back in UK to begin new life
In short:
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan have arrived back in England with their two children.
The family flew on a private jet from California to Birmingham after six years living in the United States.
The family’s announcement earlier this month that they were returning to the UK came as a surprise.
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday, six years after they moved their lives to California amid simmering tensions within the royal family.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex last week made a surprise announcement they would be relocating back to Britian with their children.
UK media reported a private jet landed at Birmingham International Airport around noon local time (9pm AEST) — a claim backed up by publicly available flight-tracking data.
It has been speculated the couple will live at a private residence in the picturesque Cotswolds region outside of London.
The couple's two children, seven-year-old Archie and Lilibet, five, have already been enrolled in a British school.
Harry and Meghan gave up their royal duties at the start of 2020 and moved to the exclusive seaside area of Montecito, near Santa Barbara, as relations with his family soured.
They pursued their own independent careers but never left the headlines as they did tell-all interviews with Oprah Winfrey, produced Netflix series and continued to take on the press in court over breaches of security.
In the last couple of years of Queen Elizabeth II's life, the couple made allegations against palace staff as being insensitive to Meghan and levelled allegations of racism at members of the royal family.
After losing his fight for government funded security protection last year, the Duke of Sussex told the BBC he could not see a world where he would feel safe returning to the UK with his family.
The prince's relationship with his father King Charles, who is living with cancer, is said to have improved in recent times, in particular after a visit last month.
The Duke visited the UK in July for his charity work with the Invictus Games and also brought the family across from their Portugal holiday home for a surprise visit, allowing the King to see his grandchildren for the first time in four years.
Prior to that, the last time the entire Sussex family was in the UK together was for the Queen's funeral in 2022.
But it's widely reported Harry is not on speaking terms with his brother and heir-to-the-throne, Prince William.
The announcement of their return came a day before a London court ruling meant Harry could be liable to pay millions of pounds to the publisher of the Daily Mail newspaper after a failed privacy lawsuit.
Meghan is reportedly in talks about a return to acting although neither her agent nor the speculated TV drama have commented.

At least 384 travellers, including 105 Indians, have been reported missing following a flash flood in the Bhote Koshi River in Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Wednesday morning, the Nepal Tourism Board said. The missing travellers include 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali nationals.
Of the 291 foreign nationals reported missing, others include citizens of Australia, the Netherlands, the United States, Malaysia, the United Kingdom and South Africa.
The nationalities of several other foreign travellers are yet to be confirmed, while 37 have been listed as non-resident Indians (NRIs).
The Embassy of India in Kathmandu has issued emergency helpline numbers for assistance and information regarding Indian nationals affected by the flash floods in Nepal.
Those seeking assistance can contact +977 985 131 6807 or +977 970 910 7500, the MEA said.
The preliminary list was compiled using information from 10 tourism and travel agencies. The Tourism Board, Tourist Police and other tourism stakeholders are working with travel agencies, guides, local authorities and security agencies to verify the whereabouts and safety of those reported missing, as cited by Nepal News.
The preliminary agency-wise records show that 92 travellers were associated with Trekkers Society, 71 with Samrat Tours & Travels, 55 with Leaf Holiday, 52 with Himalayan Glacier, 31 with Kailash Journey, 27 with Fishtail Tours & Travels, 20 with Alpine Eco Trek, 17 with Kathmandu Holiday Tours & Travels, 12 with Richa Tours & Travels and seven with Explore Vacation.
Tourists in the affected areas have been advised to remain calm, stay updated through official channels and follow safety instructions issued by authorities.
Those requiring emergency assistance can contact 1234, 1144 or the Tourist Police at 9851289445, Nepal News reported.
They can also approach the nearest police or security personnel, local administration, travel agency, guide or tour operator.
At least seventeen people have been confirmed dead and more than 25 rescued following the flash flood, Nepal Army officials said, according to local media reports.
Police said four bodies were recovered from Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot, near the Trishuli River. The Nepal Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have been deployed for search-and-rescue operations, with 14 helicopters, drones and sniffer dogs being used to locate those still missing.
The Nepal Army said six people were rescued from Syafrubesi, two from Mailung and four from Dhunche in Rasuwa. It has also established an emergency treatment centre at Military Training Centre No. 1 in Trishuli.
Four Armed Police Force personnel were initially reported missing from Rasuwa, while another report said nine personnel stationed at Timure, near the Nepal-China border, remained unaccounted for.
A sudden surge in the Bhote Koshi River struck the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area at around 9 am local time, affecting Rasuwa as well as parts of the neighbouring Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
The flooding washed away vehicles, goods, bridges and other infrastructure, while several hydropower projects also suffered damage.
Amid concerns over a potential flood threat in Bihar following heavy rainfall in Nepal, Union home minister Amit Shah spoke to Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary over the phone, news agency ANI reported.
Shah assured the Bihar government of all possible assistance to deal with the situation, while the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) is being mobilised to respond to any emergency.
Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath also expressed concern over the flood situation in Nepal and directed authorities in vulnerable districts to remain alert.

Rockstar calls GTA 6 leaks 'heartbreaking for our team' and says the game is nearly finished
Ahead of the extended look at GTA 6 on Netflix, Rockstar has addressed leaked gameplay videos in a statement.
Rockstar Games has issued a statement on the recent Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks, just ahead of an official extended look at the game. The publisher — publicly acknowledging for the first time that the clips are legitimate — called the leaked videos "heartbreaking for our team" and indicated they may include some spoilers. It added that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time."
The GTA 6 developer apologized for taking so long to bring everything to fans and for keeping official gameplay footage and other details under wraps. Rockstar said it was nearly finished making the game (which will receive many updates in the coming years, so it won't really be "finished" anytime soon).
GTA 6 is slated to arrive on November 19. Rockstar will give fans a clearer picture of what the game is all about with a deep dive that will initially stream on Netflix on August 27 before hitting YouTube several hours later. The publisher said it took longer than it hoped to prepare this "extended look" but was aware it needed to exceed fans' expectations.
An individual or group has dropped more than a dozen gameplay clips that were widely shared on social media (Rockstar issued takedown notices on many copies). The first two showed Jason — one of the two playable protagonists — shooting a few hoops at his safe house and causing chaos on the roads of GTA 6's version of South Florida. Subsequent leaks depicted him at a nudist colony and cycling along an impressively crowded beach.
The leaker, who promoted a memecoin in the clips, claimed they were protesting video game companies' alleged anti-consumer practices, such as Rockstar's decision to release the physical edition of GTA 6 as a code in a box, instead of on a disc. One of the leaked clips notably showed Jason walking around a store that sells physical copies of games.
The publisher is said to have been "all hands on deck" to figure out how the leaks happened and who is responsible. Its parent, Take-Two Interactive, sought information from Microsoft and Discord that it believed to be connected to the leak. On Monday, Discord marketing director Ryan K. Rigney said the company had "not yet been served with a subpoena" and that once Take-Two had, it would "evaluate the validity and scope before responding."
Rockstar's full statement is below:
Dear all,
We know that many of you have been waiting to hear from us regarding the events of the past week. It would be an understatement to say that having videos of Grand Theft Auto VI gameplay leak in this way has been heartbreaking for our team, and this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time. We are very sorry that everything has taken as long as it has — from getting the game finished (nearly there!) to sharing more details and official gameplay, and providing the community with everything you want to know.
We are very excited for everyone to see the extended look tomorrow. It has taken longer than we wanted to get it ready, but as with everything we do, we know we need to exceed your expectations, and we are determined to deliver at the level you expect and deserve. While it is unfortunate that the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers, we hope that everyone will wait a bit longer to experience the game for themselves on November 19.
We want to thank everyone in the community who has reached out with messages of support this past week — your words have meant more to this team than you can imagine. Ultimately, we are making this game for you, and without you, we would not have had the privilege of making games.
We look forward to sharing more with you soon.
Sincerely, Rockstar Games.

Caste divides make scorching summers harder in a parched corner of India
- Published
A couple of months ago, just after sunrise, 40-year-old Mamta began the first of as many as 10 journeys she would make that day.
Carrying three empty plastic buckets, she walked a few hundred metres to the nearest handpump in her village in Jalaun district, in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of northern India. Temperatures in parts of the region were soaring above 40C.
The taps installed under a government drinking water scheme had been dry for two years, she said, leaving most of the village's 1,000 residents dependent on a handful of handpumps.
Mamta said collecting enough water for her 11-member family and their livestock took hours. But the heat was not her only obstacle.
Mamta belongs to the Valmiki community, part of the Dalits - groups once regarded as "untouchable" under India's centuries-old caste hierarchy and which continue to face widespread discrimination.
She said she waited until members of the village's dominant castes finished using the handpump before approaching it.
"If they are standing there, we cannot fill water. We have to wait until they leave," she said.
Afterwards, she said, some upper-caste residents poured water over the pump to "cleanse" it.
"It has been happening for decades."
Bundelkhand, a semi-arid region that spans several districts in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, is notoriously drought-prone. It faced several major droughts between 2002 and 2016, making it almost a symbol for water scarcity in a country where several regions face similar hardships.
The rocky terrain of the Bundelkhand plateau means it can store little groundwater. Erratic rainfall and hotter temperatures have also made access to water unpredictable despite several government and community-led conservation efforts.
A study of more than a century of weather records found temperatures had risen across almost the entire region, and in recent summers, parts of Bundelkhand have neared 48C.
Residents and researchers say worsening heat and water stress are putting new pressure on an old divide.
As more families compete for scarce shared water, Dalits who have long faced barriers in accessing it are encountering those inequalities more often.
"Conflict over water is not new," said Mitashi Singh of the Centre for Science and Environment.
"What is changing is the role hotter summers are playing in making water scarcer and intensifying tensions that already existed."
Local officials reject claims that the region faces water shortages or caste discrimination at public water sources.
Dominant-caste residents interviewed by the BBC also denied discriminating against others, although they acknowledged growing pressure on water supplies.
Ram Gopal Singh, who is in his 50s, pointed to several abandoned village wells.
"These wells have been dry for almost 20 years," he said. Other sources had dried up or become polluted, while unreliable tap connections had pushed more families towards handpumps.
Everyone tried to collect water in the cooler morning hours, he said, leading to arguments over turns and how much each family could take.
"But there is no caste-based dispute at these handpumps," he insisted.
Dalit residents interviewed by the BBC described something different.
There is no formal queue at the pumps, they said. Instead, families try to collect water at different times to avoid confrontations.
Mamta said she usually went very early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
"The fear of being targeted stays with me throughout," she said.
About 50km away in Shahjahanpur, Shiv described a similar experience.
He said members of his community would not approach the handpump while dominant-caste families were using it.
"No matter how hot it is, even if we have to wait for hours for one bucket of drinking water, we wait because we do not have a choice," he said.
In summer, when his family needed more water, those waiting periods became more frequent.
"Even if my parents are thirsty, we sometimes wait for hours before we can drink."
Three years ago, Shiv's mother Parmi Devi said she was assaulted after an argument with a member of a dominant caste at a village handpump.
"I was thrashed and beaten up and thrown on the ground three times," she alleged.
"It was not just about water. It was because of our caste."
Devi filed a police complaint alleging assault. No arrests have been made yet.
Such disputes have surfaced repeatedly in complaints documented by the Dalit Dignity and Justice Centre (DDJC), a non-profit organisation in Uttar Pradesh.
The group said police registered 113 cases under India's law against caste-based atrocities in the area in 2025.
Kuldeep Singh Baudh of DDJC told BBC Hindi a majority of the complaints it tracked during the hottest months of May and June involved water, though the organisation has not published a detailed breakdown.
"To truly understand [the heat's] impact, you have to see it from the perspective of the communities that are the most excluded," he said.
The office of District Magistrate Rajesh Kumar Pandey rejected the allegations.
"There is not even one instance wherein caste-based discrimination is being practised when it comes to access to water in the region," it said in a statement.
The statement also disputed claims of water shortages, pointing to the federal government's Jal Jeevan Mission, which aims to provide piped drinking water to every rural household, and other local efforts to restore ponds and recharge groundwater.
There have also been wider efforts to tackle Bundelkhand's water crisis. Traditional water bodies, including ponds and check dams, have been revived across the region, while women-led groups known as Jal Sahelis work in villages to monitor supplies and promote water conservation.
Mukul Sharma, a researcher on caste and environmental politics, said increasing water supplies was only part of the solution.
Climate change is "not the origin of these injustices, but a threat multiplier", he added.
More water alone will not solve the problem if caste still shapes who gets to use it, Sharma said.
That morning in May, Mamta waited beside the handpump as other families filled their buckets, three empty plastic containers at her feet.
In cooler months, she said, she made the journey only a few times a day. In summer, it could be eight or 10, each trip determined partly by who was already at the pump.
When her turn came, she filled her buckets and carried them home. Later that day, she would return.

Ethiopia submits official bid to host Afcon 2028
- Published
Ethiopia has submitted an official bid to host the 2028 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
The country's football federation (EFF) says its government-backed proposal affirms "the nation's full readiness to host Africa's biggest footballing event".
Ethiopia has staged Afcon three times, in 1962, 1968 and 1976, but its footballing infrastructure lags well behind others on the continent.
The nation had just one stadium approved for use by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) last season but is in the process of inaugurating a new international stadium and sports complex in Addis Ababa.
That venue in the capital could provide one location for the tournament, but whether Ethiopia has enough compliant venues to host a 24-team Afcon across multiple locations remains a major question.
A number of existing regional facilities are understood not to meet Fifa or Caf standards in terms of infrastructure, facilities and overall match-day requirements.
Ethiopia played its home qualifiers for the 2026 Fifa World Cup at neutral venues in Morocco and Rwanda but did host matches in Dire Dawa earlier this year.
Last month, Caf president Patrice Motsepe said his organisation had received "exciting bids" for the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Afcons - with the tournament set to move to a four-year cycle after 2028.
Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe announced a joint Southern African bid for the 2028 finals earlier this year.
Despite reports that Morocco - hosts of the 2025 edition - could stage the tournament again in two years' time, BBC Sport Africa understands the kingdom is not in the running and instead is focusing on preparations to co-host the 2030 Fifa World Cup.
Meanwhile, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger - three countries led by military governments - have expressed interest in co-hosting in 2032.
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year, with the competition returning to East Africa for the first time since it was held in Ethiopia in 1976.
Ethiopia won the Afcon title on home soil in 1962 but the Walia Ibex, ranked 143rd in the world and 43rd in Africa, have only qualified for the tournament three times since they last hosted.
Their most recent appearance came at the 2021 edition, when they finished bottom without a win in a group containing Cameroon, Burkina Faso and Cape Verde.
Ethiopia beat Sao Tome and Principe in the preliminary round of qualifiers for next year's Afcon and have been drawn alongside Senegal, Mozambique and Sudan in Group J.
- Is holding Afcon every four years 'totally wrong' or 'good call'? 
  - Published22 January
Infrastructure and security concerns
Analysis by Kaleb Moges, BBC Africa
The EFF's announcement that it wants to host Afcon has generated mixed reactions, with critics questioning whether the country is truly prepared to host a tournament of this scale.
Ethiopia was one of just three nations to play at the first Afcon in 1957, but the 52,000-seat Bahir Dar Stadium in the north of the country is currently the only facility it posseses which is approved by Caf.
Meanwhile, the 62,000-capacity Adey Abeba International Stadium in Addis Ababa is expected to be completed next year.
Three other proposed stadiums are at much earlier stages of development and would need significant work to meet Caf's requirements in time for 2028.
However, hosting Afcon would require more than upgrading or constructing stadiums. The country would also need adequate training facilities, gyms, accommodation and entertainment venues, as well as reliable urban transport and security infrastructure.
Security is a major concern for Ethiopia's bid. Although the capital city is comparatively safe, several parts of the country continue to experience armed conflict, political unrest and other security challenges.
Addressing these concerns, alongside the infrastructure requirements, would be critical if Ethiopia is to successfully host Afcon 2028.

A lung cancer diagnosis has a way of stopping a conversation cold. Families go quiet. Plans get shelved. The assumption, almost universal, is that the outcome is already decided. Often, that assumption is wrong. When the disease is found early, meaningful treatment is possible, curative intent included. The gap between what people believe about lung cancer and what medicine can actually offer has never been wider.
Myth 1: A lung cancer diagnosis is always a death sentence
Where does this belief come from? In India, most patients present in advanced stage, and because of this, the treatment options decrease exponentially. The outcomes families witness reinforce a fatalism that’s hard to shake. Late detection is the problem, not an inherent quality of the disease itself. Lung cancer found at an early, localised stage is genuinely treatable. Surgery with curative intent is possible. The question that matters most is how soon the disease gets diagnosed.
Myth 2: Only smokers get lung cancer
Smoking is the most well-known risk factor, and for good reason. But the picture is more complicated. Prolonged exposure to indoor cooking fuel smoke or second-hand smoke carries considerable risk, as does long-term exposure to occupational carcinogens. Registry data from India has shown a steady rise in cases among women and adults who have never smoked. Adenocarcinoma, now the most commonly diagnosed lung cancer subtype in India, occurs frequently in this group. It also tends to carry specific genetic mutations that respond well to targeted treatment. Any respiratory symptom that doesn’t resolve deserves attention, irrespective of smoking history.
Myth 3: The warning signs will always be clear
This is the myth that probably causes the most harm. Lung cancer is often silent early on, and when symptoms surface, they look like something else entirely. A cough that has outstayed its welcome. Recurring chest infections. Unexplained weight loss, or breathlessness that keeps getting worse. Any of these, persisting beyond three weeks, should prompt clinical evaluation. Some features call for more urgency: coughing up blood, a voice that turns persistently hoarse, chest pain that doesn’t shift. Attributing such signs to the weather or getting older is understandable, but it is also how early lung cancer gets missed.
Why early detection changes everything
The stage at diagnosis is an important factor in how lung cancer plays out. Finding it early and getting it surgically removal with curative intent becomes a real possibility. This is where screening comes into the picture. Low-dose CT scanning picks up small nodules in the lung before a patient feels anything, creating a window for treatment that wouldn’t otherwise exist. Indian health economic research has confirmed this approach as cost-effective for those at highest risk. If you have a long smoking history and are above a certain age, it’s worth asking your doctor about screening.
Treatment can transform outcomes
The treatment landscape for lung cancer has shifted considerably. Molecular testing can now identify specific mutations within a tumour. EGFR and ALK alterations are among the most clinically significant, and therapies designed to target them have extended survival in ways that weren’t possible with chemotherapy alone. For patients whose tumours don’t carry targetable mutations, immunotherapy has opened up another avenue. These are part of standard oncology care in India today. A patient diagnosed now is working with a very different set of possibilities from someone diagnosed a decade ago.
Who should act and when
Anyone with a long smoking history, a close family member who has had lung cancer, or years of exposure to air pollutants at work or at home has reason to discuss their risk with a doctor. That conversation doesn’t need to wait for symptoms. When symptoms do appear, they shouldn’t be left to resolve on their own; in someone already carrying these risks, investigation is the right call.
A diagnosis of lung cancer is not, in itself, what limits a patient’s options. Time is. The treatments available today are genuinely different from what existed a decade ago, and outcomes for many patients reflect that. But none of it matters if the disease is found late. The most important thing anyone can do is take symptoms seriously and act on them early.
(Dr. Rajesh Shinde is director – GI (HPB–colorectal) & thoracic surgical oncology Apollo Cancer Centre – Western Region Apollo Hospitals, Navi Mumbai. drrajesh_sh@apollohospitals.com)

Trump threatens to demolish another DC landmark
The Kennedy Center becomes a hostage to Trump’s renaming demands.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is threatening that if he can’t have the Kennedy Center, no one can.
What’s going on? Trump has been trying to get his name back on the John F. Kennedy Center for Performing Arts since June, when it was removed in response to a court order. On Monday night, the Justice Department revealed its latest ploy to make that happen.
In a court filing, the DOJ argued that if its renovation plans for the Kennedy Center aren’t allowed to go forward, “the center will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down” and replaced by another structure, “such as a large outdoor amphitheater.”
Tied up in the proposed $250 million renovation are three new tributes to Trump, which the Kennedy Center board (stacked with Trump appointees) voted to add earlier this month: the text “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump” and “endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund” on the building’s facade, and the renaming of the Kennedy Center grounds as “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”
Those changes are currently being challenged in court by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), who successfully sued to undo Trump’s first renaming of the center. But the Trump administration claims her suit endangers the entire project.
What does Trump’s name have to do with the renovations? According to the DOJ filing, “an order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop.”
“There will simply not be the expertise or funding necessary to rebuild and renovate this decimated structure,” it adds.
Is that true? No. Congress already approved $257 million for the renovation last year, which the Kennedy Center board touted in a press release crediting Trump.
And far from being a draw, the Washington Post reported Tuesday, Trump’s previous renaming of the Kennedy Center caused ticket sales and donations to plummet, creating a $23 million deficit even after deep spending cuts.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Apple has announced fresh versions of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio desktop computers, alongside some new chips: the M6 and M5 Ultra.
Neither Mac desktop has undergone any physical changes on the exterior, but the long-awaited update brings these Macs back into stock after being difficult to buy for most of this year. Importantly, this serves as our first introduction to the M6 chip, which we will likely see much more of in future MacBooks.
Skipping the M5 entirely, the Mac Mini now comes in two flavors: the M6 and the M5 Pro. The M5 Pro is the same chip that's currently found in the MacBook Pro, but the M6 is brand new. It's the first Apple Silicon part to be built on 2-nanometer process technology and also adds extra cores to the mix. This is a 12-core CPU—another first for Apple—broken down into two super cores, four performances cores, and six efficiency cores.
New here are the performance cores, which Apple says are designed to speed up multithreaded tasks while preserving efficiency. Apple claims the M6 is 20 percent faster than the M5 in multithreaded performance and 40 percent faster than the M4.
The M6 comes with a faster GPU too, adding two more cores to the mix for a total of 12 GPU cores. This is also the first Mac Mini to have Neural Accelerators for faster on-device AI performance, a feature that launched in the M5 chip last year. The result is a Mac Mini that Apple claims is twice as fast as the M4 Mac Mini, along with providing higher throughput for gaming. Lastly, the M6 Mac mini also comes with what Apple calls a “dual 16-core Neural Engine," which doubles the peak AI performance.
In addition to the extra performance, however, it also comes with a $200 price increase. The M6 Mac Mini now starts at $899 for the model with 16 GB of unified memory. The Mac Mini can still be configured with up to 32 GB of unified memory, and Apple says the tiny desktop is 40 percent faster, with bandwidth now up to 170 GB per second.
The M5 Ultra Arrives
The Mac Studio is also receiving a significant update. Like the Mac Mini, it still comes in two flavors: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. This is the fourth generation of the Mac Studio to come out, with the M3 Ultra (and M3 Max) model coming out in early 2025.
Apple proudly claims that the M5 Ultra is Apple's most powerful chip ever, and the first to use a “quad-die” architecture. Apple's “Ultra” chips have always connected two Max dies together using using a technology called UltraFusion across a high-speed interconnect. The difference this time is that the M5 Max already had two dies itself, which is where the four dies come from. To keep those four chips running as fast as possible, the next version of UltraFusion increases the inter-die bandwidth to over 4.4 TB per second, allowing the whole array to function as a single CPU.
M5 Ultra Mac Studio comes with four more CPU cores for a total of 36. There are still 80 GPU cores (the same as on the M3 Ultra), but the M5-specific improvements to the GPU apply here for better overall performance.
In a briefing on the Mac Studio, Apple even discussed the ability to connect multiple Mac Studios together over Thunderbolt 5 to run frontier-level LLMs with over a trillion parameters locally, allowing the four systems to share memory. Hypothetically, that allows you to run models locally on a Mac that just weren't possible before. Apparently, four Mac Studios can even be connected in this way to run over a standard wall outlet.
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio are available for preorder starting today and will come with macOS 27 Golden Gate preinstalled. However, systems won't ship until September 22. In a briefing, Apple said this delay wouldn't be reflective of shipping times for these new Mac Mini or Mac Studio systems.

In Summary
- The iQOO Z11 is the latest device in iQOO’s mid-segment Z series.
- The phone comes with a curved display, a sleek design, and specs and features that make it a solid mid-segmenter.
- At its starting price of Rs 34,999, the iQOO Z11 is a great option for those who want a phone that is capable of handling most tasks and has flaunt value too.
iQOO’s latest mid-segmenter sports sleek curves of the display sort, packs in decent, entertainment-friendly specs, manages to squeeze a big battery into a slim frame, and tops it all with a generous serving of AI. But will all this be enough for the iQOO Z11 to click with its target audience in a time of rising prices and declining specs? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
iQOO Z11 looks and appearance: Curved display and a Pixel-like camera bar
The iQOO Z11 is a tall, slim phone that will turn heads with its appearance. It sports a curved display in front and also has curved sides, while on the back is a camera bar that reminds us of the Google Pixel. It is a tall phone at 164.4 mm, although it is very slim at just 7.99 mm, and surprisingly light for its size at just 199 grams – that’s taller, and yet lighter and slimmer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. The front is smooth glass while the back and sides are made of polycarbonate, but they can be easily mistaken for metal or glass. The camera bar on the back is made of aluminum, which gives the phone a very premium feel. It comes with IP68/69 dust and water resistance, so it can easily survive a fall in the water, and has a very reassuringly solid feel to it.
The iQOO Z11 comes in Celestial Blue and Aurora Green shades. Both have a subtly shiny look that shimmers and changes shades in the light, and also have matte finishes that do not smudge or stain easily. We got the Aurora Green shade. This phone has flaunt value without being loud – the curved display and the camera bar give it slim and tall Pixel vibes, which is not a bad thing at all.
iQOO Z11 Spec Sheet and Hardware: Solidly upper mid-segment
The iQOO Z11 comes with a 6.83-inch AMOLED display with a resolution of 2800 x 1260 and a refresh rate of 144 Hz, which is rare at this price point. Sound is handled by a pair of stereo speakers. The phone is the first in the Indian market to be powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 7500 Ultra processor, which is supposed to be a steady performer with some gaming ability as well. This is paired with RAM and storage variants of 6 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 128 GB, 8 GB/ 256 GB, and 12 GB/ 256 GB. The RAM is LPDDR4X, while the storage is UFS 3.1, which are, like the processor, not top of the line, but actually very capable. The camera bar on the back has a 50-megapixel main Sony IMX882 sensor with OIS, accompanied by an 8-megapixel ultrawide, while selfie and video call duties are handled by a 32-megapixel front-facing camera. In spite of being very slim, the iQOO Z11 comes with a large 7025 mAh battery with support for 44W charging, and a 44W charger in the box.
The iQOO Z11 runs on OriginOS 6 on top of Android 16 and comes with an assurance of three years of Android upgrades and five years of security patches. Once again, that’s par for the course for the segment. The phone also comes with not only a number of AI tools (apart from Google’s standard Gemini suite), but also with unlimited AI credits for AI captions and AI creations using iQOO’s tools, basically allowing consumers to use them without restrictions, which is rare to see at this price.
iQOO Z11 cameras: Colorfully pleasant mostly
Photography on the iQOO Z11 is largely a single-camera show – something that is beginning to become the rule in this price segment. The 50-megapixel main camera takes very pleasant snaps with ample detail. Purists might feel that the images come with slightly saturated colors, but mainstream users are unlikely to complain. Even low-light and night photography is impressively colorful. We would suggest shooting videos in the daylight, though, as low-light videos are not the best.
The front camera takes good selfies, with plenty of beautification and skin smoothing by default, although these can be toned down. The ultrawide camera is basically good for a different perspective, but its quality is not the greatest. Portraits are impressive, but lossless zoom is limited to 2x, while digital zoom goes up to 10x. There are plenty of shooting and editing options to let one do more with images, but this is a phone for casual point-and-shooters rather than enthusiasts.
iQOO Z11 performance: Doing it all well, instead of doing a few things brilliantly
The iQOO Z11 is one of the rare phones out there that does many things well. The combination of that large display and very good stereo speakers makes it a great phone for viewing content, whether it is viewing shows and films, reels, or just browsing the Web. The 7050 mAh battery comfortably keeps going for a day and a half of normal use, and the 44W charger gets the phone from empty to full in about 70-75 minutes, with half an hour generally being enough to take the phone up to 50 percent (which is enough to see off a day of use).
The Dimensity 7500 Ultra sails through routine tasks effortlessly, and we were able to switch between 6-10 apps quite easily without any lag. While the phone is not a gaming beast, we were able to play titles like Call of Duty and Asphalt after a few minor tweaks, and even Genshin Impact (with graphics toned down) ran well on the phone. The display and speakers again play key roles here. The phone never heated up excessively either, no matter what we burdened it with.
iQOO Z11 Software and UI: Unlimited AI
OriginOS 6 runs smoothly on the iQOO Z11, and there are plenty of AI tools to play around with. AI Creation is a powerful writing tool, and AI Transcript Assist works perfectly for those who love to have written records of meetings, classes, or lectures (do double-check names, though). There are also tools for AI translation, summaries, and more. They all work very smoothly indeed (though you need to log in to an iQOO account and have an Internet connection for most), with many coming with unlimited usage – something college-goers and AI addicts on a tight budget will appreciate. Of course, one also gets Google’s AI tools such as Gemini and Circle to Search.
While there is some bloatware (most of which can be uninstalled), there are a number of handy utilities and features too, including iQOO DocMaster, which lets one work with multiple document formats, the Dynamic Island-like Origin Island, and the ability to easily share information with not just Android but also iOS devices. The software seems to be a little overwhelming, but is extremely useful once one gets the hang of it. And works smoothly most of the time.
iQOO Z11 Review Verdict: Great for those who want a do-it-all, which also looks good
The iQOO Z11 is available in the following RAM and storage configurations at these prices:
6 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 34,999
8 GB/ 128 GB: Rs 39,999
8 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 44,999
12 GB/ 256 GB: Rs 49,999
Given the trend of insanely high prices, these are extremely competitive. In fact, although some might frown at the relatively modest RAM in the base 6 GB/ 128 GB model, the fact that it is priced below Rs 35,000 could tempt many users. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said on Tuesday it authorised Abbott Laboratories' glucose monitor, making it the first device that continuously monitors both ketone levels and blood sugar.
Here are some details:
The device branded as Libre Duo 10 Day is designed for a 10-day wear period for people aged 2 years and older living with diabetes.
The biowearable is designed to alert people of rising ketones that can lead to a diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) emergency, a serious health complication for people with diabetes.
Unlike earlier ketone tests that offered only separate, one-time readings, Abbott's device continuously monitors both ketone and glucose levels, displaying real-time trends.
The device can send automatic alerts, which may help patients and caregivers recognize rising ketones before DKA becomes a medical emergency.
"If glucose is the speedometer, ketones are like the check engine light—providing an alert that something may need attention," said Chris Scoggins, executive vice president of Abbott's diabetes care business.
The device brings both glucose and ketone levels together in a single dashboard, providing a more complete picture to help people with diabetes make more informed decisions, added Scoggins.
Abbott is working with leading pump companies to enable automated insulin delivery systems to connect with the sensors.
The company said the device integrates with the Libre app and expects Libre Duo 10 Day to work with devices from Insulet and Tandem in 2027.

Spurs in talks to sign Man City's Savinho and Marmoush
- Published
Tottenham are in talks with Manchester City over a double deal for forwards Savinho and Omar Marmoush.
Sources have told BBC Sport that negotiations between the clubs are progressing, although an agreement has yet to be reached.
Spurs' interest in Brazilian winger Savinho dates back to 2025, when the 22-year-old opted to remain at Etihad Stadium.
But he was limited to just seven starts in the Premier League last season, and is now minded to leave the club after joining for a £30m fee in 2024 from French club Troyes.
Marmoush, a £59m signing from Eintracht Frankfurt in 2025, fell out of favour under Pep Guardiola in 2025-26 and the 27-year-old managed eight goals in 36 appearances in all competitions.
City's valuation for the pair is unclear, but the club would expect to make a significant profit on both.
Tottenham head coach Roberto de Zerbi has revamped his midfield this summer, signing Mateus Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for a combined £185m.
But the Italian has stressed the need to strengthen his attack following the side's 17th-placed finish in the Premier League last term, scoring just 48 goals in 38 games.
Spurs remain interested in Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, but it is unclear whether the club could finance a deal for the Netherlands international as well as moves for Marmoush and Savinho.
City have already sold a host of players this summer, including Rodri, midfielder Tijjani Reijnders and second-choice goalkeeper James Trafford.
Spurs kick off their Premier League campaign away at Brentford on Saturday (17:30 BST), while City host Bournemouth on Sunday (14:00 BST).

Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
- Published
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.
It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.
The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision which severed her right leg.
Fifteen months later, her death, and the silence surrounding it, has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.
In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.
Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.
Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures. Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.
Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.
Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.
Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.
Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.
State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.
VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.
While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.
Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.
In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.
In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

  - Published8 April
Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.
Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".
Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.
The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.
"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."
Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.
Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.
This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.
Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.
Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.
On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.
Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.
In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.
But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.
Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.
Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.
"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"
