From Rs 50 to Rs 200 per kg: How UP govt's push transformed Kalanamak rice market
After the Uttar Pradesh government's One District One Product push, farmers who once struggled to find buyers for the traditional rice now say traders approach them even before the crop is harvested, offering advance payments to secure supplies.
In Uttar Pradesh’s Siddharthnagar district, Kalanamak rice has emerged as a lucrative crop for farmers after being selected under the state’s One District One Product (ODOP) scheme in 2018, with increased government promotion, better market access and value-added products helping drive up demand and prices.
Farmers who once struggled to find buyers for the traditional rice now say traders approach them even before the crop is harvested, offering advance payments to secure supplies.
Kalanamak rice, known for its distinctive aroma and nutritional properties, previously sold for around Rs 35-70 per kg, according to farmers. It now fetches around Rs 180-200 per kg in the market, while the wholesale price has risen to about Rs 20,000 per quintal.
Farmers say the sharp increase in demand has even made the rice difficult to procure, with buyers from cities including Delhi, Mumbai, Gorakhpur and Sant Kabir Nagar approaching growers for supplies.
The growing popularity of Kalanamak rice has also significantly expanded its cultivation in the district. According to officials, the crop was grown across around 2,000 hectares in 2017, before its inclusion under ODOP.
The area under cultivation has since expanded to nearly 20,000 hectares, with officials saying production needs to increase further to keep pace with demand.
Ajay Rawat, a beneficiary associated with Buddha Delights, said his family has been cultivating Kalanamak rice for nearly three generations. He said its inclusion under ODOP in 2018 helped open up national and international markets for the traditional crop and also encouraged the development of value-added products.
“We have also ventured into value-added products made from Kalanamak rice, including cookies,” Rawat said, adding that the products are positioned for their nutritional value and contain nutrients such as zinc and protein.
Rawat said he received a Rs 2.06-crore grant from the District Industries Department in Siddharthnagar under the ODOP scheme. The support helped him participate in fairs and festivals, where the products were showcased and promoted beyond the district. He said that before 2018, farmers had limited awareness about the nutritional properties of Kalanamak rice, including its low glycaemic index, and there was little organised demand for the crop.
According to Rawat, the increased promotion under ODOP has changed the market dynamics. Rice that previously struggled to find buyers at Rs 50-60 per kg now sells for around Rs 200 per kg, he said.
Farmer Pankaj Chaubey said the improvement in prices has had a direct impact on growers. He said farmers who once struggled to sell Kalanamak rice for Rs 5,000-6,000 per quintal can now command around Rs 20,000 per quintal.
Chaubey said the Alidapur belt is particularly known for producing good-quality Kalanamak rice. He added that farmers who once had to approach buyers themselves now receive calls from different parts of the country seeking supplies.
“Earlier, people would go around asking buyers to take Kalanamak rice. Now we receive calls from places such as Gorakhpur, Sant Kabir Nagar, Khaliabad, Mumbai and Delhi asking us to arrange supplies,” he said.
Another farmer, Mohit, said Kalanamak has been cultivated by his family for generations, but the crop fetched only around Rs 35-45 per kg in the past because demand was limited. The situation changed after the rice was brought under the ODOP scheme, he said.
“Now, as soon as we sow it, people from outside come and book the crop, asking us to give the produce only to them,” Mohit said, adding that some buyers also pay farmers in advance.
He said the ODOP initiative helped create awareness about Kalanamak cultivation in the Alidapur belt and brought greater recognition to the rice's nutritional properties. The growing demand in national and international markets, he added, has also boosted farmers’ confidence.
Farmer Brij Bhushan Chaudhary recalled that Kalanamak rice previously sold for around Rs 6,000-7,000 per quintal, and even finding buyers at those prices was difficult. Government employees and officials were often among the few buyers, he said.
The extensive promotion under ODOP, however, has significantly increased awareness and the market value of the rice.
Officials said the government has also focused on improving processing, packaging and marketing infrastructure around the product. Shiv Shankar, Deputy Commissioner of Industries at the District Industries Promotion and Entrepreneurship Development Centre in Siddharthnagar, said Rs 917 lakh in grants had been provided to 306 beneficiaries since the ODOP scheme was introduced in 2018.
He said the expansion in cultivation from around 2,000 hectares to nearly 20,000 hectares was largely driven by improved prices and rising demand. The administration has organised awareness programmes, buyer-seller meets and promotional campaigns in coordination with the Agriculture Department to expand the market for Kalanamak rice.
The rice is also being sold through online marketplaces, including Flipkart and Amazon, while a Common Facility Centre has been established in Madhwapur in Bansi tehsil to support packaging and processing.
The district administration has also encouraged the development of new varieties to address concerns over low productivity. Varieties such as Kiran 101, Kiran 102 and Kiran 103 have been developed to improve yields and encourage more farmers to take up Kalanamak cultivation.
Under the ODOP initiative, 10-day training programmes are organised for farmers covering cultivation practices, packaging and marketing. Officials said around 1,400 farmers have received training related to Kalanamak rice since 2018.
Farmers are also provided moisture meters to assess the moisture content of harvested paddy, while warehousing facilities are available for storing produce when required.
Balram Singh, Chief Development Officer of Siddharthnagar, said various government schemes were being implemented to increase Kalanamak rice production and promote products made from it. Subsidies are being provided to entrepreneurs involved in processing, packaging and value addition, including around Rs 2 crore in assistance to a company manufacturing products from Kalanamak rice.
With farmers, entrepreneurs and government agencies increasingly focusing on cultivation, processing and marketing, Kalanamak rice has evolved from a traditional crop with limited demand into one of Siddharthnagar’s most prominent products under the ODOP initiative.

Quote of the Day: “The past is never dead. It's not even past.” — William Faulkner
Some events may belong to another time, but their influence can continue to shape the present. Memories, decisions, conflicts and experiences from years ago can leave lasting marks on individuals, families and societies. William Faulkner’s famous observation captures this enduring connection between what has happened and what is happening now.
The quote suggests that the past does not simply disappear when time moves forward. Instead, it can remain alive through memories, consequences and the choices people make in the present. Something that happened decades ago may continue to influence relationships, beliefs, institutions or even entire communities.
At its heart, Faulkner’s statement is about the lasting power of history. People often think of the past as something finished and separate from the present. But personal and collective experiences rarely work that way. Past events can continue to affect how people understand themselves and the world around them.
For an individual, this could mean childhood experiences shaping adult behaviour, an old friendship influencing present relationships, or a difficult experience continuing to affect important decisions. Even when the event itself is over, its emotional or psychological impact can remain.
On a larger scale, the idea applies to societies and nations. Historical conflicts, political decisions, social inequalities and cultural traditions can continue to influence generations that did not experience them directly. Understanding the present, therefore, often requires looking back at what came before.
The quote also highlights the importance of confronting history rather than simply trying to forget it. Ignoring difficult experiences does not necessarily make their consequences disappear. Recognising how the past continues to influence the present can help people understand current challenges more clearly and make better choices for the future.
Faulkner’s words can also be interpreted in a more personal and philosophical way. Human beings carry memories with them, and those memories become part of who they are. Time may change circumstances, but it does not always erase the meaning attached to earlier experiences.
The statement therefore serves as a reminder that the present is rarely created from nothing. It is often the result of countless events, choices and experiences that came before it. Looking at history can provide context for the world we live in today.
In an increasingly fast-moving world, Faulkner’s observation remains relevant because societies are constantly dealing with the consequences of earlier decisions. Whether the subject is politics, culture, family relationships or personal growth, the past often provides important clues about the present.
The quote encourages reflection rather than simply looking forward. Progress does not always require forgetting what happened before. In many cases, learning from history is essential to avoiding the repetition of old mistakes.
Ultimately, Faulkner reminds us that time does not automatically separate us from our experiences. The past may have happened already, but its effects can remain very much alive.
William Faulkner was an American novelist, short-story writer and poet who became one of the most influential writers of 20th-century literature. Born in Mississippi in 1897, he drew heavily on the history, culture and social tensions of the American South in his fiction.
Faulkner was known for exploring themes such as memory, identity, race, family, guilt and the complicated relationship between the past and present. His experimental storytelling techniques and complex characters earned him international recognition.
He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1949 for his powerful contribution to modern American fiction. Among his best-known works are The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying and Absalom, Absalom!. His writing continues to be studied for its exploration of human nature and the enduring influence of history.

NZ religious sect leader jailed over death of elderly follower
- Published
A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family.
Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.
The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu.
Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music.
During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023.
She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark", along with several other female followers.
Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master".
Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables.
The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined.
In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard.
The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage".
The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice.
Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year.
On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand.
New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China.
In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded.
Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents.
Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music.
During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends".
During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang.
"Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

Tanzania's vice-president announces resignation in unprecedented move
- Published
Tanzania's Vice-President Emmanuel Nchimbi has announced he is resigning weeks after it was reported that he had fallen out with President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
The 54-year-old shared his brief resignation letter on his Instagram account, saying he wanted to respect the president's wishes. Sources in his office and the presidency confirmed the move.
Nchimbi said he would retire from public life at the end of next week - less than 10 months after being sworn in and making him the first vice-president to step down in the history of the East African nation.
He was Samia's running mate in last October's disputed presidential election, which saw hundreds killed in post-poll unrest.
The pair were sworn in last November after winning 98% of the vote.
Violent protests in the awake of voting led to the deaths of at least 500 people, according to an official enquiry.
Opposition parties and human rights groups accused the security forces of unleashing a brutal crackdown on anti-government protesters.
"I have become convinced, without doubt, that the president wants changes, and I have therefore decided to fulfil my promise," Nchimbi wrote in his resignation letter referring to the pledge he had made to Samia that he would go if she wanted another deputy.
He thanked the president and the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party for the trust they had placed in him, and to Tanzanians for their support during his time in public service.
Nchimbi said he was leaving office in accordance with the country's constitution and would continue to be a "good citizen of Tanzania".
The vice-president has made some controversial remarks in recent weeks - which may point to the possible fallout with President Samia.
Last month, he urged Tanzanians to "fight for a new constitution", arguing that there was an opportunity to secure one before 2030.
He also linked a new constitution to ways of addressing injustice, strengthening human rights, good governance and democracy.
Nchimbi previously served as secretary-general of CCM. He also held several senior positions in government, including both minister of information and home affairs, before becoming Tanzania's ambassador to Brazil and later Egypt.

Gold custody, armed security, and bullion logistics are not core competencies of a Health Department, a government doctors’ association has pointed out, questioning the administrative burden and cost involved in implementing the Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam in Tamil Nadu.
In a district-level costing of the proposed hub-and-spoke model, the Service Doctors and Post Graduates Association (SDPGA) said the hospital-based arrangement could cost roughly three times the State-wide administrative norm prescribed in the Government Order, factoring in the expenses for dedicated vaults, armed security posts, and armoured transport.
The association recommended that the scheme be delivered through a bank channel — either direct disbursal against a PICME (Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation)-linked entitlement certificate or bank-run logistics under a Memorandum of Understanding using the infrastructure that banks already operate for their own bullion, currency-chest, and cash-in-transit business.
According to the G.O., the State government had allocated ₹750.83 crore — ₹17,000 each for 4,41,667 deliveries — for procurement of one-gram gold rings. An administrative cost at 0.66% of the total budget — five crore — was sanctioned for the scheme. The administrative cost included monitoring, transport, evaluation, consumables, software, and hardware.
In a letter to the Health Secretary, SDPGA president P. Saminathan said the G.O. envisages a hub-and-spoke framework under which government hospitals take custody of, secure, and physically transport gold rings from hub centres to spoke delivery points for handing them over to beneficiaries. At the district level, the Health Department had to build a parallel bullion-security apparatus that had nothing to do with clinical care, he said.
Among the costs that need to be factored in are dedicated Reinforced Concrete Cement strong room with double locking, fire-rated vaults and dual-custody protocol at the two district hubs, biometric access and CCTV at 27 sites, six-member armed police/home guard posts each hub, additional security for every spoke and armoured cash-in-transit vehicles under annual rate contract with a driver and two escorts.
A district-level costing of this model involving two hubs and 25 spokes, and 25,000 deliveries per year, was worked out by SDPGA. It estimated an annualised capital cost of ₹12.68 lakh for strong-room and vault infrastructure at the two hubs, CCTV and biometric access at the hubs and spokes, steel safes/almirahs, besides a recurring annual cost of ₹71.50 lakh for security personnel, vehicles, insurance and digital systems. With the annual value of gold procurement estimated at ₹42.50 crore (25,000 rings x ₹17,000), the combined annualised cost of ₹84.18 lakh works out to 1.98% of the gold value, nearly three times the 0.66% administrative cost norm prescribed in the G.O.
By contrast, SDPGA said that using the existing infrastructure of scheduled banks could reduce the administrative cost to a negotiated handling fee. Even a service fee in the range of 0.15%-0.30% of the value handled (₹42.50 crore/year) would come roughly to ₹6.4 lakh to ₹12.75 lakh/year, thereby saving substantial funds and allowing health staff to focus on patient care. “The bank model is a foolproof time-tested model. Earlier, the Revenue Department implemented the Thalikku Thangam Scheme through a bank model, and the same can be brought in for the gold ring scheme,” he said.

Rahul Gandhi held the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ youth interaction programme in Pune on 22 August 2026, where he addressed students, spoke about women’s rights and criticised the BJP and RSS. The event triggered a political controversy after the BJP dubbed it “Paise Ki Goonj” and alleged that Congress had paid social media influencers to mobilise people, with BJP leaders claiming payments of up to ₹25,000–₹35,000. Congress rejected the allegations, accusing the BJP of being concerned about Gandhi’s growing appeal among young voters. As of 25 August 2026, the political row has continued. Gandhi has also written to Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis urging him to meet tribal hostel students in Pune and address their grievances (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a massive crowd gathered for Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s student interaction event, ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’, in Pune, Maharashtra. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a massive crowd gathered at Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Pune, Maharashtra in August 2026.
Fact: The video actually shows football fans celebrating a goal at the Zócalo in Mexico City during the 2026 FIFA World Cup match between Mexico and Ecuador, not the crowd gathered for Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Pune. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the same video (archived) posted on the Instagram account of Spanish sports journalist and television presenter Carlota Vizmanos on 1 July 2026. According to the caption, the crowd gathered at the Zócalo was celebrating Mexico’s goal. Vizmanos also posted several similar videos from the celebrations, which can be seen on her Instagram account (here, here).
The video shows the words “Mexico 26” at one spot in the crowd. The same text is also visible in the viral video, further indicating that both videos were recorded at the same location and during the same event.
Zócalo is the main square in central Mexico City, where football matches are broadcast live for fans to watch and celebrate together. FIFA designated the square as its central fan hub for the 2026 World Cup in Mexico City.
Taking this as a clue, we conducted a Google search and identified the distinctive thick pole visible among the crowd in the viral video. The same pole can be seen in the Constitution Plaza area of Zócalo. A comparison with Google Maps Street View further confirms that it is the same pole.
Mexico defeated Ecuador 2–0 in the FIFA World Cup Round of 32 on 30 June 2026. The match in Mexico City was delayed by one hour due to thunderstorms and lightning risk around the stadium.
To sum up, an unrelated video from Mexico is falsely shared as showing visuals of a massive crowd at Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Pune.

A US judge on Monday dismissed criminal charges against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, after the justice department said it had decided to abandon the fraud and bribery case.
The Brooklyn-based district judge Nicholas Garaufis’s decision to grant federal prosecutors’ rare attempt to toss the case came after he inquired into their reasons for doing so, including by asking Adani whether anything was promised in exchange for the dropping of the case. In November 2024, before the charges were unsealed, Adani had promised to invest $10bn in the United States.
Adani was charged in 2024 with agreeing to bribe Indian government officials so a subsidiary of his Adani Group could win approval to develop a solar energy plant, then misleading US investors by providing reassuring information about his company’s anti-corruption practices.
Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. Adani himself has not appeared in US court to respond to the charges. On 18 May, the justice department announced it would no longer pursue the case. That marked the latest instance in which federal prosecutors had sought to drop a high-profile white-collar criminal prosecution during Donald Trump’s second term in the White House.
Legal experts say US judges have little discretion to compel prosecutors to continue with criminal cases they no longer wish to pursue, but the charges cannot be formally dismissed without a judge’s approval.
Garaufis asked the justice department to justify its decision to drop the charges, writing that its “bland and conclusory” announcement did not give him enough information.
In a 4 July court filing, Trent McCotter, a senior justice department official, said the case was primarily foreign, hard to prove and inconsistent with the agency’s current priorities.
In the filing, McCotter also denied as false what he called media stories suggesting he sought to dismiss the case in part because of a promise by Adani to invest money in the United States.
In response, Garaufis asked Adani whether he was “aware of any agreement exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment”.
In a sworn declaration filed in court on 15 July, Adani said he was not aware of any such agreement. He acknowledged having previously promised to invest $10bn in the US and said his lawyers told the justice department in meetings that the pledge “might be part of a resolution of these matters”. Robert Giuffra, a lawyer for Adani, said in a 15 July court filing that the justice department had told him that it would not consider the Adani Group’s willingness to invest in the US as part of any resolution.

Boks drop Feinberg-Mngomezulu to bench for All Blacks rematch
- Published
Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu has paid the price for an indifferent showing in South Africa's defeat by New Zealand, with the fly-half dropping to the bench for Saturday's rematch in Cape Town.
The All Blacks, revitalised under new coach Dave Rennie, ran out 33-16 winners in the series opener in Johannesburg.
Feinberg-Mngomezulu was turned over five times in possession and occasionally exposed in defence, before he shifted to full-back for the Springboks in the second half of Saturday's first Test.
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has recalled 32-year-old double Rugby World Cup winner Handre Pollard at 10, while injuries to Cheslin Kolbe and Grant Williams have brought Ethan Hooker and Cobus Reinach into the starting line-up at wing and scrum-half respectively.
Siya Kolisi may return to the back row after recovering from a hamstring injury, but Erasmus has also named Paul de Villiers as a back-up at blindside flanker in case Kolisi is not ready.
Thirty-nine year-old Deon Fourie, who came off the bench to play 77 minutes of the Springboks' 2023 Rugby World Cup final win over New Zealand, could win his first cap since that occasion after being named among the replacements.
"There were a handful of positives and negatives last week, but the main thing that let us down was that we created so many chances, but mistakes at crucial times cost us," said Erasmus.
"We'll put in a lot of work this week to ensure that we are sharp in that regard this weekend because if we had used even some of those chances, the result could have been completely different."
South Africa side to face New Zealand: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Pollard, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi/De Villiers, PS du Toit, Wiese.
Replacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, Feinberg-Mngomezulu.
'I'm ready' - Mo'unga fired up for All Blacks return
New Zealand may be tempted to give Richie Mo'unga an immediate Test return as they chase a 2-0 lead in the four-match series that has been marketed as 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry'.
The 32-year-old was first-choice stand-off during their 2023 Rugby World Cup campaign, but he has been ineligible for selection while playing his club rugby in Japan since.
However, his signing for Canterbury and the Crusaders, along with an injury to Billy Proctor, has paved the way for his comeback.
Mo'unga will start at 10 in Tuesday's match against Johannesburg-based provincial side the Lions.
Mo'unga, who says his determination to return to Tests was fuelled by watching a Six Nations match while in a Japanese karaoke bar last year, is confident he can produce the form that earned him a spot in World Rugby's team of 2023.

The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.
Top-notch contrast. Outstanding color performance. Crisp motion clarity. Absolutely loaded with extra features.
TIRED
Mirror-like display finish isn’t for everyone. Stand takes up a lot of space on the desk. Expensive at full price.
RGB Stripe OLED panels are the new hotness in 2026. The new OLED panel technology is designed to improve text clarity and color performance, which potentially give a monitor like the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM a broader appeal beyond just a typical gaming monitor.
That is, perhaps, why Asus takes the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach. At a glance, it might seem like a typical 4K OLED gaming monitor. It has a 26.5-inch tandem 4K RGB Stripe OLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and HDR support with VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certification. But it's also rounded out with tons of features, which helps make the higher price of $1,200 easier to swallow.
Super Glossy, Superior Contrast
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM has the company’s unique TrueBlack display finish, which is designed to deliver an ultrahigh-contrast experience in a wide variety of lighting conditions. It does so with a high-gloss coat that minimizes the impact of ambient light across the display.
It’s not just marketing drivel. The TrueBlack finish provides noticeably deeper black levels in a bright room. The matte OLED finish on Samsung’s OLEDs looks positively hazy by comparison. Glossy OLED monitors from competing brands also look less contrast-rich, though the difference is most noticeable in a very bright room—brighter, I suspect, than most PC gaming dens.
I also feel it comes across in how colors present. Technically, the monitor’s results are modest for an OLED monitor: It has a color gamut that spanned 94 percent of DCI-P3 and 89 percent of AdobeRGB. That’s a tad more narrow than top QD-OLED monitors, which can hit up to 98 percent and 95 percent, respectively. However, the ultra-clear, high-contrast look of the panel amplifies the sense of impact. I’m not saying it’s better than the best competitors, but the PG27UCWM’s overall image quality is in the upper tier. That's at least partially due to the fact that RGB Stripe OLED also improves “color volume," which is a display's ability to maintain color that gamut had max brightness.
Unfortunately, the vivid and contrast-rich image is paired with mirror-like reflections. I could likely use the monitor to shave. It’s not a problem in a dark room, but it’s noticeable when even modest ambient light is present.
This is an important, and divisive, point. Many OLED purists adore an ultra-gloss finish because it highlights the rich contrast and color the technology can provide. Others, myself included, prefer matte displays that reduce or eliminate discernible reflections.
There’s no right answer to this question, but you’ll need to decide your preference before you make a purchase.
Great for Sharpness, Great HDR
Beneath the PG27UCWM’s glossy coat you’ll find a tandem RGB Stripe OLED panel with a native resolution of 3840 x 2160. It’s crisp. Earlier OLED monitors have used an unusual sub-pixel arrangement that could hurt image clarity, but the PG27UCWM has a more conventional RGB sub-pixel layout that eliminates the issue. You'll sometimes see this marketed as “5th-Gen QD-OLED," and it initially launched in 34-inch monitors like the Alienware AW3426DW. But finally, the PG27UCWM is bringing it to the more standard 27-inch size.
Text clarity, in particular, has always been one of the chief issues about those shopping for OLED monitors, and I no longer have complaints in that regard. The resolution helps, too, providing a pixel density of about 165 pixels per inch across the 26.5-inch panel. The panel’s sharpness was excellent with the monitor connected to both my Windows 11 desktop and my MacBook Air M4.
HDR is where the PG27UCWM’s tandem OLED panel really begins to earn its keep. My testing found it can hit up to 800 nits of brightness. While that’s not a record-setting result, it’s in line with other premium OLED monitors, which typically offer 800 to 900 nits in my testing (the best barely clear 1,000 nits). The monitor also supports Dolby Vision HDR, which is rare.
The PG27UCWM’s brightness, contrast, and resolution combine to deliver real impact in HDR games. It’s so bright that it can at times feel overwhelming. Fortunately, Asus includes HDR brightness adjustment options that let you tone down the brightness if you’d prefer.
Asus’ PG27UCWM isn’t uniquely bright in HDR though. The Alienware AW3426DW, Acer Predator X27 X1, and MSI MPG 32URXW are among the monitors I’ve tested that deliver similar HDR brightness (and some of which are significantly cheaper). Still, the PG27UCWM performs much better than least expensive OLED monitors like the entry-level Alienware AW2726DM, which can only deliver roughly 400 nits in HDR.
Motion Clarity Checks the Boxes
The PG27UCWM can reach a refresh rate of up to 240 Hz at 4K resolution. That’s standard for a high-end 4K OLED in 2026. It also provides a dual-mode feature that can reduce the resolution to 1080p in exchange for a refresh rate of up to 480 Hz. That’s less common, though many OLED monitors now offer a similar feature.
I think the 1080p/480Hz mode will prove niche, as the monitor’s motion clarity is already excellent at 4K and 240 Hz. Motion blur is minimal and small objects are easy to make out. Though perhaps most useful in games, the monitor’s motion clarity is also noticeable on a Windows 11 or macOS desktop. Scrolling text is readable and OS animations look ultrasmooth.
Still, the 480 Hz mode has uses. It’s ideal for people who like to play competitively in esports titles, yet also want to enjoy maximum image quality in single-player games. The PG27UCWM can handle both without compromise.
The PG27UCWM lists compatibility with AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA Adaptive Sync. In practice, many monitors that list support for only one of these can work with all three, as they are based on the same core technology. However, I always prefer to see official support listed, so you don’t have to guess whether adaptive sync will work with your PC or game console.
Features Galore
The PG27UCWM is more than just excellent image quality though. Asus has packed it full with a treasure trove of features to sweeten the deal.
The monitor’s design is top-notch. It includes attractive transparent plastic elements on the rear of the display and an RGB-LED logo that can be synced to other RGB-LED devices with Asus’ Aura Sync. An ergonomic stand is included and offers the usual range of adjustment for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot; VESA mounting for third-party arms and stands is possible with a provided adapter.
There’s also an 1/4-inch screw mount on the top of the stand neck. This is a common type of mount for camera and streaming equipment. You can use the mount to place a webcam or ring light above the monitor. It’s an uncommon but useful feature.
I do have one nitpick with the stand, and that’s the stand base. Asus opts for a wide base that takes up a lot of desk space. It’s not the largest I’ve seen, but I prefer the more compact stand base found with competitors like the MSI MPG 272URX and Alienware AW2725Q. On the plus side, though, the stand is remarkably solid. Most monitor stands allow a hint of wobble if I purposefully jostle my desk, but the PG27UCWM is unbothered.
Image-quality purists will be happy to see the monitor is packed with adjustments. These include multiple color space presets, color temperature and gamma modes that target precise values, and six-axis color saturation adjustment.
The monitor even has a built-in sensor that can detect ambient light and the user’s presence. This is used primarily to enable the monitor’s OLED burn-in reduction features, which can turn off the monitor automatically when you step away (if it’s not on, it won’t burn in).
Connectivity is great, too. The monitor has two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and one USB-C port with DisplayPort input for a total of four video inputs. All of the inputs can reach 4K at 240 Hz, and the DisplayPort 2.1 port offers UHBR20 data rates of up to 80Gbps, which means it can hit the 4K/240 Hz target without display stream compression.
The USB-C port offers 90 watts of power delivery for charging a connected laptop or tablet. A USB-C hub is included, as well, and provides three downstream USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 ports. The USB-A ports are accessible through the USB-C input or a USB-B input. A KVM switch is present as well. As if that wasn't all, Asus even throws in a three-year warranty for good measure.
What’s the Catch?
The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM is a great gaming monitor with a long list of features. It has a beautiful, sharp image, smooth-motion clarity, good HDR, lots of display inputs, and a USB hub. It even looks nice on a desk. The super-vivid, super-reflective TrueBlack coat won’t be to everyone’s taste, but it delivers on its promise to improve perceived contrast.
Which brings us to the only serious issue with the PG27UCWM: the price.
The monitor will set you back $1,200 at retail price. That’s a lot of clams for a 27-inch 4K OLED monitor. The PG27UCWM does a lot to justify a higher price, but I can’t broadly recommend the PG27UCWM over less expensive options like the PG27UCDM (currently $950) or MSI MPG 272URX (currently $800). Neither of those have the newer RGB Stripe OLED, of course, but that might not be enough for the average gamer to full appreciate given the hundreds of dollars of difference in price.
Still, the PG27UCWM is worth consideration if you want a flagship 27-inch 4K OLED monitor with the latest panel technology and a boatload of features when it becomes available in October. A 32-inch model will also be launched alongside it.

There was a time when sport did not need to be scheduled. It just needed a ball and a few willing accomplices.
Much of my childhood cricket was played on the rooftop of a schoolmate’s apartment building or in the narrow street in front of our house. Every ball that disappeared over the parapet meant someone had to dash down four floors to retrieve it. And even that inconvenience became a sport. We invented a contest to see who could throw the ball all the way back to the eagerly waiting players on the roof from the road below. Before long, all of us had developed what today would be called a gun throwing arm.
The game had rules that would have bewildered the MCC. One-drop, one-hand catches counted. Hit the wall directly and you were out. The street offered only one legitimate boundary that was straight down. A friend, unwilling to accept such geographical restrictions, perfected a scoop over the wicketkeeper to find the boundary behind. This was years before Tillakaratne Dilshan gave the world the Dilscoop.
As we move into adulthood, sport remains in our lives, but our relationship with it changes. We begin by playing it, then watching it and, in some cases, writing about it. Somewhere along that journey, almost without noticing, we cross the boundary from participant to voyeur.
I have been thinking about that boundary lately because my own sporting life has slowly disappeared. There were once two-hour table tennis sessions at the office that were fiercely competitive despite there being nothing at stake. There was the Saturday morning football with fellow journalists, when reputations built during the working week could be dismantled rather quickly by a misplaced pass or an embarrassing lack of stamina.
Both are now memories.
Perhaps this is simply ageing. Bodies protest, calendars fill up and weekends acquire obligations. Yet something more profound is lost when we stop playing sport. Playing reminds us that sport is difficult. It reminds us that the gap between intention and execution can be enormous. That the pass visible from the stands becomes considerably harder when someone is chasing you. That fatigue alters judgement and pressure tightens muscles.
For those of us who write about sport, perhaps this matters even more.
We demand fitness, courage, discipline and perseverance from athletes. We dissect their mistakes and occasionally question their desire. But when did we last test our own bodies against even the most modest sporting challenge?
Nobody expects a sportswriter to perform like the athletes they cover. But perhaps we should occasionally remember what it feels like to play.
Sport should not become something we merely consume.
And if we spend our lives preaching its virtues, perhaps the least we can do is, at times, practise some of them ourselves.

A man has received threats from the Taliban after his work for the Afghan police was revealed by a Ministry of Defence leak and the UK refused his application for resettlement.
Hamid* worked for the Afghan national police special unit and received certificates for his work signed by senior British figures praising his “dedication, unparalleled service and leadership”. His details were also included in an accidental 2022 leak by an MoD official that identified 18,700 Afghans who had worked with or for the British government.
Hamid said he had received a number of threats from the Taliban, including a video he shared with the Guardian in which a man cradling a rifle and sitting below a Taliban flag threatens to pursue him and cites knowledge of his previous movements.
The MoD, however, has rejected his application for resettlement under the Afghan relocations and assistance policy (Arap) scheme. His most recent rejection, received on 31 July, stated that Hamid had not provided evidence of “working alongside, in partnership with or closely supporting a UK government department”. It gave him 28 days to appeal.
Hamid said: “This is extremely painful because I have already submitted every document available to me proving my service. Furthermore, many of my former colleagues who served in exactly the same department and performed the same duties have already been relocated to the UK through the Arap scheme.
“Despite this evidence, my case continues to be refused. I believe my case raises serious questions about how some former Afghan partners of the UK continue to be treated despite years of loyal service.”
Hamid’s plea for help comes five years after the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan on 15 August 2021 after the withdrawal of US and Nato forces. The UK government launched the Arap scheme on 1 April 2021 and closed it to new applications on 1 July last year. Pre-existing applications continue to be processed.
Under Arap, high risk of death or serious injury are only taken into account if the rest of the criteria are deemed to have been met, which they have not in Hamid’s case. “Must I wait until I am captured, tortured or killed by the Taliban before my service and the danger I face are finally recognised?” he said.
“Following the Ministry of Defence data breach, my personal information was exposed, placing me at even greater risk. Since then, my life has changed completely. I cannot safely leave my home to work. I live in constant fear of being recognised or targeted.”
After the leak, the then defence secretary, John Healey, said the dataset included people who had made speculative applications under Arap and had not worked with British forces. He said being included in the leak “doesn’t give them a right to claim access to Britain”.
“It doesn’t give them a right to claim asylum. It doesn’t make them eligible for the special [Arap] scheme that Britain put in place for those who’d worked alongside or served with our forces,” he said.
Hamid said that because he was in hiding he had no reliable income and relied on his wife, who supports the family by doing small jobs from home. “This is our family’s only source of income, and even then we struggle simply to survive,” he said.
“The emotional impact has been devastating. My wife and I have become deeply exhausted, depressed and hopeless after years of fear, uncertainty, repeated refusals and financial hardship.
“I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a fair review based on the evidence I have already provided.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “Each application is considered on a case-by-case basis, assessed against the evidence provided, such as how they supported the UK mission in Afghanistan, and in line with the publicly available eligibility criteria.
“Since the Taliban takeover, the UK has resettled almost 39,000 Afghan men, women and children through Afghan resettlement schemes.”

Dolly Parton's 'Jolene' may be named after British Columbia nurse
Parton says name comes from a girl with 'red hair, green eyes and fair skin', just like Prince George fan
This story was originally published in 2016.
A Prince George woman believes she may be the inspiration for Dolly Parton's 'Jolene.'
Juline Whelan met the singer in 1972, and matches the description of the little girl Parton says inspired the title of the famous tune.
"I got the name from a little girl that had come up to the stage for an autograph in my early, early career," Parton said in an interview with Norwegian television program Lydverket in 2008.
"And I said, 'you are the prettiest thing I've ever seen.' She had this red hair, green eyes and fair skin. And I said 'what is your name?' and she said 'Jolene.'
"I said. 'I'm gonna write a song about you and if you ever hear it, you'll know it was about you.'"
Is Juline, Jolene?
Juline Whelan doesn't remember that conversation, but she does remember meeting Parton in 1972, the year before Jolene was recorded.
Whelan, then 10 years old, was on a family trip to Disneyland when her parents took her to see a country music concert featuring Parton.
"At the end of the show they said, 'anybody that wants to come up on stage for an autograph, come up and get an autograph,'" Whelan recalled.
"I loved her song Coat of Many Colors ... so I went over to Dolly Parton and got her autograph."
It wasn't until years later that Whelan realized that meeting may have inspired the country music star.
She was watching a 2015 TV movie about Parton's life, and afterwards decided to do some research.
"Her songs come from real-life events, right ... so I went and googled Jolene and thought, 'Well, I'll find out where that comes from,'" Whelan said.
What she found was the Parton interview in which she describes meeting the red-haired, green-eyed girl named Jolene.
"I was like, 'Oh wow, this sounds like me'," Whelan said. "'I was 10 and I went up to her and got an autograph and I have red hair, green eyes and white skin... I'm like 'OK,' and slowly I started to put the pieces together."
What solidifies the story for Whelan is how often her name is mistaken for "Jolene."
"Her getting my name as Jolene instead of Juline is totally normal for me, so I wouldn't have even questioned that."
"What kid wants to be 'Jolene, don't steal my man?'"
Though the name of the song was inspired by a child, the story it tells is much more adult. It's a plaintive cry from Parton, begging another woman not to steal her love away.
Parton has said that part of the story was inspired by a different redhead — a flirtatious bank teller who took an interest in her husband.
It's one of the singer's biggest hits and was named the 217th greatest song of all time by Rolling Stone magazine.
Not that Whelan appreciated it when it was first released.
"It drove me crazy," she remembered. Other kids at school and, later in life, her co-workers, would often sing the song at her.
"She's a hussy, man... what little kid wants to be 'Jolene, don't steal my man'?"
Today though, Whelan's made peace with sharing a name with one of pop culture's most famous home wreckers.
"It's an amazing song. I love the song," she laughed. "Over the years, it's annoyed me ... but I really love the song now."
Whelan is hoping she'll get a second chance to meet Parton when she performs in Vancouver on September 19, though she's not sure what she would say.
"I would probably be speechless."

The Transcendence of Dolly Parton
The late singer was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Dolly Parton transcended.
It almost didn’t matter what: class, gender, region, musical genre, partisanship. She transcended boundaries in all of them. During an era when politicians act like pop stars, pop stars are expected to engage in politics, and politics divide fiercely, Parton was perhaps the only person in the United States who commanded nearly universal affection. Her death today, at 80, leaves an absence that no contemporary cultural figure could dream of filling.
Parton’s origin story was, in the most literal sense, a rags-to-riches tale. She was born in a one-room cabin in the Appalachian Mountains of East Tennessee, one of 12 children of an illiterate sharecropper father. She memorialized her impoverished childhood in “Coat of Many Colors,” which tells of how her mother sewed a jacket from rags. When she wears it to school, “with patches on my britches / and holes in both my shoes,” her classmates mock and laugh at her. Rather than a hard-luck story, this is a triumph. Parton gets the last laugh: “But they didn’t understand it and I tried to make them see / That one is only poor only if they choose to be.” The song showcases one of the keys to Parton’s success: the ability to bare her soul while keeping a sense of humor and a smile.
Her rise to fame began when she was hired by the rhinestone-adorned country singer Porter Wagoner as a “girl singer” in his act. Parton quickly demonstrated that she had more than an attractive face and voice, writing a string of successful songs, such as “Jolene” and “My Tennessee Mountain Home.” One indication of her songwriting talent was that her most famous song was a bigger hit for another singer. Parton had initially hoped that Elvis Presley would record “I Will Always Love You,” but she refused his manager’s demand to give Presley songwriting credit, and she cut the song herself. It topped the country charts twice, but after Whitney Houston rerecorded the song for The Bodyguard’s soundtrack in 1992, it was a No. 1 pop hit for weeks.
Today, little separation exists between country music and the mainstream, but the genre garnered much less respect when Parton’s career began. She helped tear down old prejudices in an era when many music listeners might have professed to like “anything other than country.” Her success helped pave a path for later crossover stars such as Shania Twain and Taylor Swift. She pursued her own genre experimentation, too, collaborating with a range of artists. When she was nominated for the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, she protested that she wasn’t a rock musician and tried to withdraw from consideration. When the hall refused, she announced with appealing humility that she would earn the honor by making a rock album—her 49th and final—with guests including Joan Jett, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney.
Parton always maintained her connection to rural southern music. Few country stars could claim a more authentic origin. She kept her down-home accent and platinum-bouffant hairstyle, and she spoke openly about her abiding Christian faith. These traits may have allowed her to take stands that might otherwise have been controversial. (She also avoided electoral politics, and declined Presidential Medals of Freedom from both Donald Trump and Joe Biden.)
Like her predecessor Loretta Lynn, she cultivated a no-nonsense strain of feminism in her lyrics. In 1980, she starred alongside the outspoken liberals Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the movie 9 to 5, a workplace comedy in which three women conspire to get even with their sexist-pig boss. Parton agreed to take the role if she could write the theme song, and the track has proved even more enduring than the film. “It’s a rich man’s game no matter what they call it / And you spend your life puttin’ money in his wallet,” she sang. Was this working-class grievance or progressive economics? Radical feminism or mass-market entertainment? Why not both?
Parton was beloved by the gay community, and she reciprocated that affection. She also quietly fostered change using her fortune. In 1986, she opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and the theme park became the largest job provider in the area. In 1995, she launched Dolly’s Imagination Library. Starting first in her native Sevier County, and then expanding around the United States as well as in a few other countries, the program mails a book each month to children from birth to age 5, to encourage literacy and a love of reading. In 2020, she donated $1 million to help fund the development of a COVID-19 vaccine, then proudly received the shot.
In her middle age, during a perhaps less enlightened time in American society, Parton was often a punch line. Her voluptuous chest and many plastic surgeries were frequent fodder for jokes, and Parton perfected the trick of playing along with the gags while also subverting them. One of her earliest singles is titled “Dumb Blonde,” but it warns, “This dumb blonde ain’t nobody’s fool.” In a 2002 New York Times interview, she said, “Hopefully people can see beneath the hair to know there’s a brain, beneath the boobs to know there’s a heart, and behind all the other stuff to know there’s some talent.”
If that wasn’t always the case, Parton got her wish in the end. Admiration for her became an unshakable conviction across cultural lines. One sign of Parton’s status is that even Trump is on his best behavior, treating her death with a reverence he usually reserves only for his biggest public admirers, of whom she was not one. The president ordered flags flown at half-staff for a week to mark her death. It is a fitting farewell for an artist who united Americans in a way that few people ever have or will.

A video of Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi is going viral on social media (here, here, and here), allegedly showing him making controversial remarks about women and rape. In the video, he is purportedly heard saying, “Eighty per cent of rapes are caused by women. Rape happens in India, and rape does not happen in Bharat. The girl has a place; she should be in a cage; there should be control over her. She shouldn’t be working, and boys should be given full freedom.” Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Rahul Gandhi making controversial remarks about rape and women.
Fact: The video has been edited. In the original video, Rahul Gandhi was not making these statements himself; he was quoting past controversial remarks made by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and former Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar while criticising their views. The viral clip deliberately removes his attribution, making it appear as though he was expressing these views himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to the original video uploaded on the official YouTube channel of the Congress party on 22 August 2026. The video is from the Congress’s “Chhatraon Ki Goonj” event held in Pune on the same day. The viral clip appears at the 1:00:12 timestamp. In the original video, Rahul Gandhi refers to statements previously made by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat and former Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar. Gandhi attributes to Bhagwat the statement that rape happens in “India” and not in “Bharat”, while attributing to Khattar the remark that 80% of rapes are caused by women. Gandhi then describes these remarks as reflecting a mindset that he says they are fighting.
This makes it clear that the viral video has been edited to remove the portion in which Gandhi identifies Bhagwat and Khattar as the sources of these remarks, making it appear as though he himself made the statements.
We also conducted a Google keyword search and found (here, here) that, during RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat’s visit to Silchar on 4 January 2013, he made a controversial remark about rape incidents, saying that such crimes occur more in “India” and less in “Bharat”. The statement sparked controversy at the time. Then-RSS spokesperson Ram Madhav clarified that Bhagwat was referring to Indian traditions of respecting women and saying that people who moved away from these values could become involved in criminal cases.
Similarly, in November 2018, then Haryana Chief Minister Manohar Lal Khattar made a controversial remark (here, here) about rape and molestation cases. He said that 80–90 per cent of such incidents involved people who knew each other and suggested that some cases arose after people had been in relationships for a long time.
To sum up, this viral video of Rahul Gandhi making controversial remarks about rape and women is edited.

A landslide struck the China-Nepal border in Tibet's Gyirong county on Wednesday, leading to "major casualties" and leaving several people missing at the Gyirong Port, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
The landslide occurred at around 10.30am (local time) and began on the Nepalese side before hitting the key border crossing in China.
Devastating footage showed people scrambling to safety as a massive wall of mud, water and debris swept through the Gyirong Port. CCTV footage showed roads and buildings being inundated within seconds, with floodwaters and debris tearing through parts of the border crossing.
Authorities closed roads leading to the checkpoint for seven days as rescue operations continued.
The destruction cut roads leading to the port and knocked out power and communications on the Chinese side, while authorities warned of "major casualties" and missing people. Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered an "all-out" search and rescue operation.
Across the border in Nepal, the flash floods destroyed villages, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure. Nepal's Tourism Board said 384 travellers were initially reported missing, including 291 foreign nationals; at least 105 Indians were among those unaccounted for.
The disaster remained fluid, with the death toll rising through the day and authorities warning that the full scale of the casualties and destruction was still being assessed.
China has sent about 200 rescuers, along with geologists and engineers, to the site, with additional personnel on standby. Rescue teams brought heavy machinery, reconnaissance drones, 3D laser scanners and life-detection equipment, Xinhua reported.
Gyirong Port is Tibet's main foreign trade port and handles most of China's trade with Nepal. Two-way freight and passenger clearance resumed there in 2022 after the Covid-19 pandemic, and the port has since become a major route for Chinese exports to Nepal, including electric vehicles.
The landslide also disrupted a strategically important trade corridor between China and Nepal. China allows trade and transit through six border points with Nepal, five of them in Shigatse, while the two countries have been pursuing a wider Trans-Himalayan connectivity network under China's Belt and Road Initiative.

Hollywood's summer box office is glowing, but the numbers come with startling caveats
Summer blockbusters — including the smash hits Spider Man: Brand New Day, and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey — have busted plenty of blocks this year. American cineplexes are on track to rake in more dollars than they have in a decade, a gratifying outcome after years of losing audiences to streaming.
And while the big box office numbers come with equally big caveats, it's reasonable to revel in the good news first. With Spidey entertaining superhero fans, the Michael Jackson biopic Michael capturing the pop music crowd, The Odyssey for folks who like epics, The Devil Wears Prada 2 for fashionistas, and Toy Story 5 for kids, Hollywood has managed to have something for everyone this summer.
It even found room for a couple of unexpected, low-budget thrillers from YouTube creators — Obsession and Backrooms — that together added $460 million dollars to the North American box-office pot.
All of which has theater owners cheering, and Tinseltown's trade papers buzzing about what's shaping up to be a $4.5 billion dollar summer, easily topping not just the Barbenheimer summer of 2023 but also the Lion King/Avengers: Endgame summer of 2019. (In Hollywood, "summer" means the first Friday in May through Labor Day.)
This is great news for a film industry that seemed to lose its way when the pandemic accelerated the growth of streaming services six years ago. For a few months in 2020, when theaters shut down entirely, movie studios became reluctant-but-active participants in the weaning of audiences away from the habit of attending movies in cinemas.
Disney sent its Pixar attractions, reliably successful in theaters, straight to Disney+, Warner Bros. made Dune, its most promising blockbuster, available for home viewing on HBO Max the same day it opened in more than 4,000 theaters. Other studios delayed openings or sent films straight to streaming services that would normally have gone first to theaters.
And movie patrons, once they had been trained to look for the latest movies in their living rooms, had to be strenuously wooed back to cinemas with films that were spectacle-oriented, star-studded, and in every sense bigger than what was available at home.
More money
It took a while, but in dollar terms, the industry has now recovered. Five 2026 films (Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Toy Story 5, Michael, and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie) have each earned more than $1 billion dollars worldwide, more than in any year since the start of the pandemic. And that's before the presumed Christmas bonanza that fans are already calling "DunesDay" — when rival blockbusters Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday both open on December 18 — a one-two punch that's expected to cap the best year American theaters will have had since $10-billion years were commonplace in the 2010s.
But there are some notable differences now.
Fewer screens
Cineplexes are crowded partly because the pandemic left the industry with fewer of them. According to research firm Omdia, there were 44,283 movie screens in North America at the end of 2019. By the end of last year, more than 7,000 of those screens had permanently shuttered.
Fewer moviegoers
And the industry's recovering box office numbers mask another issue — dollars are up, but attendance is down. Data and analytics company S&P Global reports that through mid-August in the year before the pandemic, cinemas sold 795.9 million tickets. This year's ticket sales for that same period, although they're up from the last couple of years, are still only 547.1 million; a drop of almost a quarter of a billion admissions.
A shortfall that enormous would have been catastrophic if prices hadn't risen. Seven years ago the trade group Cinema United tallied the average movie ticket at around $9. Today, audience fondness for pricey premium formats like IMAX has pushed the average adult ticket price above $13, according to research firm EntTelligence. (Audiences are paying $18.46 for premium format and $12.87 for standard tickets, per EntTelligence data.)
So, fewer patrons, but bigger event films like The Odyssey.
Fewer movies
And there's one other difference: In the summer of 2019, about 400 movies played in theaters; this year, barely 300 will. That means on average, each individual film is doing better, but there aren't as many choices for folks who've had a good time and want to come back, the audiences that multiplex theaters were designed to capture.
So, what Hollywood is looking at as it concludes its most successful summer in years is more dollars, but fewer theaters, fewer patrons, and fewer movies — not really, as Miranda Priestly of The Devil Wears Prada might put it, a great look for an industry in recovery.
Studios and cinemas will need to grapple with whether their current business model is sustainable. But this summer, after a long slog back to profitability, they can be forgiven for basking in a slew of box office records including — when Spider-Man: Brand New Day first joined The Odyssey and Toy Story 5 in theaters — the highest collective take for a single weekend in Hollywood history.

Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature.
Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd.
The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister.
Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released.
“The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India.
The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations.
They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance.
Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits.
Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies.
The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations.
The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said.
The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned.
The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35.
Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

When people in India are used to buying all sorts of medicines over the counter (OTC), the challenge is the enforcement of laws which make prescription mandatory, said Hyderabad-based paediatrician Sivaranjani Santosh even as she welcomed the Centre’s decision to make all syrups, including cough syrups, as prescription-only.
Why India has restricted chlorpheniramine, phenylephrine medicines for children under 4 | Explained
Many in the pharmaceutical trade as well are uncertain how effectively the new rules can be enforced among consumers accustomed to buying medicines over the counter (OTC).
On Tuesday (June 16) the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, ending the OTC sale of syrups, including cough syrups. Following the amendment, cough lozenges, pills and tablets will continue to be available over the counter, but syrups will require a prescription.
Dr. Santosh welcomed the move, saying concerns over overdoses, incorrect dosing and indiscriminate use of cough-and-cold preparations justified tighter controls. Many formulations contain ingredients such as terbutaline, levosalbutamol, salbutamol, chlorpheniramine maleate and phenylephrine, which could add to complications if used inappropriately, she said.
ALSO WATCH Watch: Why are prescriptions now mandatory for cough syrups? | Above the Fold | 16.06.2026
Doubts over implementation were echoed by pharmacists. Uday Kumar of Mor Chemists and Druggists said consumers increasingly expected immediate relief and questioned whether a blanket prescription requirement would work in the long run. “Everyone wants to recover instantly. If they fall sick today, they want to become well tomorrow,” he said.
Mr. Kumar argued that counterfeit, adulterated and unbranded medicines posed a bigger challenge. He added that identifying genuine and fake products was difficult and laboratory testing often took months.
Neelesh Kanodia, who runs Yash Agencies, distinguished between codeine-based cough syrups and regular formulations. “I don’t think the blanket rule will continue in the long run. But restrictions on codeine-containing syrups will continue,” he said. According to Mr. Kanodia, codeine-containing cough syrups were already largely dispensed against prescriptions only, whereas commonly used formulations had traditionally been available over the counter.
Meanwhile, the Telangana Chemists and Druggists Association (TCDA) moved quickly to inform retailers about the new rules. Krishna Kumar, treasurer of the association, said broadcast messages had been sent to pharmacies across the State immediately after the notification was issued. “We also circulated those messages in Telugu so that they reach even the remote corners of the State,” he said.
Mr. Kumar said Telangana had around 39,000 pharmacies, of which nearly 18,000 were located in Hyderabad.
A Hyderabad-based pharmacist who runs a prominent store in Panjagutta and requested anonymity said implementation was likely to vary across regions. “Large and reputed pharmacies in metropolitan cities and affluent areas would comply with the rules but enforcement in smaller localities and towns could prove more difficult,” he said.
He added that consumer behaviour is a major obstacle. Patients often reuse old prescriptions instead of returning to doctors, while consultation fees, travel costs and waiting times discourage repeated visits.

U.S. drugmakers Merck and Moderna said Wednesday a personalized cancer treatment had shown success in reducing the recurrence of melanoma tumors in a late-stage trial hailed by experts as a "breakthrough."
The news sent shares in Moderna soaring 145% to $154 while Merck's stock was up more than 12% to $152.
The drug, called "intismeran autogene," is based on the same messenger RNA (mRNA) technology behind Covid-19 vaccines.
Researchers have for years been trying to apply mRNA treatments against cancer, but this was the first time such a drug showed positive results in a large, late-stage clinical trial.
"Today marks an extraordinary milestone for Moderna, for mRNA science and, most importantly, for patients with cancer," Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said in a statement.
The trial lasted approximately a year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomized into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab -- the current standard-of-care drug -- while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.
The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.
Proof of principle
Lennard Lee, an oncologist and assistant professor at the University of Oxford who was not involved in the trial, called the results "very encouraging," adding: "We should now look forward to seeing the complete data."
Oncologist Marco Gerlinger, a professor at London's Barts Cancer Institute, added that beyond being good news for patients with melanoma, it was "proof of principle that personalised cancer vaccines work."
"I think it is fair to call it a breakthrough in the development of new cancer immunotherapies," he added, while also noting the press release was short on details.
The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient's tumor and identifying its unique mutational signature, or "fingerprint," then using mRNA technology to fight it.
Messenger RNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions encased in tiny fat bubbles that temporarily enter cells, causing them to produce targets that train the body's immune system.
The technology was first conceived decades ago but came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.
Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.
"Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumor types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers," said Bancel.

Bengaluru residents appear to have taken advantage of the Greater Bengaluru Authority’s (GBA) abandoned vehicle clearance drive with some ulterior motives.
Of the 6,000 vehicles flagged on the ASTraM app for clearance, nearly 50% were found to be false complaints, many of which were allegedly filed amid feuds between neighbours over parking spaces on the road.
Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda had announced the abandoned vehicle clearance drive as part of a citywide footpath clearance exercise being jointly undertaken with the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP). To encourage citizen participation, the BTP created a window on its ASTraM app through which residents could upload details and photographs of vehicles that had been abandoned for a long period, along with their location.
The response was overwhelming, with more than 6,000 vehicles flagged within two weeks of the announcement. However, when the BTP and Bengaluru corporations began verifying the complaints, they found that only around 3,000 were genuine, while the rest had been wrongly flagged.
In a city where many households own multiple vehicles amid a shortage of parking space, vehicles are often parked on roads for extended periods. Disputes over such parking spaces are also common. In several cases, residents angry with their neighbours over parking have uploaded photographs of vehicles that had remained parked in the same spot for a few days, alleging that they had been abandoned, according to BTP sources.
A senior traffic police officer said many families use two-wheelers to commute to work while leaving their cars parked outside their homes . “Such cars have also been flagged as abandoned,” he said.
“In some cases, people have flagged vehicles belonging to neighbours who had travelled to their hometowns after parking their vehicles on the streets,” the officer said. There have also been instances of garage owners parking customers’ vehicles on roads, which were subsequently flagged as abandoned by residents annoyed by the parking.
While no action has been taken against those who made such complaints, the police have urged citizens to flag only genuine cases, pointing out that verifying false complaints places an additional burden on personnel.
“It is a waste of time and manpower to verify such cases, which could otherwise be used to provide citizen services. Citizens should therefore refrain from making such complaints,” the officer said.
According to corporation sources, more than 1,000 vehicles have been cleared so far under the drive. These include vehicles whose owners contacted the corporation after notice stickers were pasted on them and subsequently removed the vehicles themselves after paying the prescribed fines.

Far-right Israeli lawmaker damages Palestinian memorial with sledgehammer
- Published
A far-right member of the Israeli parliament has badly damaged a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer in the occupied West Bank while under military escort.
The incident has drawn strong criticism from Palestinians and across the political spectrum in Israel.
Video footage showed Zvi Sukkot, a member of the far-right Religious Zionism party, and several others striking the stone memorial in the Palestinian village of Madama.
In the video, Sukkot - who has a history of provocative anti-Palestinian acts - says: "This is something we cannot leave standing here, because any place that glorifies terrorism, we must remove it."
Rami Nasar, the head of the village council in Madama, said that the monument was erected in 2008 to remember Palestinians killed in the battle of Karameh - a day-long military confrontation between Israeli forces and those of both the PLO and Jordan in 1968.
It also memorialises Palestinians killed in the first and second intifada.
Nasar said it was intended to honour those who had been killed in conflict with Israel, whatever their political affiliation.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said its soldiers had been present during the incident. The Israeli military said it had approved a tour of monuments in the area for Sukkot and was providing security.
But the IDF said he and the others involved had acted deceptively and without authorisation.
It said soldiers eventually stopped Sukkot and escorted his group out of Madama after reporting the incident to their commanders.
In a number of previous incidents involving settler violence, soldiers have been filmed standing by without intervening.
The incident has further raised the temperature in the West Bank, where increasing attacks by settlers on Palestinians in recent months have drawn international condemnation.
Madama itself has been the target of several attacks by settlers.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has issued a statement criticising Sukkot's actions. It read: "Taking the law into one's own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combating terrorism and incitement to violence."
Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming general election, Gadi Eisenkot, said that Sukkot's behaviour was "a disgrace for anyone who claims to represent the public and be a leader".
